papers.title: Stemma: Induced Decision Regions Reveal LLM Provenance
papers.abstract: LLM provenance testing asks whether a suspect LLM belongs to the same lineage as a source. Existing black-box methods largely infer this relationship from response-level characteristics, but these characteristics may shift under adaptation or deployment even when the underlying meaning remains unchanged, weakening the reliability of provenance evidence. To address this limitation, we introduce induced decision regions by mapping open-ended outputs into a finite decision space, thereby abstracting away surface-form variation and reframing provenance testing as measuring the inheritance of decision regions. Empirical analysis shows that the source's induced regions are preserved more strongly in related models than in unrelated models. Building on this signal, we propose Stemma, a practical black-box LLM fingerprinting method that operationalises stability, robustness, and specificity as complementary probe-selection principles for reliably estimating induced decision region inheritance. Across 770 source-suspect pairs drawn from 56 public checkpoints and spanning diverse model-weight transformations, Stemma achieves 0.967 AUC and 87.8% TPR at 1% FPR, substantially outperforming four representative baselines. It further achieves 0.995 AUC and 93.5% TPR at 1% FPR on 1,260 pairs covering 91 deployment instances, demonstrating robustness to diverse inference-time deployment settings.

summary.takeaway: 引入 induced decision regions，使黑盒 LLM 溯源更稳健。
summary.problem: 现有指纹方法依赖表面输出相似性，易受适配和部署影响。
summary.method: Stemma 依据稳定性、鲁棒性、特异性挑选 probes，测量决策区继承。
summary.evidence: 在 770 对（56 检查点）上达 0.967 AUC，1% FPR 时 TPR 87.8%，在 1,260 对部署实例上达 0.995 AUC，TPR 93.5%，显著超越四个基线。
summary.limitations: 效果依赖精心挑选的 probes，随机 probes 只能提供有限区分力。
summary.why_for_you: 对可信 LLM 研究者，Stemma 提供了在模型适配和部署后仍可验证来源的实用指纹方法。

signals.text: 引入 induced decision regions，将开放式输出映射到有限决策空间，实现更稳健的来源判别。
Stemma 通过稳定性、鲁棒性、特异性三原则挑选 40 条 probes，测量决策区继承度。
在 770 对（56 检查点）上达 0.967 AUC，1% FPR 时 TPR 87.8%，但随机 probes 仅提供有限区分力。

deep_dive.overview: 本文针对 LLM 溯源面临的表面输出易变问题，提出将生成答案映射到有限决策空间的 induced decision regions 概念，并基于此构建 Stemma 指纹系统。Stemma 通过三大探针选择原则（稳定性、鲁棒性、特异性）从 3,000 条 MMLU 题目中挑选 40 条高信息 probes，随后在源模型和嫌疑模型上测量这些 probes 的决策区继承程度。实验在 56 个公开检查点的 770 对源‑嫌疑模型以及 91 种部署实例的 1,260 对上进行，指标包括 AUC、pAUC、1% FPR 下的 TPR 与 d′，结果显著优于 LLMmap、LLMPrint、MPT 与 ZeroPrint 四个基线，并在不同模型族、适配方式和部署设置下保持鲁棒。消融分析表明，探针的稳定性与特异性是提升低 FPR 性能的关键，而探针数量与候选池规模对整体表现影响有限。

methodology.title: Probe selection pipeline
methodology.detail: 从 3,000 条随机抽取的 MMLU 问题构建候选池，首先剔除与黄金答案相同的题目以提升特异性，然后过滤掉在等价输入变体下不稳定或对边界敏感的 probes，最后依据继承度得分排序，选取前 40 条作为指纹探针。

methodology.title: Decision region mapping
methodology.detail: 对每个 probe，使用源模型生成多次输出并通过预定义的映射函数将文本答案映射到有限的决策标签集合，从而抽象掉表面形式差异，形成源模型的 induced decision region。

mechanism.title: Induced decision regions
mechanism.detail: 将开放式生成答案映射到离散决策空间，使得相同语义的不同表述落入同一决策区，继承度即嫌疑模型在相同 probe 上落入相同决策区的比例。

mechanism.title: Region inheritance measurement
mechanism.detail: 计算嫌疑模型对每个 probe 的决策标签与源模型的匹配率，聚合得到整体继承分数，用作溯源判别的连续评分。

experiments.title: Benchmark setup
experiments.detail: 770 source‑suspect 对，来源于 56 个公开检查点，涵盖微调、合并、压缩、蒸馏等权重变换；另有 1,260 对覆盖 91 种部署实例。基线包括 LLMmap、LLMPrint、MPT、ZeroPrint。评估指标为 AUC、pAUC（FPR∈[0,0.05]）、1% FPR 下的 TPR 与 d′。

experiments.title: Ablation studies
experiments.detail: 分别评估随机 probes、仅使用非黄金池、不同候选池规模（1k‑6k）以及 probe 预算（10‑80），结果显示稳定性与特异性过滤对低 FPR 表现贡献最大，性能在 40 条 probes 后趋于饱和。

findings.title: Superior provenance discrimination
findings.detail: Stemma 在整体数据上取得 0.967 AUC（预训练源）和 0.995 AUC（部署实例），1% FPR 下 TPR 分别为 87.8% 与 93.5%，显著高于所有基线。

findings.title: Robustness to deployment variations
findings.detail: 在聊天模板与原始完成提示的接口不匹配情况下，基线性能接近随机，而 Stemma 仍保持高区分度，说明决策区继承信号对提示变化不敏感。

findings.title: Probe budget efficiency
findings.detail: 性能在 probe 数量达到约 40 条后基本稳定，进一步增加预算对 AUC 与 pAUC 的提升有限，表明方法在查询成本上具备可控性。

contributions: 提出 induced decision regions 概念，重新定义 LLM 黑盒溯源。
设计 Stemma 指纹系统，基于稳定性、鲁棒性、特异性三原则进行 probe 选择。
提供大规模实验验证，展示在多模型族、适配方式和部署设置下的鲁棒性。
limitations: 效果依赖于精心挑选的 probes，随机 probes 只能提供有限区分力。
评估局限于公开检查点和已测试的部署实例，未覆盖所有可能的模型压缩或对抗扰动情形。
open_questions: 在更极端的模型压缩、量化或对抗攻击下，决策区指纹能否保持可靠？
能否将 induced decision regions 扩展到多模态或视觉语言模型的溯源任务？

papers.title: Empirical Evaluation of Out-Of-Distribution Performance of Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) have emerged as novel approaches for tabular predictive tasks, demonstrating competitive predictive performance to ensemble tree-based models. Most TFMs are trained and evaluated on independent and identically distributed data, but this assumption changes in real-world scenarios due to distribution shifts, which compromise the robustness of models. Limited research has been conducted of TFMs under distribution shifts. We present an empirical evaluation of Out-Of-Distribution (OOD) performance of nine TFMs, spanning diverse pre-training strategies and architectures: TabPFNv2, TabPFNv2.5, TabPFNv2.6, TabPFNv3, TabICL, TabICLv2, Mitra, LimiX and TabFM. Three real-world datasets from the TableShift study were considered (HELOC, Voting, Childhood Lead), covering label, socioeconomic, and geographic shift types. Our results show that all evaluated TFMs degrade systematically under distribution shift regardless of pre-training strategy, with shift gaps ranging from 0.003 to 0.060 depending on shift type. The relationship between in-distribution and OOD predictive performance documented for classical tabular models extends into TFMs. We also identified a scalability gap, as high-performing models demand significant memory and computational resources beyond what standard deployment infrastructure can support. This study extends existing benchmarks for OOD in tabular data, providing evidence to support their adoption in high-stakes domains characterized by structural distribution shifts.

summary.limitations: 研究未对 TFMs 在目标任务上进行微调，且因计算资源限制排除了一些结果，导致对适应能力和可扩展性的洞察受限。
summary.evidence: 所有 TFMs 在分布漂移下表现出一致的性能下降，shift gap 在 0.003 至 0.060 ROC-AUC 之间，且无模型实现 OOD 与 ID 性能持平。
summary.why_for_you: 了解 TFMs 的 OOD 鲁棒性和可扩展性限制，对在高风险真实环境中部署可信的表格模型至关重要，尤其面对结构性分布漂移。
summary.problem: 尽管 TFMs 在表格预测任务中应用日增，但其对 OOD 场景的鲁棒性仍未得到充分研究。
summary.takeaway: Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) 在不同数据集和预训练策略下，面对分布漂移时预测性能系统性下降。
summary.method: 对九种采用不同预训练策略的 TFMs 在三个人真实数据集（包含标签、社会经济和地理分布漂移）进行实证评估。

signals.text: 在真实数据上预训练的 TFMs（如 TabPFN 变体）获得更高的 ID 与 OOD ROC-AUC 分数，但其 shift gap 与合成先验模型相似，表明其更擅长 ID 拟合而非固有的 OOD 鲁棒性。
评估使用默认推理配置且未进行任务特定微调，采用 ROC-AUC 作为指标，在三个 TableShift 数据集（HELOC、Childhood Lead、Voting）上衡量 OOD 性能下降。
性能下降随漂移类型而异：社会经济漂移（Childhood Lead）导致最大下降，标签漂移（HELOC）中等，地理漂移（Voting）最小，进一步确认 TFMs 对分布漂移的系统性脆弱性。

deep_dive.overview: 本研究评估了九种 Tabular Foundation Models (TFMs) 在三个人真实数据集（分别呈现标签、社会经济和地理分布漂移）上的 OOD 表现。核心问题是已展示竞争性 ID 性能的 TFMs 能否在真实分布变化下保持鲁棒性。作者使用 TableShift 基准数据集，覆盖真实、合成及混合预训练策略的模型，在未微调的情况下测量 ID 与 OOD 测试集的 ROC-AUC，并以差值定义 shift gap。结果显示所有 TFMs 在 OOD 条件下均出现系统性性能下降，且无模型实现 ID 与 OOD 性能持平。值得注意的是，真实数据预训练的模型在绝对分数上领先，但并未缩小相对 shift gap，表明预训练语料更有利于 ID 拟合而非 OOD 泛化。研究还指出高性能 TFMs 在资源受限环境下的可扩展性挑战，限制其部署。上述发现扩展了现有表格基准，为在结构性分布漂移的高风险应用中部署 TFMs 提供关键洞见。

methodology.title: 数据集选择与偏移类型
methodology.detail: 从 TableShift 中选择了三个数据集，以代表多样的分布偏移：HELOC（标签偏移）、Childhood Lead（社会经济偏移）和 Voting（地理偏移）。每个数据集包括由领域特定变量定义的训练、分布内测试和 OOD 测试划分。

methodology.title: 模型选择与预训练策略
methodology.detail: 评估了九种 TFM，包括 TabPFN 变体（v2、v2.5、v2.6、v3）、TabICL 变体、Mitra、LimiX 和 TabFM，涵盖真实数据预训练、结构因果模型的合成先验以及混合方法。

methodology.title: 评估协议
methodology.detail: 模型在默认推理模式下使用，未进行微调。对 ID 和 OOD 测试划分计算 ROC-AUC，shift gap 定义为两者分数的差值。实验在五个随机种子上重复，以报告均值和标准差。

methodology.title: 性能指标与报告
methodology.detail: 由于数据集存在类别不平衡，选择了 ROC-AUC。由于资源限制，省略了在大规模 Voting 数据集上计算成本高的模型（TabFM、LimiX）的结果。

mechanism.title: 未提供明确机制
mechanism.detail: 论文未提出解释分布偏移下性能下降的正式机制或理论模型；而是提供了跨 TFM 系统性性能下降的实证证据。

experiments.title: TableShift 数据集上的 OOD 性能评估
experiments.detail: 在 HELOC、Childhood Lead 和 Voting 数据集上评估了九个 TFM，数据集呈现不同的分布漂移。使用 ROC-AUC 在 ID 和 OOD 划分上评估模型，结果取五个随机种子平均。

experiments.title: 不同预训练策略的比较
experiments.detail: 比较了在真实数据、合成先验和混合先验上预训练的模型，以评估预训练语料对 OOD 鲁棒性的影响。

experiments.title: 资源与可扩展性评估
experiments.detail: 研究指出高性能 TFM（尤其是 TabFM 和 LimiX）的计算和内存需求，限制了在更大数据集上的评估，凸显了可扩展性差距。

findings.title: 系统性的 OOD 性能下降
findings.detail: 所有九个 TFM 在 OOD 测试划分上的 ROC-AUC 均低于 ID 划分，漂移差距在 0.003 至 0.060 之间，证实了对分布漂移的脆弱性。

findings.title: 预训练语料影响 ID 而不影响 OOD 鲁棒性
findings.detail: 真实数据预训练的 TFM 取得更高的绝对性能，但相较于合成先验模型并未降低相对漂移差距，表明其固有 OOD 泛化能力有限。

findings.title: 漂移类型影响性能下降幅度
findings.detail: 社会经济漂移（Childhood Lead）导致最大性能下降，标签漂移（HELOC）适中，地理漂移（Voting）最小，展示了对漂移类型的依赖性鲁棒性。

findings.title: 可扩展性限制实际部署
findings.detail: 高性能 TFM 需要大量计算资源，超出标准部署基础设施能力，限制了其在资源受限环境中的适用性。

contributions: 首次对九种不同TFM进行OOD性能的全面实证评估。
展示了尽管采用多样的pre-training策略，TFM仍缺乏对distribution shifts的内在鲁棒性。
扩展了针对表格数据的OOD基准，使用覆盖多种shift类型的真实数据集。
识别出限制高性能TFM在实际环境中部署的scalability差距。
limitations: 评估使用默认推理且未进行fine-tuning，可能低估了适应能力。
计算资源限制导致部分模型在大数据集上的结果未报告，限制了完整性。
未提供对观察到的OOD退化的理论或机制解释。
研究聚焦于分类任务，未评估回归或其他表格任务。
open_questions: fine-tuning或适应策略能否提升TFM在默认推理之外的OOD鲁棒性？
哪些架构或训练修改能增强TFM的内在OOD泛化能力？
TFM在其他类型的distribution shifts或回归任务中的表现如何？
哪些方法能解决scalability挑战，以实现TFM在资源受限环境中的部署？

papers.title: DataOrchestra: Learning to Orchestrate Per-Example Curation of Pretraining Data
papers.abstract: Pretraining data processing is critical to the downstream performance of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, many existing approaches define a fixed processing strategy at the corpus or domain level and apply it uniformly to many examples, without adapting to the needs of each example. We propose DataOrchestra, a framework that unifies different processing operations and orchestrates an example-specific pipeline for each example. Given a chunk of pretraining data, an orchestrator decides whether to drop, untouch, or clean it. For a chunk to be cleaned, it selects one or more downstream operations, ranging from programmatic editing to different forms of LLM-based rewriting. For each rewriting step, it further generates a concrete instruction, which is executed by the corresponding downstream tool model. We pretrain models from 0.5B to 7B from scratch on web data processed by DataOrchestra and observe stable average gains over individual data-processing methods across 11 benchmarks. DataOrchestra is also effective for math continued pretraining and outperforms stronger processing baselines, while reducing processing compute by skipping unnecessary downstream operations.

summary.method: 编排器预测 drop/untouch/clean 决策，并为噪声剪枝、表面校正和教学增强工具生成块级指令。
summary.evidence: 在 DataOrchestra 处理的数据上预训练的 0.5B‑7B 模型将平均准确率提升至 40.13（对比最强基线的 38.88），覆盖 11 项基准，并跳过不必要的操作。
summary.why_for_you: 通过提供学习的、逐例的策展机制，直接解决 LLM 的数据选择问题。
summary.takeaway: DataOrchestra 学会为每个示例选择预处理流水线，带来一致的下游提升。
summary.problem: 现有数据处理流水线对所有预训练示例使用单一固定策略，忽视示例的特定需求。
summary.limitations: 在可得来源中未说明。

contributions: 逐例编排多种数据处理操作
统一框架，将 NP、SR、PA 与学习决策相结合
实证展示不同模型规模和语料库下的准确率提升与计算节省

signals.text: DataOrchestra 引入逐例编排框架，统一噪声剪枝、表面校正和教学增强。
编排器预测 drop/untouch/clean 决策，并为下游工具模型生成块级改写指令。
DataOrchestra 训练的 7B 模型实现 40.13 平均准确率（对比 38.88 基线），但计算节省依赖不可验证的 verifier LLM 检查。

mechanism.title: 自适应流水线选择
mechanism.detail: 编排器将每个块路由至最少必要的操作集合，允许部分块被丢弃或保持不变，从而节省计算。

mechanism.title: 指令生成
mechanism.detail: 在每个改写阶段，编排器生成具体的自然语言指令，引导下游工具模型（如基于 LLM 的改写）。

deep_dive.overview: DataOrchestra 提出统一框架，为每个示例定制预训练数据处理。编排器先决定 drop、untouch 或 clean，然后在噪声剪枝 (NP)、表面校正 (SR) 与教学增强 (PA) 中选择，并为工具模型生成具体指令。细粒度计划演化利用 verifier LLM 剔除无效阶段。实验在网页语料上预训练 0.5B‑7B 模型，跨 11 项基准实现稳定的平均准确率提升，并通过跳过不必要的改写降低计算。消融实验验证计划演化和指令生成的重要性。

methodology.title: 编排器训练
methodology.detail: 在 160K 由 DataMan 打分的文档块上训练模型，学习输出粗粒度计划（drop、untouch、NP/SR/PA 标记）。

methodology.title: 粗粒度计划生成
methodology.detail: 教师 LLM 为每块打分 (0‑5) 并给出 NP、SR、PA 的二元判断；得分低于 2 的决定触发丢弃。

methodology.title: 细粒度计划演化
methodology.detail: 执行选定阶段后，verifier LLM 检查幻觉、事实损失或微小变化（Levenshtein > 98%），并剔除无效阶段。

experiments.title: 预训练与基准评估
experiments.detail: 在 DataOrchestra 处理的网页数据上，从头预训练 0.5B、1.5B、7B 参数模型；下游性能在 11 项基准（ARC‑E、ARC‑C、MMLU、HellaSwag、WinoGrande、PIQA、CommonsenseQA、SIQA、RACE、OpenBookQA、SciQ）上测量，采用最近三个 checkpoint 的平均准确率。

experiments.title: 基线与对比
experiments.detail: 基线包括 raw data、ProX（行级噪声去除）、RePro、ReWire 及其混合；DataOrchestra 始终优于它们，7B 模型实现 40.13 平均准确率，对比 ProX 的 38.88。

experiments.title: 计算节省分析
experiments.detail: 约 35% 的块被丢弃或保持不变；NP 删除最多 token，SR 稍减 token，PA 增加 token，符合其设计目标。

open_questions: 该方法在更大模型（>100B）和更广域数据上如何扩展？
指令质量对改写效果的影响如何，能否进一步优化？
能否用更廉价的启发式方法替代 verifier LLM 而不损失质量？

findings.title: 性能提升
findings.detail: DataOrchestra 在不同模型规模上实现稳定的平均准确率提升，规模更大的模型相对基线的提升幅度更大。

findings.title: 计算高效利用
findings.detail: 跳过不必要的清洗阶段降低有效 EFLOPs，同时保持或提升下游质量。

findings.title: 消融洞察
findings.detail: 去除细粒度计划演化使平均准确率从 40.13 降至 39.0；再去掉指令生成进一步降至 38.5，验证其贡献。

limitations: 依赖教师和 verifier LLM 进行计划生成与验证，缺乏量化开销或鲁棒性分析。

papers.title: FlowCTS: On-policy Continuous Trajectory Supervision of Flow Models
papers.abstract: While on-policy distillation (OPD) effectively addresses sparse rewards and exposure bias in large language model post-training, its extension to flow models remains underexplored. To this end, we propose Flow Continuous Trajectory Supervision (FlowCTS), which matches subsequent student and reference trajectories initialized from the same student-visited state. Using the integral relation between trajectories and velocity fields, we derive a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound and discretize it into practical objectives parameterized by the number of supervision steps. Under a multi-reference setup, single-state FlowCTS-OPD outperforms vanilla KL-based OPD with faster convergence. FlowCTS-OPD improves GenEval from 0.90 to 0.93, OCR from 0.90 to 0.92, and PickScore from 22.75 to 23.06, while outperforming a mixed-reward RL baseline across all target metrics. Further analysis reveals a clear temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla KL-based OPD arising from its auxiliary SDE transition kernels. Beyond on-policy setting,FlowCTS also consistently outperforms vanilla SFT , particularly on OCR, while increasing supervision steps exhibit a trade-off between richer trajectory information and greater optimization difficulty.

summary.takeaway: FlowCTS introduces a continuous trajectory supervision objective for flow models that improves on-policy distillation performance and convergence speed over vanilla KL-based OPD.
summary.problem: Extending on-policy distillation to flow models is challenging due to their continuous velocity field parameterization lacking natural next-step conditional distributions.
summary.method: FlowCTS supervises the discrepancy between student and reference continuous trajectories from the same student-visited state using a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound discretized into multi-step objectives.
summary.evidence: FlowCTS-OPD improves GenEval from 0.90 to 0.93, OCR from 0.90 to 0.92, and PickScore from 22.75 to 23.06, converging faster than vanilla KL-based OPD and outperforming mixed-reward RL baselines.
summary.limitations: Increasing the number of supervision steps introduces a trade-off between richer trajectory information and greater optimization difficulty, with no consistent improvements observed.
summary.why_for_you: FlowCTS provides a novel dense supervision framework for flow models in on-policy distillation, addressing temporal supervision mismatch and offering a new scaling dimension relevant to LLM post-training.

signals.text: FlowCTS-OPD achieves balanced multi-objective performance, matching GenEval and OCR experts while retaining competitive PickScore, demonstrating the effectiveness of trajectory-derived supervision in multi-reference on-policy distillation.

The method derives a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound on continuous trajectory supervision, discretized into a finite number of steps parameterized by K, enabling both single-state and multi-step supervision in flow models.

Analysis reveals a temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla KL-based OPD caused by auxiliary SDE transition kernels, which FlowCTS overcomes by focusing supervision on early denoising stages where student-reference discrepancy is largest.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the challenge of applying on-policy distillation (OPD) to flow models, which differ from autoregressive language models by parameterizing continuous velocity fields without natural next-step conditionals. The authors propose Flow Continuous Trajectory Supervision (FlowCTS), which supervises the discrepancy between student and reference continuous trajectories initialized from the same student-visited state. By deriving a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound and discretizing it into practical objectives parameterized by supervision steps, FlowCTS enables dense trajectory supervision beyond token-level next-step objectives. Experiments demonstrate that FlowCTS-OPD outperforms vanilla KL-based OPD in convergence speed and multi-objective metrics (GenEval, OCR, PickScore), and also surpasses mixed-reward RL baselines. The method extends to off-policy supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with consistent gains, especially on OCR. The authors identify a temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla OPD due to auxiliary SDE kernels, which FlowCTS mitigates by focusing supervision on early denoising stages where discrepancies are largest. Increasing supervision steps introduces a trade-off between richer trajectory information and optimization difficulty, highlighting a new scaling dimension for flow models.

methodology.title: Flow Continuous Trajectory Supervision (FlowCTS)
methodology.detail: FlowCTS supervises the discrepancy between student and reference continuous trajectories starting from the same student-visited state. It derives a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound on the trajectory discrepancy and discretizes this into a finite number of optimization steps parameterized by K, covering single-state velocity matching and multi-step trajectory supervision.

methodology.title: On-policy Distillation with FlowCTS (FlowCTS-OPD)
methodology.detail: In the on-policy setting, the shared starting state is sampled from the current student rollout. FlowCTS-OPD applies the discretized trajectory supervision objective to improve convergence and performance over vanilla KL-based OPD by focusing on velocity matching along the trajectory.

methodology.title: Extension to Off-policy Supervised Fine-Tuning (FlowCTS-SFT)
methodology.detail: FlowCTS generalizes beyond on-policy distillation by allowing the shared starting state to be sampled from off-policy data trajectories, enabling supervised fine-tuning with the same trajectory-derived objective, which improves OCR performance while maintaining other metrics.

methodology.title: Temporal Supervision Analysis
methodology.detail: The method analyzes the temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla KL-based OPD caused by auxiliary SDE transition kernels that concentrate supervision in late denoising stages, whereas FlowCTS provides dense supervision in early stages where student-reference discrepancy is largest.

mechanism.title: Velocity-Matching Upper Bound
mechanism.detail: FlowCTS leverages the integral relation between continuous trajectories and velocity fields to derive a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound on the discrepancy between student and reference trajectories. This bound is discretized into practical objectives parameterized by the number of supervision steps K, enabling tractable optimization.

mechanism.title: Temporal Supervision Mismatch in KL-based OPD
mechanism.detail: Vanilla KL-based OPD constructs transition kernels via an auxiliary stochastic differential equation (SDE), which concentrates supervision in late denoising stages, causing a temporal mismatch with the student’s rollout distribution. FlowCTS addresses this by supervising the entire trajectory starting from the student-visited state.

experiments.title: On-policy Distillation Evaluation
experiments.detail: FlowCTS-OPD is evaluated on GenEval, OCR, and PickScore metrics using multi-reference Flow-GRPO models. It outperforms vanilla KL-based OPD, improving GenEval from 0.90 to 0.93, OCR from 0.90 to 0.92, and PickScore from 22.75 to 23.06, with faster convergence and better out-of-distribution generalization.

experiments.title: Off-policy Supervised Fine-Tuning Evaluation
experiments.detail: FlowCTS-SFT is tested with off-policy starting states, showing consistent improvements over vanilla supervised fine-tuning (SFT), particularly on OCR, while maintaining comparable GenEval and PickScore performance.

experiments.title: Training Budget Control Ablation
experiments.detail: A controlled study compares FlowCTS-OPD with K=1 and K=2 supervision steps, controlling for total supervised state evaluations. Results indicate that K=2 supervision yields better GenEval and compositional correctness, suggesting benefits from multi-step trajectory constraints beyond training budget effects.

experiments.title: Sampling Method Comparison
experiments.detail: Comparison of SDE and ODE sampling for generating student-visited states during on-policy distillation shows that SDE sampling consistently achieves higher GenEval performance, especially during early optimization.

findings.title: Improved Multi-objective Performance
findings.detail: FlowCTS-OPD achieves balanced performance across GenEval, OCR, and PickScore, matching expert models on GenEval and OCR while retaining competitive PickScore, demonstrating effective multi-reference trajectory supervision.

findings.title: Faster Convergence
findings.detail: FlowCTS-OPD converges faster than vanilla KL-based OPD across all three metrics, reaching expert-level performance substantially earlier, indicating the efficiency of the velocity-matching trajectory objective.

findings.title: Temporal Supervision Mismatch Identified
findings.detail: Vanilla KL-based OPD suffers from temporal supervision mismatch due to auxiliary SDE transition kernels focusing supervision on late denoising stages, whereas FlowCTS provides dense supervision in early stages where discrepancies are largest.

findings.title: Trade-off with Supervision Steps
findings.detail: Increasing the number of supervision steps K introduces a trade-off: richer trajectory information improves compositional and structural correctness but may suppress fine-grained details and increase optimization difficulty.

findings.title: Off-policy Gains on OCR
findings.detail: FlowCTS-SFT improves OCR performance over vanilla SFT while maintaining comparable GenEval and PickScore, validating the trajectory supervision formulation beyond on-policy distillation.

contributions: Proposed FlowCTS, a continuous trajectory supervision framework for flow models enabling dense on-policy distillation.
Derived a temporally weighted velocity-matching upper bound discretized into multi-step objectives parameterized by supervision steps.
Extended FlowCTS to both on-policy distillation and off-policy supervised fine-tuning settings with empirical validation.
Identified and addressed temporal supervision mismatch in vanilla KL-based OPD caused by auxiliary SDE transition kernels.
Introduced supervision step count as a new scaling dimension balancing trajectory information richness and optimization difficulty.
limitations: Increasing supervision steps does not consistently improve performance and introduces optimization challenges.
The trade-off between richer trajectory supervision and fine-grained detail preservation requires further exploration.
Temporal supervision mismatch analysis is limited to auxiliary SDE kernels; other flow model variants are not analyzed.
Evidence on generalization beyond evaluated datasets and tasks is not provided.
open_questions: How can the trade-off between supervision step count and optimization difficulty be better managed or mitigated?
Can FlowCTS be adapted or extended to other types of generative models beyond flow models?
What are the theoretical guarantees or bounds on convergence and generalization for FlowCTS in large-scale settings?
How does FlowCTS interact with different sampling methods or velocity field parameterizations in flow models?

papers.title: Simulating Tenant Responses to Energy Policy Interventions with Transaction-Cost-Aware LLM Age
papers.abstract: Recent studies use Large language models (LLMs) to simulate human opinions and decisions by prompting models with demographic, attitudinal, or persona-based descriptions. Yet such simulations rarely model the practical, cognitive, or social frictions that shape how people respond to policy interventions. Perceived transaction cost (PTC) provides a useful lens for modeling the practical frictions that shape policy responses, such as information burden, administrative effort, coordination demands, and perceived uncertainty. We use this lens to develop a friction-aware persona modeling approach for LLM-based simulation. In the context of energy-efficient renovation (EER), tenants are represented not only by who they are demographically, but by how they perceive the costs, benefits, barriers, and uncertainties associated with proposed renovation plans. Using survey data collected from 1,068 citizens in the Netherlands, comprising approximately 40,548 survey question and answer pairs, we compare prompt-only and fine-tuned settings across GPT-3.5-turbo, Ministral-8B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and evaluate supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) for local open-weight models. Results show that incorporating PTC-based personas and reasoning consistently improves model performance across both prompt-only and fine-tuned settings, suggesting that PTC-based persona design provides a useful bridge between institutional policy theory and interpretable LLM-based policy simulation. Code is available at https://github.com/xiaweijie1996/socialagent.

summary.takeaway: Incorporating perceived transaction cost (PTC)-based personas and reasoning into LLM simulations significantly improves the fidelity of tenant responses to energy-efficient renovation policies.
summary.problem: Current LLM-based simulations inadequately model the practical, cognitive, and social frictions influencing human responses to policy interventions, limiting their interpretability and accuracy.
summary.method: The authors develop a friction-aware persona modeling framework that integrates PTC-based personas and reasoning prompts into LLMs, comparing prompt-only and fine-tuned approaches across GPT-3.5-turbo, Ministral-8B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models.
summary.evidence: Using a dataset of 1,068 Dutch citizens with 40,548 survey Q&A pairs, experiments show consistent performance improvements when PTC personas and reasoning are included, validated across prompt-only and fine-tuned settings with supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization.
summary.limitations: The study focuses on energy-efficient renovation in Dutch social housing tenants, limiting generalizability; also, the paper does not provide detailed quantitative metrics for all model comparisons or address potential biases in LLM-generated responses.
summary.why_for_you: This work bridges institutional policy theory and LLM-based policy simulation by introducing a theoretically grounded, interpretable persona design that models practical frictions, advancing trustworthy and context-sensitive LLM applications in policy research.

signals.text: Incorporating PTC-based personas that capture perceived barriers and benefits such as financial sensitivity and immediate utility seeking improves LLM simulation fidelity in replicating tenant responses to energy policy.

The method uses a three-layer prompt design combining system instructions, PTC persona descriptions, and PTC reasoning prompts, alongside fine-tuning local open-weight models with QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization.

Experimental results on 40,548 survey question-answer pairs demonstrate that models with PTC persona and reasoning prompts achieve lower mean absolute error (MAE) in predicting tenant responses compared to demographic-only or no-PTC baselines.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the gap in LLM-based policy simulation where existing models inadequately represent the practical frictions—such as information burden, administrative effort, and uncertainty—that influence human responses to energy policy interventions. The authors propose a novel persona modeling framework grounded in perceived transaction cost (PTC) theory, which enriches LLM prompts with personas reflecting tenants' perceived barriers and benefits related to energy-efficient renovation (EER). They implement a structured prompt design with system instructions, PTC persona descriptions, and reasoning checklists, and evaluate this approach on a large-scale Dutch survey dataset. The study compares prompt-only GPT-3.5-turbo baselines with fine-tuned local models (Ministral-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) using supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization. Results consistently show that PTC-aware personas and reasoning improve model accuracy in simulating tenant responses, suggesting that this approach effectively bridges institutional policy theory and interpretable LLM simulation, thereby enhancing the trustworthiness and contextual relevance of LLMs in policy research.

methodology.title: PTC Persona Construction
methodology.detail: Tenant personas are constructed from survey indicators measuring perceived benefits (comfort, health, energy savings) and barriers (rent increases, disruption, distrust, uncertainty). These personas capture practical frictions and motivations relevant to energy-efficient renovation decisions.

methodology.title: Prompt Design
methodology.detail: Each survey instance is converted into a structured prompt with three layers: a system instruction to maintain persona consistency, a PTC persona prompt describing barrier- or benefit-oriented traits, and a PTC reasoning prompt that guides the model to reflect on burdens, uncertainties, and personal gains before answering.

methodology.title: Model Adaptation via QLoRA
methodology.detail: Local open-weight models (Ministral-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) are fine-tuned using QLoRA with 4-bit NF4 quantization and LoRA adapters. Two training regimes are used: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learning directly from survey examples, and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizing outputs with an explicit reward function.

methodology.title: Evaluation Setup
methodology.detail: Models are evaluated on a dataset of 1,068 Dutch citizens with 40,548 survey question-answer pairs, split into training (4,600 attitude-related pairs) and test sets. Performance is measured by mean absolute error (MAE) across benefit- and barrier-related questions under varying prompt and fine-tuning conditions.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models but relies on the theoretical framework of perceived transaction costs to represent practical frictions influencing policy responses, operationalized via persona prompts and reasoning checklists.

experiments.title: Prompt-Only Baseline Evaluation
experiments.detail: GPT-3.5-turbo is evaluated under three prompting conditions: no PTC information, PTC persona only, and PTC persona plus reasoning prompts, demonstrating incremental improvements in response accuracy.

experiments.title: Fine-Tuning Local Models
experiments.detail: Ministral-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct models are fine-tuned using QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on 4,600 attitude-related survey pairs, with evaluation on the remaining data to assess gains from adaptation and PTC prompting.

experiments.title: Performance Metrics and Analysis
experiments.detail: Mean absolute error (MAE) is used to quantify prediction accuracy across survey questions, showing that models incorporating PTC personas and reasoning outperform demographic-only or no-PTC baselines consistently across benefit- and barrier-related questions.

findings.title: PTC Persona Improves Simulation Fidelity
findings.detail: Adding PTC persona prompts to GPT-3.5-turbo reduces MAE compared to demographic-only prompts, indicating better alignment with tenant responses influenced by perceived barriers and benefits.

findings.title: PTC Reasoning Further Enhances Performance
findings.detail: Including PTC reasoning prompts alongside personas yields additional accuracy gains, suggesting that explicit reflection on transaction costs aids LLM decision modeling.

findings.title: Fine-Tuning with SFT and GRPO Boosts Accuracy
findings.detail: QLoRA-based supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization on local open-weight models further improve prediction accuracy beyond prompt-only baselines, validating the benefit of model adaptation.

findings.title: Consistent Gains Across Models and Settings
findings.detail: Performance improvements from PTC-based persona design and reasoning are observed across GPT-3.5-turbo, Ministral-8B-Instruct, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, demonstrating robustness of the approach.

contributions: Introduces a novel PTC-aware persona modeling framework for LLM-based simulation of policy responses.
Develops a structured prompt design combining system instructions, PTC persona descriptions, and reasoning prompts.
Demonstrates empirical improvements in simulating tenant responses to energy-efficient renovation policies using a large-scale Dutch survey dataset.
Evaluates and compares prompt-only and fine-tuned LLM settings including supervised fine-tuning and Group Relative Policy Optimization.
Bridges institutional policy theory and interpretable LLM simulation to enhance trustworthy AI applications in energy policy research.
limitations: Focus on Dutch social housing tenants limits generalizability to other populations or policy contexts.
Lack of detailed quantitative metrics for all model comparisons restricts comprehensive performance assessment.
Potential biases and variability in LLM-generated responses are acknowledged but not deeply analyzed.
No formal causal or mechanistic model is provided beyond theoretical framing of transaction costs.
open_questions: How well does the PTC-aware persona framework generalize to other policy domains and cultural contexts?
Can the approach be extended to model dynamic decision-making processes over time rather than static survey responses?
What are the best practices to mitigate biases and ensure fairness in LLM-based policy simulations conditioned on PTC personas?
How can explicit causal mechanisms linking transaction costs to policy responses be integrated into LLM simulation frameworks?

papers.title: D-Score: A Spectral Hidden-State Signal for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Language Models can produce fluent text that is false, unsupported by the available evidence, or inconsistent with information that appears to be internally represented by the model. We study hallucination detection from the geometry of hidden activations and introduce the D-Score, a simple spectral statistic computed from a single forward pass. For a fixed model, layer, and tolerance parameter, the D-Score counts how many singular directions of the hidden activation matrix have singular values that remain close to the leading one. We use this quantity as a hallucination score, classifying an input text as hallucinated when its D-Score is larger than a pre-defined quantity. The motivation is that, when a model processes a text that conflicts with information available in its own internal state, the hidden representation may encode both the asserted content and some form of counter-evidence, uncertainty, correction, or lack of support; this can make the hidden trajectory spread across additional singular directions. We formalize this intuition through a lightweight spectral argument and evaluate the resulting detector on FAVA-Annotation and RAGTruth. The experiments indicate that the D-Score is a strong hidden-state signal for hallucination detection, while requiring no external verifier, no retrieval step, and no multiple generations.

summary.takeaway: The D-Score effectively detects hallucinations in Large Language Models by analyzing hidden activations without external resources.
summary.problem: Hallucination in LLMs leads to the generation of false or unsupported claims, hindering their reliability.
summary.method: The D-Score quantifies hallucination by counting singular directions in hidden activation matrices during a single forward pass.
summary.evidence: Experiments on FAVA-Annotation and RAGTruth demonstrate that the D-Score outperforms existing methods across multiple models.
summary.limitations: The D-Score's performance is sensitive to the choice of tolerance parameter and layer selection.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding the D-Score can enhance the reliability of LLMs in applications requiring factual accuracy.

signals.text: The D-Score measures how many singular values of hidden activations remain close to the leading one, indicating the coherence of the hidden trajectory.
The method requires only a single forward pass through the model, eliminating the need for external verifiers or multiple generations.
Evaluation results show that the D-Score achieves strong performance metrics on datasets like FAVA-Annotation and RAGTruth, outperforming traditional methods.

deep_dive.overview: This research addresses the challenge of hallucination in Large Language Models (LLMs) by introducing the D-Score, a spectral statistic derived from hidden activations. The D-Score quantifies the coherence of hidden state trajectories during a single forward pass, providing a direct measure of hallucination without relying on external data or multiple model evaluations. The authors validate the effectiveness of the D-Score through experiments on FAVA-Annotation and RAGTruth, demonstrating its superior performance compared to existing methods, thus offering a promising approach to enhance the reliability of LLM outputs.

methodology.title: D-Score Calculation
methodology.detail: The D-Score is computed by analyzing the singular values of the hidden activation matrix from a fixed model and layer. It counts how many singular values exceed a predefined tolerance, indicating the concentration of the hidden trajectory.

methodology.title: Model Configuration
methodology.detail: The method operates on a fixed model and layer, with a tolerance parameter that determines the threshold for classifying hallucinations. This configuration allows for consistent evaluation across different inputs.

methodology.title: Single Forward Pass
methodology.detail: The D-Score is derived from a single forward pass through the model, making it computationally efficient. This approach avoids the complexities of retrieval-based or consistency-based methods.

mechanism.title: Geometric Argument
mechanism.detail: The paper posits that unsupported claims lead to a spread in the hidden trajectory across multiple singular directions, which can be detected by the D-Score. This reflects the model's internal uncertainty when processing conflicting information.

experiments.title: Evaluation on FAVA-Annotation
experiments.detail: The D-Score was tested on the FAVA-Annotation dataset, where it demonstrated superior performance metrics compared to existing hallucination detection methods.

experiments.title: Evaluation on RAGTruth
experiments.detail: In experiments on RAGTruth, the D-Score outperformed traditional approaches, indicating its robustness across different datasets and model architectures.

findings.title: D-Score Effectiveness
findings.detail: The D-Score effectively identifies hallucinations, achieving strong results on multiple benchmarks, indicating its potential as a reliable detection tool.

findings.title: Sensitivity to Parameters
findings.detail: The performance of the D-Score is sensitive to the choice of tolerance parameter and layer selection, which can affect its detection capabilities.

findings.title: Internal Geometry Insights
findings.detail: The research provides insights into how the internal geometry of LLMs can reveal information about the truthfulness of generated claims.

contributions: Introduction of the D-Score as a novel method for hallucination detection in LLMs.
Operational definition of model-internal hallucination based on unsupported claims.
Geometric argument explaining the relationship between hallucinations and hidden trajectory spread.
limitations: The D-Score's effectiveness is contingent on the appropriate selection of the tolerance parameter and layer.
The method's performance may vary across different model architectures and datasets.
open_questions: How can the D-Score be adapted for different model architectures beyond those tested?
What are the implications of varying the tolerance parameter on the D-Score's reliability?
Can the D-Score be integrated with other detection methods to enhance overall performance?

papers.title: LLM-SoccerArena: Benchmarking LLMs on Real-World Predictions in Sports
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly support decisions about uncertain future events, yet evaluating their ability to forecast real-world outcomes remains difficult. In particular, existing benchmarks are typically static and retrospective, and therefore cannot test how information is synthesized by LLMs to predict future events under uncertainty. We introduce LLM-SoccerArena (https://llm-soccerarena.com), a prospective live benchmark that evaluates how well LLMs forecast real-world sports events before the outcomes are known. LLM-SoccerArena provides (1) a prospective live benchmark protocol, (2) a public open-source platform, and (3) a factorial benchmark design together with tournament-related questions (e.g., which team will win). LLM-SoccerArena automatically records timestamped, schema-validated forecasts of unresolved events, together with prompts, model versions, tool traces, and costs. The factorial design varies along four dimensions: (1) model version (e.g., GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8); (2) information access; (3) prompting strategy, and (4) forecast horizon. We demonstrate LLM-SoccerArena through a large-scale evaluation of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, in which seven LLMs generated forecasts for all 104 matches and 15 tournament-related questions. We provide a detailed analysis of model performance across information access, prompting strategy, and forecast horizon. As a result, LLM-SoccerArena provides new evidence about the forecasting performance of state-of-the-art LLMs. For example, LLMs with web access outperform those without, but only by a small margin (i.e., a 0.023 improvement in Brier score). Overall, LLM-SoccerArena provides a flexible, open-source platform for prospective benchmarking of unresolved events. LLM-SoccerArena will be continuously updated, and can be directly applied to future national and international tournaments and league competitions.

summary.takeaway: LLM-SoccerArena introduces a novel prospective benchmark for evaluating LLMs' forecasting abilities in sports.
summary.problem: Existing benchmarks for LLM forecasting are static and retrospective, failing to assess real-time predictive capabilities.
summary.method: The study employs a factorial design to evaluate LLMs across various dimensions, including model version and information access.
summary.evidence: In a large-scale evaluation of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, LLMs with web access showed a 0.023 improvement in Brier score over those without.
summary.limitations: The benchmark does not provide curated statistics or domain features beyond basic event information.
summary.why_for_you: This research is crucial for understanding how LLMs can be effectively utilized in real-world decision-making under uncertainty.

signals.text: LLM-SoccerArena's factorial design allows for systematic comparisons of LLM forecasts across different model versions, prompting strategies, and information access, enhancing the understanding of LLM capabilities.
The benchmark protocol records timestamped forecasts, ensuring that predictions are made before outcomes are known, thus providing a genuine assessment of forecasting ability.
The evaluation of seven LLMs during the 2026 FIFA World Cup revealed that models with web access achieved a Brier score improvement of 0.023, indicating a slight advantage in predictive accuracy.

deep_dive.overview: LLM-SoccerArena addresses the challenge of evaluating LLMs' forecasting abilities by providing a prospective live benchmark that records predictions before outcomes are known. This benchmark is designed to overcome the limitations of static, retrospective evaluations by allowing LLMs to synthesize evolving information into probabilistic judgments. The study demonstrates its effectiveness through a large-scale evaluation of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, where it captures the performance of various LLMs under different conditions, revealing insights into their predictive capabilities and the impact of information access and prompting strategies.

methodology.title: Prospective Live Benchmark Protocol
methodology.detail: LLM-SoccerArena records timestamped forecasts for unresolved events, ensuring that predictions are made before outcomes are known, thus preventing artifacts from memorization.

methodology.title: Factorial Design
methodology.detail: The benchmark varies across four dimensions: model version (e.g., GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8), information access (web search vs. no web search), prompting strategy (scoreline vs. outcome probabilities), and forecast horizon (timing of predictions).

methodology.title: Evaluation Metrics
methodology.detail: Performance is assessed using accuracy and Brier score, allowing for a quantitative comparison of forecasting abilities across different LLMs and conditions.

methodology.title: Data Collection
methodology.detail: The benchmark automatically collects prompts, model versions, tool traces, and costs associated with each prediction, facilitating a comprehensive analysis of LLM performance.

mechanism.title: Information Synthesis
mechanism.detail: LLM-SoccerArena tests the ability of LLMs to synthesize evolving information into probabilistic judgments, reflecting their reasoning capabilities under uncertainty.

experiments.title: 2026 FIFA World Cup Evaluation
experiments.detail: Seven LLMs generated forecasts for all 104 matches and 15 tournament-related questions, allowing for a detailed analysis of model performance across various conditions.

experiments.title: Impact of Information Access
experiments.detail: The evaluation revealed that LLMs with web access outperformed those without, achieving a Brier score improvement of 0.023, indicating the importance of real-time information.

experiments.title: Prompting Strategies Analysis
experiments.detail: Different prompting strategies were tested, showing that direct score predictions led to varying levels of agreement between predicted scorelines and overall match outcomes.

findings.title: Performance of LLMs with Web Access
findings.detail: LLMs with web access achieved a Brier score improvement of 0.023 over those without, highlighting the advantage of real-time information.

findings.title: Effectiveness of Factorial Design
findings.detail: The factorial design allowed for systematic comparisons, revealing that different prompting strategies significantly influenced forecasting accuracy.

findings.title: Prospective Benchmarking Success
findings.detail: LLM-SoccerArena successfully recorded predictions before outcomes were known, providing a genuine assessment of LLM forecasting abilities.

contributions: Introduces a novel prospective live benchmark for evaluating LLM forecasting abilities in sports.
Provides a public open-source platform for continuous updates and evaluations.
Establishes a factorial design for systematic comparisons of LLM performance across various conditions.
limitations: The benchmark does not include curated statistics or domain features beyond basic event information.
Limited qualitative insights into reasoning traces or evidence from LLM-generated justifications.
open_questions: How can LLMs be further improved to enhance their forecasting accuracy in dynamic environments?
What additional factors could be integrated into the benchmark to better assess LLM reasoning capabilities?

papers.title: Reason-Mediated Behavioral Models for Auditing LLM Social Simulators
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as social simulators, including as synthetic survey respondents. Most evaluations ask whether simulated outcomes resemble human outcomes. We argue that this is necessary but too weak: a simulator can match the final answer while using the wrong rationale-derived reason pattern. We study this problem through a 94-person sunscreen concept test in which each respondent evaluated three product concepts and wrote open-ended rationales. We map those rationales into signed reason states $Z$, where positive signs support adoption and negative signs block it. This gives a practical audit: holding respondent descriptors $D$, category context $K$, and concept treatment $X$ fixed, do human rationale-derived reasons help predict behavior $Y$, and can an LLM simulate the same reason state without seeing the human rationale or outcome? Human rationale-derived reasons substantially improve held-out prediction of purchase intent. LLM-simulated reasons are more brittle: they often sound plausible, but frequently echo the concept board rather than recover the respondent's acceptance or rejection path. The paper contributes an evaluation framework for social simulators. Reason states do not identify natural causal effects by themselves, but they provide an interpretable test of whether a simulator's stated reasons align with human evidence.

summary.takeaway: Human rationale-derived reasons significantly enhance the prediction of purchase intent in LLM social simulators.
summary.problem: Existing evaluations of LLMs as social simulators often overlook the importance of the rationale behind decisions.
summary.method: The study employs a sunscreen concept test with 94 respondents to map rationales into signed reason states for auditing LLM predictions.
summary.evidence: Human rationale-derived reasons improve held-out prediction of purchase intent, while LLM-simulated reasons often fail to capture the underlying acceptance or rejection paths.
summary.limitations: The study's small sample size limits the generalizability of its findings.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding the alignment of LLM outputs with human reasoning is crucial for developing trustworthy AI systems.

signals.text: Human rationale-derived reasons significantly improve the prediction of purchase intent, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.625 compared to 0.918 for zero-Z control.
The study introduces a reason-mediated behavioral model that maps respondent descriptors, category context, and concept treatment into signed reason states, facilitating a practical audit of LLMs.

LLM-simulated reasons are found to be brittle, often echoing concept boards rather than accurately reflecting the respondent's acceptance or rejection paths, leading to a mean reason intersection over union (IoU) of only 0.201.

deep_dive.overview: This research addresses the inadequacy of current evaluations of LLMs as social simulators, which typically focus on outcome similarity to human responses. By analyzing a sunscreen concept test with 94 respondents, the authors introduce a reason-mediated behavioral model that maps human rationales into signed reason states. The findings reveal that human-derived reasons significantly enhance the prediction of purchase intent, while LLM-simulated reasons often fail to capture the necessary rationale, indicating a gap in LLM performance that must be addressed for trustworthy AI applications.

methodology.title: Concept Test Study
methodology.detail: The study involved 94 English-speaking Indian women aged 22-40 who evaluated three sunscreen concepts. Respondents provided purchase intent ratings, rationales, and demographic information, allowing for a comprehensive analysis of the factors influencing their decisions.

methodology.title: Reason-State Construction
methodology.detail: A reason codebook was developed to map open-ended rationales into signed reason states, categorizing reasons into families such as value, proof trust, and safety. This structured approach enables the reuse of reason states across different concept tests.

methodology.title: Predictive Readout Training
methodology.detail: A readout function was trained to predict purchase intent based on fixed respondent descriptors, category context, concept treatment, and mapped reason states. This model was evaluated against LLM-simulated reasons to assess predictive accuracy.

mechanism.title: Reason-Mediated Behavioral Model
mechanism.detail: The model posits that fixed human-readable reason states can mediate the relationship between stimuli and responses, allowing for an interpretable audit of LLM outputs against human reasoning.

experiments.title: Sunscreen Concept Test
experiments.detail: The experiment involved 94 respondents rating three sunscreen concepts, with outcomes measured in terms of purchase intent, believability, and differentiation. The main target was to assess the predictive accuracy of human versus LLM-simulated reasons.

experiments.title: Voice-Pool Simulation
experiments.detail: The voice-pool estimator maintained multiple response modes (skeptic, balanced, enthusiast) to generate candidate reason states and purchase-intent distributions, comparing these with oracle selections to evaluate model performance.

experiments.title: Robustness Checks
experiments.detail: Various robustness checks were conducted, including respondent bootstrap intervals and reason-family ablations, to validate the predictive capabilities of the reason-mediated model against different baselines.

findings.title: Improved Prediction with Human Reasons
findings.detail: The study found that incorporating human rationale-derived reason states improved the prediction of purchase intent, achieving a mean absolute error of 0.625.

findings.title: Brittleness of LLM-Simulated Reasons
findings.detail: LLM-simulated reasons were shown to be less effective, with a mean IoU of 0.201, indicating a failure to accurately reflect the human reasoning process.

findings.title: Negative Result for LLM Reason Simulation
findings.detail: The research highlighted that LLM-simulated reasons, while fluent, often failed to align with the human acceptance or rejection paths, demonstrating a critical limitation in current LLM capabilities.

contributions: Definition of a reason-mediated behavioral model for auditing LLM social simulators.
Demonstration that human rationale-derived reasons enhance predictive accuracy for purchase intent.
Identification of limitations in LLM-simulated reasoning capabilities.
limitations: The small sample size of 94 respondents limits the generalizability of the findings.
The study does not establish causal relationships, focusing instead on predictive accuracy.
open_questions: How can LLMs be improved to better simulate human reasoning paths?
What larger-scale studies are needed to validate the findings across diverse populations?
Can the reason-mediated model be adapted for other types of social simulations beyond consumer behavior?

papers.title: X$^3$-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment
papers.abstract: While large audio-language models have achieved remarkable progress in auditory perception, they still lag behind text-based large language models in deep logical reasoning, primarily due to the scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data. To bridge this gap, we propose X$^3$-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that transfers reasoning capabilities from a powerful text teacher to an audio-language student. During training, the student generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on its own acoustic perception, while the teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. We further construct a three-tier symmetric corpus covering textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and spoken-dialogue reasoning involving paralinguistic cues. This design extends cross-modal distillation beyond textually recoverable content to reasoning grounded in non-linguistic events, prosody, and conversational context. Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR demonstrate that X$^3$-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving the model's existing capabilities under domain shift.

summary.takeaway: X³-OPD introduces a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework that effectively transfers deep reasoning capabilities from a text-based teacher to a large audio-language student model, substantially improving audio-grounded reasoning.
summary.problem: Large audio-language models lag behind text-only LLMs in multi-step logical reasoning due to scarcity of high-quality audio reasoning data and limitations of offline distillation methods.
summary.method: X³-OPD trains an audio-language student to generate reasoning trajectories conditioned on acoustic inputs while a frozen text teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers via a policy gradient-based distillation loss.
summary.evidence: Experiments on MMSU, MMAU, BIG Bench Audio, and MMAR benchmarks show X³-OPD achieves substantial improvements in audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality, outperforming strong baselines including standard supervised fine-tuning and offline distillation.
summary.limitations: The current three-tier symmetric corpus underrepresents complex musical reasoning and specialized non-linguistic soundscapes, and the text-based teacher’s token-level supervision biases learning toward semantic logic while under-penalizing perceptual and paralinguistic errors.
summary.why_for_you: X³-OPD advances on-policy distillation techniques for trustworthy LLMs by addressing cross-modal reasoning gaps and providing a scalable framework for transferring logical reasoning into audio-language models.

signals.text: X³-OPD’s three-tier symmetric corpus includes textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning grounded in complex acoustic scenes, and prosody-aware spoken dialogue, enabling supervision beyond textually recoverable content.

The method employs token-level KL-style supervision from a frozen text teacher with privileged access to ground-truth answers, guiding the student’s acoustic-conditioned reasoning trajectories via a policy gradient objective maximizing cross-modal advantage.

Compared to offline distillation and standard supervised fine-tuning baselines, X³-OPD reduces cross-modal exposure bias and mitigates performance drops on perceptual tasks while achieving remarkable gains on reasoning-heavy axes such as semantics and audio temporal grounding.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the reasoning gap between large audio-language models (LALMs) and text-only LLMs caused by limited audio reasoning data and the shortcomings of offline distillation. The authors propose X³-OPD, a cross-modal on-policy distillation framework where the audio student model generates reasoning trajectories conditioned on acoustic inputs, and a frozen text teacher provides token-level guidance using matched textual inputs and verified answers. The approach leverages a novel three-tier symmetric corpus spanning textual reasoning rendered into speech, audio-event reasoning, and spoken dialogue with paralinguistic cues, thus extending supervision beyond textually recoverable content. The distillation objective maximizes a cross-modal advantage defined as the log-probability gap between teacher and student outputs, implemented via policy gradient optimization. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that X³-OPD substantially improves audio-grounded reasoning and chain-of-thought quality while largely preserving perceptual capabilities under domain shifts. The method effectively reduces cross-modal exposure bias inherent in offline distillation, enabling robust reasoning transfer from text to audio modalities.

methodology.title: Three-tier Symmetric Corpus Construction
methodology.detail: The dataset comprises 27.8K Tier-1 instances of textual reasoning rendered into speech, 32K Tier-2 audio-event reasoning samples with captions, and 12K Tier-3 prosody-aware spoken dialogues. Each instance includes paired text and audio inputs with questions and verified answers under a uniform schema, enabling cross-modal supervision.

methodology.title: Cross-Modal On-Policy Distillation
methodology.detail: During training, the audio student rolls out reasoning trajectories conditioned on its acoustic input. The frozen text teacher, with access to matched text input and ground-truth answers, scores these trajectories token-by-token using KL-style supervision, providing dynamic corrective feedback exactly where the student deviates.

methodology.title: Policy Gradient Optimization with Cross-Modal Advantage
methodology.detail: The distillation loss maximizes the expected cross-modal advantage, defined as the log-probability difference between teacher and student outputs at each token. Multiple rollouts per sample are used to estimate gradients, enabling the student to learn robust reasoning aligned with the teacher’s logical distribution.

methodology.title: Training Configuration and Baselines
methodology.detail: The student model is initialized from Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Thinking with trainable acoustic encoder and LLM backbone; the teacher is Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking, frozen. Training includes an offline warm-start supervised fine-tuning pass followed by on-policy distillation with AdamW optimizer and vLLM rollout sampling.

mechanism.title: Cross-Modal Advantage Mechanism
mechanism.detail: The cross-modal advantage A(yt) is computed as the difference between the teacher’s log-probability of token yt given text input and ground-truth answer, and the student’s log-probability of yt given acoustic input. This advantage guides the policy gradient update to align the student’s reasoning trajectory with the teacher’s logical manifold, mitigating exposure bias.

experiments.title: Benchmark Evaluation on MMSU, MMAU, and BIG Bench Audio
experiments.detail: X³-OPD is evaluated on multiple audio-grounded reasoning benchmarks covering semantics, phonology, style, traits, sound, speech, and music. It outperforms strong baselines including GPT-4o-Audio and Qwen3-Omni-Thinking on reasoning-heavy axes, demonstrating improved chain-of-thought quality and reasoning accuracy.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies
experiments.detail: Comparisons against standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and offline guided knowledge distillation (GKD) baselines show that X³-OPD’s on-policy distillation reduces performance degradation on perceptual tasks and achieves superior reasoning gains, validating the effectiveness of dynamic teacher feedback.

experiments.title: Out-of-Distribution Generalization
experiments.detail: The model is stress-tested on held-out MMAR benchmark and domain-shifted datasets such as WorldSense and DailyOmni, showing that X³-OPD largely preserves existing capabilities under domain shifts while enhancing reasoning robustness.

findings.title: Improved Reasoning Performance
findings.detail: X³-OPD achieves the highest scores on semantic and reasoning-heavy axes across MMSU, MMAU, and BIG Bench Audio benchmarks, e.g., semantic accuracy improvements over baselines by several percentage points, demonstrating effective reasoning transfer.

findings.title: Mitigation of Perceptual Performance Drops
findings.detail: Unlike offline distillation baselines that regress on perceptual axes such as phonology, style, and music, X³-OPD substantially reduces these drops by providing on-policy corrective signals, preserving perceptual understanding.

findings.title: Limitations in Perceptual and Specialized Audio Domains
findings.detail: Despite improvements, X³-OPD slightly trails the base model on purely perceptual tasks like MMAU-Music, reflecting underrepresentation of complex musical reasoning and specialized non-linguistic soundscapes in the training corpus.

contributions: Proposed X³-OPD, a novel cross-modal on-policy distillation framework for transferring reasoning from text LLMs to audio-language models.
Constructed a large-scale three-tier symmetric corpus spanning textual reasoning, audio-event reasoning, and prosody-aware spoken dialogue for unified cross-modal supervision.
Developed a policy gradient-based distillation objective leveraging token-level KL supervision with privileged teacher access to ground-truth answers.
Demonstrated substantial improvements on multiple audio-grounded reasoning benchmarks and robustness under domain shifts.
Identified and mitigated cross-modal exposure bias inherent in offline distillation approaches.
limitations: The three-tier corpus does not yet cover the full diversity of acoustic phenomena, notably complex musical reasoning and specialized non-linguistic soundscapes.
The text-based teacher’s token-level supervision is blind to non-semantic acoustic cues, biasing learning toward semantic logic and under-penalizing perceptual and paralinguistic errors.
Residual performance gaps remain on purely perceptual axes despite on-policy distillation improvements.
The framework currently lacks multi-dimensional reward mechanisms incorporating direct audio-based rewards or environmental verifiers.
open_questions: How can multi-dimensional reward models incorporating audio-based signals and environmental verifiers be integrated to better capture non-semantic acoustic cues?
What methods can expand the training corpus to include more diverse and complex acoustic phenomena such as specialized soundscapes and musical reasoning?
How can on-policy distillation be further optimized to balance improvements in reasoning with preservation of perceptual capabilities?
Can the framework be extended to incorporate multi-modal inputs beyond audio and text, such as video, to enhance reasoning robustness?

papers.title: Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score (CM-LRS): From Plausible to Bankable
papers.abstract: In capital-markets workflows the question is rarely whether a large language model can produce a fluent draft, but whether the draft is bankable: defensible in front of a counter-party or a regulator, with the documents in hand. Existing methods address parts of that gap: open-domain QA benchmarks reward surface accuracy, and finance benchmarks (FinanceBench, FinQA, ConvFinQA) advance document-grounded and numerical QA but evaluate at the question-answer layer rather than the workflow outputs practitioners defend. We introduce CM-LRS, a Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score, evaluating outputs at the workflow-output layer across seven dimensions: factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability/auditability. Each is scored 0-5 against a rubric anchored on signals reviewers in regulated settings use; the aggregate is tunable to the workflow. We demonstrate CM-LRS on five workflows (DCM transaction-terms extraction, precedent retrieval, issuer profile synthesis, M&A transaction-comparable reasoning, ECM transaction-terms extraction) over public SEC EDGAR filings, a public UK takeover release, and fictional synthetic supplements, scoring four models against four independent LLM judges spanning three model families. Three findings. First, the frontier closed-source models cluster within 0.22 points on four-judge averaged CM-LRS (Sonnet 4.6 = 4.31, Opus 4.7 = 4.30, GPT-5.5 = 4.09); all four judges place the open-weights baseline (Llama 3.3 70B = 3.15) last. Second, that gap concentrates on retrieval (2.23) and synthesis (2.15), not extraction (0.84). Third, Decision Usefulness shows the widest cross-model dispersion of any dimension (4.0 points on issuer profiling) and top-tier inter-judge agreement (mean r = 0.52). Plausibility is cheap. Bankability is the bar.

summary.takeaway: CM-LRS is a novel, multi-dimensional evaluation metric assessing capital-markets LLM outputs at the workflow-output layer to determine bankability rather than mere plausibility.
summary.problem: Existing LLM evaluation benchmarks focus on question-answer accuracy but fail to assess whether outputs are defensible and verifiable in regulated capital-markets workflows.
summary.method: CM-LRS scores LLM outputs across seven dimensions—factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability—using a rubric anchored in real-world reviewer signals.
summary.evidence: Evaluation of five capital-markets workflows with four models and four independent judges shows frontier closed-source models cluster closely in CM-LRS scores, with open-weights baselines lagging, especially on retrieval and synthesis tasks.
summary.limitations: The paper notes the need for inter-rater reliability studies, calibration of dimension weights against real reviewer decisions, and extension to drafting workflows, indicating current limitations in generalizability and calibration.
summary.why_for_you: CM-LRS provides a rigorous, deployment-readiness metric tailored for high-stakes regulated environments, enabling trustworthy LLM evaluation beyond surface-level accuracy.

signals.text: The Decision Usefulness dimension (D6) shows the widest cross-model score dispersion (up to 4.0 points on issuer profiling) and high inter-judge agreement (mean Pearson r = 0.52), making it a key production-readiness indicator.
CM-LRS employs a seven-dimension rubric scored 0–5, each anchored on practical signals used by regulated environment reviewers, enabling tunable aggregation to specific capital-markets workflows.

The open-weights Llama 3.3 70B baseline scores roughly one point lower than frontier closed-source models on CM-LRS, with the largest gaps concentrated in retrieval (2.23 points) and synthesis (2.15 points) workflows rather than extraction (0.84 points).

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the critical gap in evaluating large language models (LLMs) for capital-markets workflows, where the key question is whether outputs are bankable—defensible and verifiable in regulated settings—rather than merely plausible or fluent. Existing benchmarks focus on question-answer accuracy but do not assess the full workflow output that practitioners must defend. CM-LRS introduces a seven-dimension rubric evaluating factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability/auditability, each scored 0–5 against rubrics grounded in real reviewer signals. The metric is demonstrated on five representative capital-markets workflows using public and synthetic data, scoring outputs from four models across three model families with four independent judges to control bias. Results show frontier closed-source models cluster closely in reliability scores, outperforming an open-weights baseline especially in retrieval and synthesis tasks. Decision Usefulness emerges as the most discriminative and reliable dimension for deployment readiness. CM-LRS thus provides a comprehensive, deployment-focused evaluation framework for trustworthy LLM use in regulated financial domains.

methodology.title: Seven-Dimension Rubric
methodology.detail: CM-LRS evaluates LLM outputs on seven dimensions: factual accuracy, evidence traceability, numerical consistency, workflow completeness, source discipline, decision usefulness, and reviewability/auditability. Each dimension is scored from 0 to 5 based on a rubric anchored on signals used by reviewers in regulated capital-markets environments.

methodology.title: Workflow-Output Layer Evaluation
methodology.detail: Unlike prior benchmarks that assess question-answer pairs, CM-LRS evaluates the entire workflow output, reflecting the actual deliverables bankers and analysts defend in front of regulators and counterparties.

methodology.title: Cross-Model and Cross-Judge Validation
methodology.detail: The framework is applied to five capital-markets workflows using four LLMs (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Llama 3.3 70B) scored by four independent judges spanning three model families to control for self- and family-bias.

methodology.title: Aggregate and Tunable Scoring
methodology.detail: Dimension scores are aggregated into a tunable composite CM-LRS score, allowing adaptation to specific workflow requirements and highlighting dimensions that require reviewer attention.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism or Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal mechanisms but relies on a rubric-based scoring system grounded in practical reviewer signals and cross-validation to assess reliability dimensions.

experiments.title: Five Capital-Markets Workflows
experiments.detail: CM-LRS is demonstrated on DCM transaction-terms extraction, precedent retrieval, issuer profile synthesis, M&A transaction-comparable reasoning, and ECM transaction-terms extraction workflows using public SEC EDGAR filings, a UK takeover release, and synthetic supplements.

experiments.title: Model and Judge Evaluation
experiments.detail: Outputs from four models (Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and Llama 3.3 70B) are scored by four independent LLM judges from three model families, including in-panel and out-of-panel judges, to mitigate bias.

experiments.title: Dimension-Level Scoring and Justifications
experiments.detail: Judges provide per-dimension scores (0–5) with textual justifications, enabling granular analysis of strengths and weaknesses per workflow and model, exemplified by a worked example scoring 4.86 aggregate.

findings.title: Frontier Models Cluster Closely
findings.detail: The three frontier closed-source models cluster within a 0.22-point band on four-judge averaged CM-LRS (Sonnet 4.6 = 4.31, Opus 4.7 = 4.30, GPT-5.5 = 4.09), indicating similar high reliability.

findings.title: Open-Weights Baseline Lags
findings.detail: The open-weights Llama 3.3 70B baseline scores 3.15 on average, roughly one point below frontier models, with the largest performance gaps in retrieval (2.23 points) and synthesis (2.15 points) workflows.

findings.title: Decision Usefulness is Most Discriminative
findings.detail: Decision Usefulness (D6) shows the widest cross-model dispersion (up to 4.0 points on issuer profiling) and strong inter-judge agreement (mean Pearson r = 0.52), making it the clearest indicator of production readiness.

findings.title: Extraction Workflows Show Smaller Gaps
findings.detail: Performance gaps between frontier and baseline models are smaller on extraction workflows (0.84 points), suggesting these tasks are less challenging for open-weights models.

findings.title: Rubric Enables Rapid Review
findings.detail: The rubric’s per-dimension scores and justifications allow reviewers to quickly identify and verify specific claims, facilitating efficient auditability and reviewability.

contributions: Introduction of CM-LRS, a seven-dimension rubric evaluating LLM outputs at the workflow-output layer for capital-markets applications.
Demonstration of CM-LRS on five representative capital-markets workflows with public and synthetic data.
Cross-model and cross-judge evaluation protocol controlling for self- and family-bias across three model families.
Identification of Decision Usefulness as a key dimension for deployment readiness with strong inter-judge reliability.
Public release of rubrics, prompts, and demonstration tasks to enable community extension and critique.
limitations: Lack of inter-rater reliability studies to quantify consistency across judges beyond Pearson correlations.
Current rubric weights and aggregation are not calibrated against real-world reviewer decisions or deployment outcomes.
Evaluation limited to extraction, retrieval, synthesis, and reasoning workflows; drafting workflows remain unaddressed.
No formal mechanistic or causal model underpinning the rubric scoring is provided.
open_questions: How can CM-LRS dimension weights be calibrated against actual deployment decisions and regulatory outcomes?
What is the inter-rater reliability of CM-LRS across a broader set of human reviewers beyond LLM judges?
Can CM-LRS be extended effectively to drafting workflows and other regulated domains beyond capital markets?
How do different prompt engineering or retrieval augmentation strategies impact CM-LRS scores across workflows?

papers.title: From Static Bibliometrics to Dynamic Knowledge Graphs: An LLM-Powered Framework for Modernizing Science, Technology, and Innovation (STI) Analytics
papers.abstract: Bibliometric indicators - citation counts, h-indexes, co-authorship networks - have long anchored science, technology, and innovation (STI) analytics, yet suffer from temporal lag, semantic shallowness, and an inability to capture the non-linear dynamics of contemporary knowledge ecosystems. Dynamic knowledge graphs and large language models (LLMs) have each been proposed as remedies, but neither is sufficient alone: existing scholarly knowledge graphs remain largely static, while LLM-driven pipelines are prone to hallucination, opacity, and corpus bias without structured grounding. This paper proposes a hybrid, symbolic-first framework integrating all three traditions under explicit methodological constraint. Organized across five layers - an open scholarly data backbone, a dynamic versioned knowledge graph, a constrained LLM-assisted semantic augmentation layer, a multi-layer validation pipeline, and an analytics layer - the framework positions LLMs strictly as generators of provisional candidate enrichments. Candidates become analytically admissible only after passing structural, evidentiary, comparative, and selective expert validation, with full provenance recorded at every stage. The analytics layer supports both established bibliometric indicators and extended graph-based analyses, including trend emergence detection, science-to-technology pathway mapping, and policy-oriented gap analysis. The framework's central theoretical contribution is treating validation as the mediating principle between semantic flexibility and epistemic discipline, enabling STI analytics that is semantically richer and temporally more responsive than static bibliometrics while remaining aligned with the evidentiary standards of science-of-science research. Governance considerations addressing reproducibility, bias, and auditability are also discussed.

summary.takeaway: A hybrid, symbolic-first framework integrating bibliometric baselines, dynamic knowledge graphs, and constrained LLM semantic augmentation enables semantically richer, temporally responsive, and methodologically accountable STI analytics.
summary.problem: Traditional bibliometric indicators are temporally lagged, semantically shallow, and inadequate for capturing the nonlinear, dynamic knowledge flows in modern science, technology, and innovation ecosystems.
