AGFO adaptively gates the activation of feedback rewards during RL training, invoking the expensive LLM-as-judge only every n steps and only when feedback quality is below a threshold, reducing overhead by 83%.
Score-only RL training degrades feedback quality significantly (RFE score drops from 0.6978 to 0.5608), whereas joint optimization with AGFO maintains high feedback quality comparable to GPT-5.5.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the challenge of jointly optimizing automated essay scoring (AES) and automated feedback generation (AFG) using large language models (LLMs). Prior work focused on prompt engineering or supervised fine-tuning, lacking systematic reinforcement learning (RL) approaches and scalable feedback evaluation. The authors propose RLAES, which integrates a novel Rubric-based Feedback Evaluation (RFE) framework comprising 166 binary rubric items assessed by an LLM-as-judge, enabling interpretable and measurable feedback quality. To mitigate the computational cost of frequent feedback evaluation, Adaptive Gated Feedback Optimization (AGFO) selectively activates feedback rewards during RL training based on a threshold, reducing overhead by 83%. Additionally, Adjacent Contrastive Reasoning (ACR) improves ordinal score calibration by contrasting adjacent score levels. Experiments on the ASAP dataset demonstrate that RLAES-AGFO achieves superior scoring performance (QWK=0.803) among LLM-based methods and maintains feedback quality comparable to GPT-5.5, avoiding the feedback degradation observed in score-only RL. This unified RL framework advances trustworthy AES and AFG by providing scalable, interpretable, and jointly optimized scoring and feedback generation.

methodology.title: Rubric-Based Feedback Evaluation (RFE)
methodology.detail: RFE decomposes feedback quality into 166 fine-grained binary rubric items, each evaluated independently by an LLM-as-judge, producing a structured reward signal for RL. This framework enables interpretable, essay-grounded feedback evaluation that aligns with expert preferences.

methodology.title: Adaptive Gated Feedback Optimization (AGFO)
methodology.detail: AGFO uses Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to jointly optimize scoring and feedback rewards. It adaptively gates feedback reward activation every n steps, invoking the LLM-as-judge only if the feedback reward falls below a threshold τ, reducing computational cost while maintaining feedback quality.

methodology.title: Adjacent Contrastive Reasoning (ACR)
methodology.detail: ACR improves ordinal score calibration by explicitly contrasting model outputs at adjacent score levels, enhancing the model's ability to discriminate fine-grained score differences and improving scoring accuracy.

methodology.title: Reinforcement Learning Setup
methodology.detail: The model is trained with GRPO using a combined reward of score accuracy and feedback quality. The score reward is scaled by a factor α and normalized by the score range. Feedback rewards are computed via RFE. Training uses LoRA for parameter-efficient fine-tuning on Qwen3.5-9B with a batch size of 8, learning rate 2e-5, and cosine scheduler.

mechanism.title: Rubric Reward Computation
mechanism.detail: The rubric reward r(x, ŷ) is computed as a weighted average of binary rubric item indicators cj(x, ŷ), where each cj is assigned by an LLM-as-judge independently. This decomposes complex feedback quality into assessable components, enabling structured RL rewards.

mechanism.title: Adaptive Gating Mechanism
mechanism.detail: Every n training steps, the feedback reward is computed; if it is below threshold τ, the gate remains open to optimize feedback; otherwise, feedback reward is skipped to save computation. This balances training efficiency and feedback quality.

experiments.title: Dataset and Evaluation
experiments.detail: Experiments use the ASAP dataset with 12,978 essays across 8 prompts, employing five-fold cross-validation with joint prompt training. Scoring is evaluated by quadratic weighted kappa (QWK), and feedback quality by RFE scores using GPT-5.5 as the LLM judge.

experiments.title: Baselines
experiments.detail: Baselines include LLM prompt engineering methods (GPT-3.5, GPT-4 with rubric and few-shot prompting, Llama-3-8B-Instruct) and post-training methods. The base model for RLAES is Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuned with LoRA.

experiments.title: Training Setup
experiments.detail: RLAES is trained for 25 epochs with GRPO, batch size 8, learning rate 2e-5, and temperature 0.9 for rollout sampling. Feedback reward weight λf=1, score scaling α=0.1, gating period n=30, and threshold τ=0.8.

findings.title: Superior Scoring Performance
findings.detail: RLAES-AGFO achieves a QWK of 0.803 on ASAP, outperforming all LLM-based baselines including GPT-4 variants and prompt engineering methods.

findings.title: Maintained Feedback Quality
findings.detail: RLAES-AGFO attains an average RFE feedback score of 0.8399, comparable to GPT-5.5's 0.8334, while score-only RL degrades feedback quality significantly to 0.5608.

findings.title: Efficiency Gains
findings.detail: AGFO reduces the computational cost of feedback evaluation by approximately 83% compared to full feedback optimization, enabling practical RL training with rubric rewards.

findings.title: Joint Optimization Benefits
findings.detail: Joint optimization of scoring and feedback rewards via AGFO improves both scoring accuracy and feedback quality without trade-offs, unlike score-only RL.

contributions: Proposed RLAES, a unified RL framework jointly optimizing AES and AFG with rubric-based rewards.
Developed Rubric-based Feedback Evaluation (RFE) with 166 binary rubric items and LLM-as-judge for interpretable feedback quality measurement.
Introduced Adaptive Gated Feedback Optimization (AGFO) to reduce feedback evaluation overhead during RL training.
Designed Adjacent Contrastive Reasoning (ACR) to improve ordinal score calibration.
Demonstrated state-of-the-art scoring and high-quality feedback generation on the ASAP benchmark.
limitations: Feedback evaluation using LLM-as-judge is computationally expensive, necessitating gating mechanisms.
Feedback evaluation was conducted on a single fold due to budget constraints, limiting robustness assessment.
The approach depends on the quality and coverage of the predefined rubric items, which may not capture all feedback nuances.
No explicit mechanism or theoretical analysis is provided for the interaction between scoring and feedback rewards.
open_questions: How well does RLAES generalize to other essay datasets or languages beyond ASAP?
Can the rubric-based evaluation framework be extended or adapted to other open-ended NLP tasks?
What are the effects of different rubric item designs or weighting schemes on feedback quality and scoring accuracy?
How can human-in-the-loop feedback be integrated to further improve rubric reward reliability and reduce bias?

papers.title: Inference-Time Steering for Cross-Lingual Factual Consistency in LLMs
papers.abstract: Although Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate remarkable multilingual fluency, their internal knowledge representations remain disproportionately biased toward high-resource languages. This leads to cross-lingual factual inconsistency, where they shift their empirical answer distributions based solely on the prompt language. We investigate whether these biases can be mitigated at inference time, forcing an English-prompted model to answer as if it were queried in target languages (German, Spanish, Bulgarian), and evaluate four intervention strategies: zero-shot contextual steering (persona prompting), internal representation manipulation via Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), and lightweight weight modification via Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) trained on benchmark-derived factual data as well as conceptual generalization data. To assess alignment, we curate a multilingual factual dataset alongside a novel generalization benchmark comprising culturally rooted queries to determine whether factual interventions transfer to broader target-centric preferences. Experiments on Gemma 3 12B Instruct reveal persona prompting to be the strongest overall intervention, balancing efficacy, safety, and out-of-domain generalization. While CAA yields sharp inconsistency benchmark shifts, it is configuration-sensitive and risks knowledge degradation. DPO-based adapters offer permanent, yet narrower and less transferable gains. These findings suggest that cross-lingual inconsistency is at least partly a selection problem, and that simple contextual interventions may outperform more invasive methods for robust, transferable alignment.
papers.comment: 8 pages (21 in total), 2 figures, 4 tables. Original manuscript for a Guided Research project conducted at the Technical University of Munich, detailing the complete methodology, full data pipeline, and comprehensive experimental results. A related, condensed subset of this work was subsequently adapted and published at the StereACuLT 2026 workshop

summary.takeaway: Zero-shot persona prompting effectively mitigates cross-lingual factual inconsistency in LLMs at inference time, outperforming deeper mechanistic and parameter-based interventions in robustness and transferability.
summary.problem: Large Language Models exhibit cross-lingual factual inconsistency due to biased internal knowledge representations favoring high-resource languages, leading to unreliable multilingual factual recall.
summary.method: The paper evaluates four inference-time interventions—persona prompting, Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) adapters trained on benchmark and generalization data—to steer English-prompted LLMs toward target language factual preferences.
summary.evidence: Experiments on Gemma 3 12B Instruct show persona prompting consistently improves Jensen–Shannon distance and target preference metrics across German, Spanish, and Bulgarian, with statistically significant gains and superior safety and generalization compared to CAA and DPO.
summary.limitations: CAA steering is highly sensitive to hyperparameter tuning and risks knowledge degradation, while DPO adapters yield narrower, less transferable improvements; the study is limited to Gemma 3 12B and three target languages.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a rigorous comparative analysis of inference-time steering methods for cross-lingual factual alignment, offering practical, lightweight interventions relevant for trustworthy and efficient multilingual LLM deployment.

signals.text: Persona prompting significantly reduces cross-lingual Jensen–Shannon distance (JSD) in German and Bulgarian, achieving p < 0.05 and p < 0.01 respectively, indicating effective alignment of English-prompted model outputs with target language factual distributions.

Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) manipulates the model’s residual stream by adding a steering vector derived from contrast pairs of English-preferred and target-preferred completions, enabling mechanistic preference realignment during inference.

CAA’s effectiveness depends on precise layer selection and multiplier scaling, with optimal configurations varying by language; misconfiguration can degrade performance, as seen with Spanish under broad contrast pair settings where JSD worsened.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the problem of cross-lingual factual inconsistency in LLMs, where models biased toward English produce divergent factual answers when prompted in different languages. It hypothesizes that such biases can be mitigated at inference time by steering the model’s output distribution to reflect target language preferences without costly retraining. To test this, the authors curate a multilingual factual dataset and a novel cultural generalization benchmark, then evaluate four intervention strategies on Gemma 3 12B Instruct: zero-shot persona prompting, Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA), and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) adapters trained on benchmark and generalization data. Persona prompting, a shallow contextual intervention, consistently improves alignment metrics and generalizes well, suggesting the model already encodes target knowledge but defaults to English-centric answers. CAA, a mechanistic activation manipulation, achieves strong but fragile improvements sensitive to hyperparameters. DPO adapters provide permanent but narrower gains. These results support the view that cross-lingual inconsistency is partly a selection problem and that simple contextual cues can outperform more invasive methods for robust, transferable alignment.

methodology.title: Persona Prompting
methodology.detail: A zero-shot contextual steering method that augments English prompts with natural language instructions to adopt the perspective of a target language demographic, leveraging in-context learning to shift output distributions without modifying model parameters or activations.

methodology.title: Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA)
methodology.detail: An inference-time intervention that adds a directional steering vector to the model’s residual stream activations, computed from contrast pairs of English-preferred and target-preferred completions, to mechanistically realign the model’s internal representations toward target language preferences.

methodology.title: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) Adapters
methodology.detail: Lightweight parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapters trained on preference triples derived from benchmark or generalization datasets, optimizing the model to prefer target language completions over English-centric ones, enabling permanent but narrower alignment shifts.

methodology.title: Multilingual Factual Dataset and Generalization Benchmark
methodology.detail: A curated dataset of atomic factual triples across six languages designed for repeated-sampling evaluation of answer distributions, and a culturally rooted generalization benchmark with 50 second-person multiple-choice queries per target language to test transfer of interventions beyond benchmark facts.

mechanism.title: Cross-Lingual Factual Inconsistency as a Selection Problem
mechanism.detail: The paper posits that LLMs share a common semantic space for multilingual inputs but exhibit biased output distributions due to the final language transition step favoring English-centric knowledge; thus, inference-time interventions can steer output selection without altering underlying representations.

experiments.title: Baseline Cross-Lingual Inconsistency Measurement
experiments.detail: Evaluated four state-of-the-art LLMs (Gemma 3 12B, gpt-oss-20b, Qwen 3 30B-A3B, Llama 4 Maverick) on a multilingual factual benchmark using repeated open-ended sampling and Jensen–Shannon distance to quantify answer distribution shifts across English, German, Spanish, Bulgarian, Korean, and Swedish.

experiments.title: Intervention Evaluation on Gemma 3 12B Instruct
experiments.detail: Compared persona prompting, CAA steering, and DPO adapters trained on benchmark and generalization data across three contrast pair strategies (v0, v1, v2), measuring improvements in JSD and target preference metrics, statistical significance, and transfer to a novel cultural generalization benchmark.

findings.title: Effectiveness of Persona Prompting
findings.detail: Persona prompting improved cross-lingual alignment in 8 of 9 cases, with statistically significant JSD reductions for German (p < 0.05, CLES=0.705) and Bulgarian (p < 0.01, CLES=0.672–0.690), demonstrating that simple contextual cues can induce substantial preference shifts without parameter changes.

findings.title: CAA Steering Performance and Fragility
findings.detail: CAA improved JSD in 8 of 9 cases with large effect sizes for Bulgarian (p < 0.01, CLES=0.741) and German (p < 0.01, CLES=0.705), but required careful tuning of intervention layer and multiplier; broader contrast sets (v2) sometimes degraded performance, indicating sensitivity and risk of knowledge degradation.

findings.title: DPO Adapter Gains and Transfer
findings.detail: DPO adapters trained on benchmark-derived data provided permanent alignment improvements but with narrower scope and less transfer to out-of-benchmark cultural generalization compared to prompting, highlighting trade-offs between permanence and generality.

contributions: Curated a high-quality multilingual factual dataset spanning six languages for distributional evaluation of cross-lingual factual consistency.
Developed a novel culturally rooted generalization benchmark to test transfer of alignment interventions beyond benchmark-specific facts.
Conducted a rigorous comparative study of four inference-time steering methods—persona prompting, CAA, and two DPO adapter variants—on Gemma 3 12B Instruct.
Demonstrated that zero-shot persona prompting is the strongest overall intervention balancing efficacy, safety, and out-of-domain generalization.
Provided evidence that cross-lingual inconsistency is partly a selection problem addressable by simple contextual interventions rather than invasive parameter updates.
limitations: CAA steering is highly sensitive to hyperparameter choices and can degrade model knowledge if misconfigured.
DPO adapters yield narrower and less transferable gains compared to prompting, limiting their generalization to broader cultural contexts.
Experiments are limited to the Gemma 3 12B Instruct model and three target languages, restricting generalizability to other architectures or languages.
The study does not provide mechanistic explanations beyond the steering vector concept, leaving deeper causal understanding of cross-lingual bias unaddressed.
open_questions: Can inference-time steering methods be effectively generalized to larger or different LLM architectures beyond Gemma 3 12B?
How can the fragility and hyperparameter sensitivity of CAA be mitigated to ensure safe and robust mechanistic interventions?
What are the underlying representational mechanisms causing cross-lingual factual inconsistency beyond selection bias?
Can permanent parameter updates be designed to combine the transferability of prompting with the permanence of DPO adapters?

papers.title: Adopting Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards for Molecular Generation
papers.abstract: Leveraging large language models (LLMs) for molecular generation has shown remarkable potential in chemical and drug design. Current methods primarily rely on supervised training or fine-tuning with limited datasets, which are insufficient to capture complex molecular design objectives. While some approaches attempt to guide generation toward specific goals, they often lack direct optimization mechanisms, making it difficult to align generated molecules with desired properties. To tackle these challenges, we propose \textbf{LLMol}, a principled reinforcement learning framework that directly incorporates verifiable rewards for targeted molecule generation. The key insight is to formulate molecular design as a goal-conditioned sequence prediction task, where verifiable rewards serve as explicit supervision to drive generation toward desired objectives. LLMol follows a two-stage training paradigm combining supervised learning and reinforcement learning. In the first stage, large language models are supervised fine-tuned to capture chemical syntax and molecular distributions. In the second stage, we introduce Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), which directly integrates property-based reward signals to guide molecular generation toward task-specific objectives. To address the high variance and instability common in discrete sequence optimization, we adopt Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a stable on-policy algorithm that smooths reward signals and improves training robustness. This framework enables LLMol to effectively handle a range of molecular design tasks, including single-property targeting (e.g., penalized logP, QED) and structure-constrained optimization. Experimental results demonstrate that LLMol consistently outperforms existing methods, achieving higher success rates and improved efficiency across diverse molecular benchmarks.

summary.takeaway: LLMol leverages a two-stage training paradigm combining supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, achieving state-of-the-art molecular generation performance on multiple property optimization tasks.
summary.problem: Existing LLM-based molecular generation methods lack direct optimization mechanisms to align generated molecules with complex, multi-objective chemical design goals.
summary.method: LLMol formulates molecular design as a goal-conditioned sequence prediction task and applies Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to optimize property-based reward signals.
summary.evidence: Experimental results on the ZINC250K dataset show LLMol achieves a 46.91% success rate in logP targeting, significantly outperforming baselines, while maintaining high validity, novelty, and diversity.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed ablation studies isolating the contributions of RLVR components or extensive evaluation on multi-property optimization beyond single-property and similarity-constrained tasks.
summary.why_for_you: LLMol’s integration of verifiable reward-driven reinforcement learning with large language models offers a robust and efficient approach to property-constrained molecular generation, relevant for advancing trustworthy and efficient LLM-based design.

signals.text: LLMol achieves a 46.91% success rate in generating molecules within a narrow logP range on ZINC250K, vastly outperforming the supervised fine-tuned model's 0.46% and prior baselines.

The Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) algorithm stabilizes reinforcement learning by smoothing reward signals and using group-based Monte Carlo rollouts, improving training robustness without requiring a critic model.
LLMol maintains high chemical diversity (0.893) close to the LIMO baseline (0.914) despite reinforcement learning optimization, indicating RLVR does not compromise exploration of molecular space.

deep_dive.overview: LLMol addresses the challenge of aligning molecular generation with complex chemical objectives by framing molecular design as a goal-conditioned sequence prediction problem. It first fine-tunes a large language model (Qwen-3, 4B parameters) on molecular string data (simplified SELFIES) to learn chemical syntax and distributions. Subsequently, it applies Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to directly optimize property-based reward functions, such as penalized logP and QED, using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to reduce variance and stabilize training. This two-stage approach enables precise control over molecular properties while preserving validity, novelty, and diversity. Experiments on the ZINC250K dataset demonstrate that LLMol significantly outperforms diverse baselines across multiple molecular generation tasks, achieving higher success rates and efficiency. The framework’s use of verifiable, deterministic rewards and stable policy optimization represents a principled advancement in LLM-driven molecular design.

methodology.title: Molecule Representation
methodology.detail: LLMol adopts a simplified SELFIES molecular string representation that removes square brackets and inserts spaces between semantic units, reducing token length and vocabulary complexity to improve LLM tokenization efficiency and modeling.

methodology.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
methodology.detail: The base Qwen-3 4B parameter LLM is fine-tuned on over 200,000 molecules from ZINC250K using LoRA to reduce trainable parameters. The objective is to learn chemical syntax and molecular distributions, enabling valid and novel molecule generation.

methodology.title: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR)
methodology.detail: RLVR integrates explicit property-based reward functions computed via RDKit to guide molecular generation toward task-specific objectives. The policy is optimized using GRPO, an on-policy algorithm that uses group-based Monte Carlo rollouts and reward whitening to stabilize training.

methodology.title: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)
methodology.detail: GRPO estimates relative advantages by comparing grouped rollout returns, avoiding the need for a critic model. It standardizes rewards through whitening and supports deterministic verifiable rewards, improving stability and exploration in discrete sequence optimization.

mechanism.title: Reward-Driven Goal-Conditioned Sequence Prediction
mechanism.detail: Molecular generation is formulated as a goal-conditioned sequence prediction task where the LLM generates molecular strings conditioned on desired property values. Verifiable reward functions provide explicit supervision signals to guide the policy toward molecules satisfying these properties.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanistic Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal mechanistic equations or causal models but describes the use of verifiable reward functions and policy optimization algorithms to achieve property alignment.

experiments.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning Evaluation on ZINC250K
experiments.detail: LLMol’s SFT stage is evaluated on validity, novelty, and diversity metrics against baselines such as JT-VAE, LIMO, and MOLGEN, achieving 100% validity and novelty, and competitive diversity (0.8473).

experiments.title: LogP Targeting Task
experiments.detail: LLMol is evaluated on generating molecules within a narrow logP range, achieving a 46.91% success rate compared to 0.46% for SFT-only and outperforming prior methods, while maintaining high diversity (0.893).

experiments.title: QED and Penalized logP Maximization
experiments.detail: LLMol optimizes drug-likeness metrics (QED and penalized logP) using RLVR, outperforming baselines in maximum scores and efficiency, with training times significantly reduced (2 hours for LLMol vs. up to 30 hours for others).

experiments.title: Similarity-Constrained Optimization
experiments.detail: LLMol demonstrates the ability to improve molecular properties while preserving structural similarity to known compounds, validating its applicability to constrained molecular design tasks.

findings.title: RLVR Significantly Improves Property Targeting
findings.detail: In logP targeting, RL-augmented LLMol achieves a 46.91% success rate, a 100x improvement over supervised fine-tuning alone (0.46%), demonstrating the effectiveness of verifiable reward integration.

findings.title: High Validity and Novelty Maintained
findings.detail: LLMol achieves 100% validity and novelty on ZINC250K, indicating that reinforcement learning does not degrade chemical correctness or exploration of novel molecules.

findings.title: Training Efficiency Gains
findings.detail: LLMol completes reinforcement learning training in approximately 2 hours, substantially faster than several baselines requiring up to 30 hours, highlighting the efficiency of GRPO and LoRA parameter reduction.

findings.title: Diversity Preservation
findings.detail: Despite optimization for specific properties, LLMol maintains a high diversity score (0.893), close to the LIMO baseline (0.914), ensuring broad chemical space exploration.

contributions: Proposed LLMol, a two-stage molecular generation framework combining supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
Introduced Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) to directly optimize property-based reward functions in molecular generation.
Developed Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), a stable on-policy RL algorithm that smooths reward signals and avoids critic models.
Demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on multiple molecular design tasks including logP targeting, QED maximization, and similarity-constrained optimization.
Adopted a simplified SELFIES representation to improve tokenization efficiency for LLM-based molecular modeling.
limitations: Lack of ablation studies isolating the impact of GRPO and reward design on final performance.
Limited evaluation on multi-property or multi-objective optimization beyond single-property and similarity constraints.
No detailed analysis of failure modes or robustness to noisy or conflicting reward signals.
Absence of mechanistic or theoretical analysis explaining why GRPO outperforms other RL algorithms in this context.
open_questions: How does LLMol perform on multi-objective molecular optimization tasks involving conflicting property constraints?
Can the GRPO algorithm be generalized or adapted to other discrete sequence generation domains beyond molecular design?
What are the effects of different verifiable reward function designs on the stability and convergence of RLVR?
How robust is LLMol to noisy or approximate reward signals derived from imperfect property predictors?

papers.title: AdaFlash: Adaptive Speculative Decoding via On-Policy Distilled Diffusion Drafters
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding, in which a lightweight draft model first generates a draft sequence that is then verified in parallel by the target model, has become a prevalent paradigm for accelerating large language model inference. Recent work such as DFlash further boosts drafting efficiency by leveraging diffusion drafters, whose parallel denoising mechanism enables draft generation in a single forward pass. In this work, we uncover a central pitfall of diffusion drafters: bidirectional attention is a double-edged sword. On one hand, it endows the model with parallel generation and global contextual modeling capabilities; on the other hand, this inherent global dependency introduces high variance at both the domain-level and the token-level: acceptance rates fluctuate substantially across different domains, and draft token quality also varies heterogeneously at different token positions. To tackle this issue, we propose AdaFlash framework, comprising two components: (i) an on-policy distillation (OPD) algorithm with reverse-KL divergence tailored for diffusion drafters, bringing stable convergence and effectively reducing domain-level variance; and (ii) an adaptive length head that dynamically adjusts the candidate sequence length on the fly, substantially lowering the verification cost of the target model and handling token-level variance. Experiments demonstrate that AdaFlash consistently improves speedup rate during deployment, with especially significant gains in high-concurrency scenarios, achieving up to approximately 66% higher throughput than previous state-of-the-art methods.

summary.takeaway: AdaFlash improves speculative decoding efficiency by using on-policy distillation and adaptive length adjustment to reduce variance in diffusion drafters, achieving up to 66% higher throughput than prior methods.
summary.problem: Diffusion drafters with bidirectional attention suffer from high domain-level and token-level variance, causing unstable acceptance rates and inefficient verification costs in speculative decoding.
summary.method: AdaFlash employs an on-policy distillation algorithm with reverse-KL divergence and entry-wise clipping to stabilize training and an adaptive length head to dynamically adjust draft sequence length during inference.
summary.evidence: Experiments on eight diverse datasets with Qwen3 models demonstrate AdaFlash consistently outperforms baselines like DFlash and OSD, achieving higher speedups and accepted lengths, especially under high concurrency.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed analysis on the impact of AdaFlash on model quality beyond acceptance rates, nor does it explore the effect of different diffusion drafter architectures extensively.
summary.why_for_you: AdaFlash offers a novel on-policy distillation approach tailored for diffusion-based speculative decoding, addressing variance issues critical for stable and efficient on-policy distillation in large language models.

signals.text: Bidirectional attention in diffusion drafters enables parallel generation but introduces high variance in acceptance rates across domains and token positions, leading to unstable speculative decoding performance.

AdaFlash's on-policy distillation uses a reverse-KL divergence loss with entry-wise divergence clipping and a mixture loss incorporating hard-label supervision on the target top-1 token to reduce domain-level variance and stabilize convergence.

Adaptive length head dynamically adjusts the candidate draft length per request, reducing verification cost by avoiding wasted computation on tokens unlikely to be accepted, thus handling token-level variance effectively.

deep_dive.overview: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference by generating draft sequences with a lightweight model and verifying them in parallel with a target model. Diffusion drafters, leveraging bidirectional attention and parallel denoising, enable one-step draft generation but suffer from high variance in acceptance rates both across domains and token positions. This variance degrades speedup and wastes computation. AdaFlash addresses these issues with two key innovations: an on-policy distillation algorithm tailored for diffusion drafters that uses reverse-KL divergence with entry-wise clipping and a mixture loss to stabilize training and reduce domain-level variance; and an adaptive length head that dynamically adjusts draft sequence length to reduce verification overhead and handle token-level variance. Extensive experiments on eight benchmark datasets and multiple concurrency levels demonstrate AdaFlash consistently outperforms prior methods like DFlash and OSD, achieving up to 66% higher throughput, especially in high-concurrency scenarios. Ablations confirm the necessity of both components and on-policy updates for optimal performance.

methodology.title: On-Policy Distillation (OPD)
methodology.detail: OPD trains the diffusion drafter online using reverse-KL divergence loss tailored for diffusion models, incorporating entry-wise divergence clipping to prevent large gradient variance and a mixture loss that adds hard-label supervision on the target model's top-1 token, stabilizing convergence and reducing domain-level variance.

methodology.title: Adaptive Length Head
methodology.detail: A lightweight module predicts the optimal candidate draft length dynamically per input during inference, allowing the system to reduce verification cost by truncating draft sequences where acceptance probability is low, thus addressing token-level variance in acceptance rates.

methodology.title: Diffusion Drafter Architecture
methodology.detail: The diffusion drafter uses bidirectional attention and a mask-and-denoise mechanism to generate all draft tokens in a single forward pass, significantly reducing per-token drafting overhead compared to autoregressive drafters.

methodology.title: Online Update Mechanism
methodology.detail: AdaFlash updates the drafter parameters during deployment using on-policy samples from the target model, enabling adaptation to domain shifts and maintaining high acceptance rates across diverse tasks.

mechanism.title: Variance Induced by Bidirectional Attention
mechanism.detail: Bidirectional attention enables global context modeling and parallel token generation but creates global dependencies that increase variance in draft quality both across domains and token positions, leading to fluctuating acceptance rates and inefficiencies in speculative decoding.

experiments.title: Benchmark Evaluation
experiments.detail: AdaFlash was evaluated on eight datasets spanning math reasoning (MathQA, GSM8K), code generation (OpenCodeInstruct, CodeAlpaca), dialogue (ShareGPT), and mixed domains (Blend), using Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B as target models, measuring speedup relative to autoregressive decoding and average accepted length under concurrency levels from 1 to 128.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies
experiments.detail: Ablations on GSM8K with Qwen3-8B showed that entry-wise divergence clipping and mixture OPD loss each improve accepted length and speedup, while the adaptive length head is critical for maintaining speedup at high concurrency by dynamically adjusting verification length.

experiments.title: Hardware Generalization
experiments.detail: AdaFlash was tested on Huawei Ascend 910C NPU with Qwen3-8B, demonstrating consistent speedup gains over DFlash across concurrency levels, confirming its applicability beyond GPU hardware.

experiments.title: Decoding Temperature Effects
experiments.detail: Evaluations under greedy decoding (T=0) and stochastic sampling (T=1) showed that although sampling reduces average accepted length, AdaFlash maintains substantial speedup, indicating robustness across decoding regimes.

experiments.title: From-Scratch Training
experiments.detail: AdaFlash can train diffusion drafters from scratch without pre-trained weights, achieving higher accepted length and speedup than the EAGLE-3 baseline on GSM8K, demonstrating its utility beyond online adaptation.

findings.title: Domain-Level Variance Reduction
findings.detail: On-policy distillation with reverse-KL and divergence clipping significantly reduces domain-level acceptance rate variance, improving stable convergence and speedup across diverse domains.

findings.title: Token-Level Variance Mitigation
findings.detail: The adaptive length head effectively lowers verification cost by dynamically adjusting draft length, preventing wasted computation on low-acceptance tokens and maintaining speedup at high concurrency.

findings.title: Superior Speedup Performance
findings.detail: AdaFlash achieves up to 5.32× speedup at concurrency 1 and maintains 1.34× speedup at concurrency 128 on MathQA with Qwen3-8B, outperforming DFlash and OSD baselines consistently across datasets.

findings.title: Robustness Across Hardware and Decoding Modes
findings.detail: AdaFlash's speedup gains generalize to NPU hardware and remain substantial under both greedy and stochastic decoding, confirming its practical deployment viability.

findings.title: Effective From-Scratch Training
findings.detail: Training a diffusion drafter from scratch with AdaFlash yields a 1.84× speedup and higher accepted length than EAGLE-3, validating the method's effectiveness beyond fine-tuning.

contributions: Identification of high domain-level and token-level variance as a central pitfall in diffusion-based speculative decoding.
Development of an on-policy distillation algorithm with reverse-KL divergence and entry-wise clipping tailored for diffusion drafters.
Introduction of an adaptive length head to dynamically adjust draft sequence length during inference.
Comprehensive empirical validation demonstrating significant speedup and robustness across datasets, concurrency levels, hardware, and decoding regimes.
Demonstration of AdaFlash's capability for both online adaptation and from-scratch training of diffusion drafters.
limitations: Lack of detailed analysis on the impact of AdaFlash on final output quality metrics beyond acceptance rates and speedup.
Limited exploration of different diffusion drafter architectures or alternative distillation losses.
No explicit discussion on the computational overhead introduced by the adaptive length head module.
Absence of theoretical guarantees or formal analysis of convergence properties for the on-policy distillation algorithm.
open_questions: How does AdaFlash affect the semantic or factual quality of generated sequences beyond acceptance rate metrics?
Can the on-policy distillation framework be extended to other non-autoregressive or hybrid drafting architectures?
What are the trade-offs between adaptive length prediction accuracy and computational overhead in large-scale deployments?
How does AdaFlash perform under extreme domain shifts or in zero-shot generalization scenarios?

papers.title: Benchmarking Generalization in Financial Statement Fraud Detection: robust evaluation and novel tasks
papers.abstract: Financial statement fraud detection (FSFD) is crucial for market integrity but faces challenges from increasingly sophisticated schemes and under-utilized textual data in financial reports. Existing methods often rely on random data splits, leading to overoptimistic performance estimates that do not reflect real-world generalization to new companies or future periods. To address this recurring problem with the state of the art, we propose a robust FSFD framework leveraging Large Language Models (LLMs) to integrate both structured financial data and unstructured textual information from financial reports. We provide a more realistic evaluation through a novel and challenging benchmark task called Company-Isolated FSFD (CI-FSFD). We construct and make publicly available a comprehensive U.S. company dataset combining financial statements, summarized MD&A text, and fraud labels. Our approach achieves the best performance on the challenging CI-FSFD task, demonstrating the critical value of textual data and robust evaluation for reliable financial fraud detection.

summary.takeaway: The paper introduces a novel Company-Isolated FSFD (CI-FSFD) benchmark and demonstrates that fine-tuned LLMs leveraging both structured financial data and summarized MD&A text outperform baselines in realistic fraud detection scenarios.
summary.problem: Existing financial statement fraud detection methods rely on random data splits that inflate performance and fail to generalize to unseen companies or future periods.
summary.method: The authors propose a robust FSFD framework integrating structured financial features with LLM-processed summarized MD&A text, evaluated under a novel company-isolated data split to ensure realistic generalization.
summary.evidence: Experiments on a newly constructed multimodal U.S. company dataset show that the fine-tuned Fino-1 8B LLM model achieves top performance on the challenging CI-FSFD task, outperforming logistic regression, MLP, tree ensembles, and adapted RCMA baselines.
summary.limitations: The paper notes the poor zero-shot performance of pretrained LLMs on FSFD, indicating the necessity of task-specific fine-tuning and does not provide mechanistic explanations for model decisions.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a rigorous evaluation framework and a multimodal dataset that enable statistically sound generalization assessment of LLM-based FSFD models, directly relevant to statistical theory and robustness in LLM applications.

signals.text: The novel CI-FSFD task enforces company isolation in data splits, preventing leakage of company-specific patterns and yielding more realistic generalization metrics compared to random splits.

The LLM-based framework combines 122 engineered financial features with summarized MD&A text processed by fine-tuned LLMs, enabling multimodal fraud classification that surpasses traditional baselines.
Zero-shot evaluation of pretrained LLMs on FSFD tasks shows poor performance, underscoring the importance of fine-tuning on domain-specific multimodal data for effective fraud detection.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the critical issue of overoptimistic performance in financial statement fraud detection caused by random data splits that allow models to memorize company-specific patterns. To overcome this, the authors propose the Company-Isolated FSFD (CI-FSFD) task, which enforces strict separation of companies between training and testing folds, thus better simulating real-world deployment scenarios. They construct a comprehensive U.S. company dataset integrating structured financial indicators with unstructured textual data from Management Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) sections, linked to fraud labels from SEC AAERs. Their method leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) fine-tuned to process summarized MD&A text alongside structured features, enabling robust multimodal fraud classification. Experimental results demonstrate that their LLM-based approach, particularly the fine-tuned Fino-1 8B model, achieves superior performance on the CI-FSFD benchmark compared to logistic regression, MLP, tree-based ensembles, and an adapted RCMA model. The study highlights the critical role of textual data and robust evaluation protocols in advancing reliable financial fraud detection.

methodology.title: Company-Isolated Data Splitting
methodology.detail: The dataset of 10,159 firm-quarter observations is split into 5 folds ensuring that all data from a given company is exclusively in either training or testing sets within each fold, preserving industry distribution and fraud ratio (~5%). This prevents leakage of company-specific patterns.

methodology.title: Multimodal Dataset Construction
methodology.detail: Structured financial data (122 engineered features) is combined with summarized textual data from MD&A sections processed by LLM-based summarization. Fraud labels are derived from SEC AAERs through a two-stage, manually audited temporal linking process ensuring high-fidelity ground truth.

methodology.title: LLM-based Fraud Detection Framework
methodology.detail: A fine-tuned LLM model (Fino-1 8B) processes summarized MD&A text and integrates it with structured financial features for binary fraud classification. The model is trained under the CI-FSFD setting to optimize detection performance.

methodology.title: Baseline Models and Hyperparameter Optimization
methodology.detail: Baselines include LR-DECHOW logistic regression, MLP, Random Forest, LightGBM, XGBoost, and an adapted RCMA model. Hyperparameters are optimized via Bayesian optimization (Hyperopt) maximizing average AUC over validation folds.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide mechanistic or theoretical explanations for how LLMs integrate textual and structured data or for the causal factors behind improved fraud detection performance.

experiments.title: Evaluation on Classic FSFD vs CI-FSFD
experiments.detail: Models are evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation under both random splits (Classic FSFD) and company-isolated splits (CI-FSFD) on the constructed dataset, measuring AUC to assess generalization.

experiments.title: Baseline Comparisons
experiments.detail: The LLM-based approach is benchmarked against logistic regression (LR-DECHOW), MLP, Random Forest, LightGBM, XGBoost, and an adapted RCMA model, all trained on structured features, with and without textual data.

experiments.title: Zero-shot LLM Evaluation
experiments.detail: Pretrained LLMs are evaluated in zero-shot mode on FSFD tasks, showing poor performance, highlighting the necessity of fine-tuning on domain-specific multimodal data.

findings.title: Company Isolation Reduces Inflated Performance
findings.detail: Performance metrics under CI-FSFD are significantly lower than under random splits, confirming that random splitting inflates results by allowing company-specific memorization.

findings.title: Textual Data Enhances Fraud Detection
findings.detail: Inclusion of summarized MD&A text improves detection performance, especially under CI-FSFD conditions where structured data alone is less informative.

findings.title: Fine-tuned LLMs Outperform Baselines
findings.detail: The fine-tuned Fino-1 8B LLM model achieves the highest AUC on CI-FSFD, surpassing traditional machine learning baselines and the adapted RCMA model.

findings.title: Zero-shot LLMs Are Ineffective
findings.detail: Pretrained LLMs without fine-tuning perform poorly on FSFD tasks, indicating that domain adaptation is critical for effective fraud detection.

contributions: Introduction of the Company-Isolated FSFD (CI-FSFD) task for realistic evaluation of fraud detection generalization.
Creation and public release of a comprehensive multimodal U.S. company dataset integrating structured financial data, summarized MD&A text, and high-fidelity fraud labels from SEC AAERs.
Development of an LLM-based framework that effectively combines structured and textual data for improved fraud detection.
Empirical demonstration that fine-tuned LLMs outperform traditional baselines under robust evaluation settings.
limitations: The study does not provide mechanistic insights or theoretical explanations for the integration of textual and structured data by LLMs.
Zero-shot LLM performance is poor, indicating reliance on fine-tuning which may limit out-of-domain generalization.
The evaluation focuses on U.S. companies and SEC AAER labels, which may limit applicability to other regulatory environments or fraud types.
Details on computational costs and scalability of the LLM-based approach are not discussed.
open_questions: How can mechanistic understanding of LLM multimodal integration improve interpretability and trust in FSFD models?
Can zero-shot or few-shot LLM capabilities be enhanced to reduce dependence on extensive fine-tuning for fraud detection?
How does the approach generalize to international datasets or different regulatory contexts beyond U.S. SEC AAERs?
What are the trade-offs between model complexity, interpretability, and deployment feasibility in real-world FSFD systems?

papers.title: A Geometric Perspective on Stabilizing Value Conflict Resolution
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle to navigate value conflicts when trained with the compressed scalar rewards of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). To address this challenge, we investigate how chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can help improve performance in this domain. Geometrically, we show that CoT correlates with further smoothing the model's loss landscape in its sharpest direction, helping resolve the optimization instability of traditional scalar rewards. We also demonstrate via relevant downstream benchmarks that value conflict-focused CoT may generalize to different kinds of moral reasoning, demonstrating that this CoT has the potential to be an effective mechanism for better moral reasoning. To capitalize on this potential, we create a new value conflict-focused CoT design that further smooths the sharpest direction of the loss landscape and increases moral reasoning performance. This finding shows that explicitly modifying and improving the design of reasoning dynamics offers a promising avenue for improving model performance on user requests with complex value conflicts, advancing pluralistic alignment in LLMs.
papers.comment: Accepted to ICML Workshop on High-Dimensional Learning Dynamics

summary.takeaway: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning smooths the sharpest direction of the LLM loss landscape, stabilizing value conflict resolution and improving moral reasoning performance.
summary.problem: LLMs trained with scalar rewards from RLHF struggle with unstable optimization and flawed moral reasoning when resolving conflicting human values.
summary.method: The authors design a value conflict-focused annealing-inspired CoT framework that mimics thermodynamic annealing phases to smooth the loss landscape and improve reasoning dynamics.
summary.evidence: Hessian top eigenvalue analysis shows annealing CoT achieves the lowest maximum curvature (λmax ≈ 1218), indicating the flattest minimum and best stability, with corresponding improved benchmark moral reasoning accuracy.
summary.limitations: Performance improvements from CoT are within the margin of error, and experiments focus on binary value conflicts without scaling to higher-dimensional pluralistic value spaces.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a geometric and mechanistic understanding of how CoT reasoning dynamics can be explicitly designed to stabilize LLM training on value conflicts, advancing trustworthy pluralistic alignment.

signals.text: Annealing-inspired CoT reduces the top Hessian eigenvalue from 4083 (base RLHF) to 1218, indicating a much smoother loss landscape in the sharpest direction and more stable optimization.

The annealing CoT method structures reasoning into three cognitive phases—high-temperature exploration, cooling trade-off weighing, and low-temperature decisive action—mimicking thermodynamic annealing to resolve value conflicts.

Benchmark results on moral reasoning datasets show annealing CoT outperforms base RLHF, base SFT, and standard CoT models, achieving the highest accuracy by a larger margin, demonstrating improved moral reasoning capability.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the instability and flawed moral reasoning in LLMs trained with scalar rewards from RLHF when resolving conflicting human values. The authors hypothesize that chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can mitigate this by smoothing the loss landscape's sharpest direction, stabilizing optimization. They draw an analogy to geometric frustration in physics and thermodynamic annealing, designing an annealing-inspired CoT framework with three cognitive phases to guide the model from broad exploration to decisive trade-offs. Empirical Hessian analysis confirms that annealing CoT achieves the flattest minima, reducing the top eigenvalue significantly compared to base RLHF and standard CoT. Correspondingly, moral reasoning benchmarks show improved performance, although some gains are within error margins. The work highlights the importance of explicitly designing reasoning dynamics to improve pluralistic alignment and suggests that internal reasoning design complements external reward engineering. Limitations include focus on binary value conflicts and lack of scaling to more complex pluralistic environments.

methodology.title: Data Generation
methodology.detail: Prompts eliciting value conflicts were generated using the ConflictScope pipeline with Claude 3.5 Sonnet, covering diverse conflicting value pairs. An ensemble of LLMs (GPT 5 Nano, Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite, Claude 4.5 Haiku) generated two reasoning traces per prompt: a standard unstructured CoT and an annealing-inspired CoT with structured cognitive phases.

methodology.title: Annealing-inspired CoT Design
methodology.detail: The CoT reasoning is structured into three phases: (1) high-temperature broad exploration weighing values, (2) cooling phase weighing trade-offs, and (3) low-temperature decisive action making hierarchical trade-offs. This design mimics thermodynamic annealing to resolve geometric frustration in value conflicts.

methodology.title: Loss Landscape Analysis
methodology.detail: The authors analyze the Hessian top eigenvalue (λmax) of the loss landscape to quantify sharpness and stability. Lower λmax indicates a flatter, more stable minimum. They visualize 3D eigenplane loss landscapes by perturbing model weights along top eigenvectors to qualitatively assess optimization geometry.

methodology.title: Model Training and Evaluation
methodology.detail: Models trained include base RLHF, base supervised fine-tuning (SFT), standard CoT, and annealing CoT. Evaluation metrics include Hessian eigenvalues for stability and benchmark accuracy on moral reasoning datasets such as MMLU Moral Scenarios, DecodingTrust Machine Ethics, and SafetyBench.

mechanism.title: Geometric Frustration and Annealing Analogy
mechanism.detail: Value conflict resolution in LLMs is analogous to geometric frustration in condensed matter physics, where incompatible constraints create a rugged, spiky energy landscape. Annealing, a thermodynamic process of heating and gradual cooling, resolves frustration by guiding the system to a stable, low-energy configuration. The annealing-inspired CoT framework translates this principle into cognitive phases that smooth the loss landscape and stabilize optimization.

experiments.title: Loss Landscape Visualization and Hessian Analysis
experiments.detail: The authors visualize 3D loss landscapes along top Hessian eigenvectors for base RLHF, base SFT, standard CoT, and annealing CoT models. Quantitatively, the top eigenvalue λmax decreases from 4083.87 (base RLHF) to 1218.04 (annealing CoT), indicating progressive smoothing and stability.

experiments.title: Moral Reasoning Benchmark Evaluation
experiments.detail: Models are evaluated on multiple moral reasoning benchmarks including MMLU Moral Scenarios, DecodingTrust Machine Ethics, and SafetyBench. Annealing CoT achieves the highest accuracy (e.g., 41.67% on MMLU Moral Scenarios) outperforming base RLHF and standard CoT, demonstrating improved moral reasoning performance.

findings.title: Scalar Reward Optimization Instability
findings.detail: Direct scalar reward optimization via RLHF leads to a sharp, cliff-like loss landscape with a high top Hessian eigenvalue (~4083), indicating unstable value conflict resolution.

findings.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning Smoothing Effect
findings.detail: Supervised fine-tuning on responses reduces the top eigenvalue to ~1402, smoothing the loss landscape into a ravine-like shape and improving stability.

findings.title: CoT Further Smooths Loss Landscape
findings.detail: Standard CoT reduces the top eigenvalue further to ~1346, and annealing CoT achieves the lowest eigenvalue (~1218), indicating the flattest minima and most stable optimization.

findings.title: Performance Gains on Moral Reasoning
findings.detail: Annealing CoT outperforms other methods on moral reasoning benchmarks by a larger margin, e.g., 41.67% accuracy on MMLU Moral Scenarios compared to 24.67% for base RLHF, demonstrating improved moral reasoning capability.

contributions: Demonstration that value conflict-focused annealing CoT design flattens the sharpest direction of the loss landscape and improves moral reasoning performance.
Geometric analysis linking CoT reasoning dynamics to smoothing of the loss landscape beyond supervised fine-tuning effects.
Release of a new dataset and code for standard and annealing CoT reasoning traces on value conflict prompts.
Empirical evidence that scalar reward optimization is ill-equipped for stable value conflict resolution in LLMs.
Proposal of explicit reasoning dynamics design as a promising avenue for advancing pluralistic alignment.
limitations: Performance improvements from CoT are within the margin of error, limiting statistical significance.
Experiments focus on binary value conflicts without scaling to N-dimensional pluralistic value spaces.
No formal mapping of trade-offs between internal reasoning design and external reward engineering is provided.
Mechanistic explanations are analogical and lack formal mathematical modeling.
open_questions: How can CoT methods be scaled from binary to N-dimensional pluralistic value conflicts in LLMs?
What are the formal trade-offs between improving value conflict resolution via internal reasoning dynamics versus external RLHF reward design?
Can the annealing-inspired CoT framework be generalized to other forms of complex reasoning beyond moral value conflicts?
What are the precise mechanistic underpinnings linking loss landscape geometry changes to improved moral reasoning performance?

papers.title: PPL-Factory: Task-Aware and Budget-Aware Data Selection from Language Modeling to Reasoning
papers.abstract: Not all training samples contribute equally to large language model fine-tuning. Selecting informative training samples can reduce the computational cost while preserving downstream performance. Many existing data selection methods rely on indirect heuristics, such as data quality, diversity or reasoning trace length. However, the effectiveness of these fixed criteria is task-dependent and difficult to generalize across diverse downstream tasks. Perplexity-based data selection provides a simple and model-aware solution to estimate the sample difficulty, but existing approaches typically score the entire training sequence and ignore the difference in learning objectives of language modeling and reasoning tasks. In this paper, we propose PPL-Factory, a simple and interpretable data selection framework that combines task-aware perplexity-based scores and data budget-aware selection criteria. Experiments on GSM8K demonstrate that PPL-Factory outperforms other state-of-the-art data selection methods using only $1\%$ of the training set. With $10\%$ of the data, PPL-Factory exceeds full-data fine-tuning accuracy by 0.9 on GSM8K and 4.8 on MATH. Overall, our results demonstrate that task-aware and budget-aware perplexity-based selection provides an effective and applicable approach for efficient fine-tuning.

summary.takeaway: PPL-Factory effectively selects informative training samples for LLM fine-tuning, enhancing performance while reducing computational costs.
summary.problem: Existing data selection methods struggle with task dependency and computational efficiency in LLM fine-tuning.
summary.method: PPL-Factory combines task-aware perplexity-based scoring with budget-aware selection criteria for improved data selection.
summary.evidence: Experiments show PPL-Factory outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving 0.9 and 4.8 accuracy improvements on GSM8K and MATH with only 10% of the data.
summary.limitations: The paper does not address the performance of PPL-Factory under extremely low data budgets beyond the tested scenarios.
summary.why_for_you: This framework is crucial for optimizing data selection in LLMs, aligning with your research interests in efficient data utilization.

signals.text: PPL-Factory outperforms existing methods, achieving a 0.9 accuracy increase on GSM8K and 4.8 on MATH using only 10% of the training data.
The framework employs a budget-aware selection criterion that adapts to varying data budgets, ensuring effective sample selection across tasks.
Perplexity scores are computed using negative log-likelihood (NLL), providing a model-aware measure of sample difficulty tailored for both language modeling and reasoning tasks.

deep_dive.overview: The research addresses the inefficiencies in data selection for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) by introducing PPL-Factory, a framework that integrates task-aware perplexity scoring with budget-aware selection criteria. This approach allows for the effective identification of informative training samples, significantly enhancing model performance while minimizing computational costs. The strongest evidence comes from experiments on GSM8K and MATH, where PPL-Factory demonstrated superior performance compared to existing methods, achieving notable accuracy improvements with a fraction of the training data.

methodology.title: Task-Aware NLL Scoring
methodology.detail: PPL-Factory computes task-specific NLL scores using a frozen pre-trained LLM, adapting the scoring mechanism to reflect the unique learning signals of language modeling and reasoning tasks.

methodology.title: Budget-Aware Selection
methodology.detail: The framework implements a selection strategy that adjusts based on the available data budget, prioritizing informative samples while maintaining coverage of the training distribution.

methodology.title: Data Selection Problem Formulation
methodology.detail: The selection process is framed as an informative-coverage maximization problem, balancing the utility of selected examples against the need to preserve the original data distribution.

mechanism.title: Perplexity-Based Scoring
mechanism.detail: PPL-Factory utilizes perplexity as a measure of difficulty, aligning with the next-token prediction objective, and adapts it for reasoning tasks by combining reasoning and answer NLL scores.

experiments.title: GSM8K Evaluation
experiments.detail: PPL-Factory was tested on the GSM8K dataset, achieving a 0.9 accuracy improvement over full-data fine-tuning using only 10% of the training set.

experiments.title: MATH Benchmarking
experiments.detail: In experiments on the MATH dataset, PPL-Factory outperformed full-data fine-tuning by 4.8 accuracy points while utilizing just 10% of the training data.

experiments.title: Comparison with Other Methods
experiments.detail: The framework was benchmarked against random, embedding-based, gradient-based, and influence-based methods, demonstrating superior performance with lower computational costs.

findings.title: Performance Improvement on GSM8K
findings.detail: PPL-Factory achieved a 0.9 accuracy increase on GSM8K with only 10% of the training data, showcasing its efficiency.

findings.title: Performance Improvement on MATH
findings.detail: The method exceeded full-data fine-tuning accuracy by 4.8 on MATH, indicating its effectiveness in selecting informative samples.

findings.title: Task-Aware Adaptation
findings.detail: The framework successfully adapts perplexity scoring for both language modeling and reasoning tasks, enhancing the relevance of selected samples.

contributions: Introduction of PPL-Factory, a novel data selection framework for LLM fine-tuning.
Demonstration of task-aware and budget-aware selection criteria that improve model performance.
Empirical validation of the framework on multiple datasets, establishing its effectiveness.

No comparative analysis with peer-reviewed methods is provided.

What are the long-term effects of using budget-aware selection on model generalization?

papers.title: Rethinking Heterogeneous LLM Merging: A Weighted Model Averaging Perspective
papers.abstract: Can large language models with substantially different parameter spaces be merged by direct weighted averaging, without training or semantic alignment? Existing heterogeneous fusion methods typically introduce distillation, adapters, learned latent spaces, routing, or feature alignment, leaving open whether a simpler recipe can work for genuinely different billion-parameter checkpoints. We revisit this counterintuitive question through training-free dimensional adaptation followed by ratio-controlled interpolation. In union-style merging, we expand the smaller model into the larger parameter space; in intersection-style merging, we truncate the larger model into the smaller parameter space. Across Qwen-family model pairs and benchmarks covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, language understanding, commonsense reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following, deterministic expansion largely preserves the source model function, and small-ratio interpolation can improve over strong source checkpoints by transferring complementary capabilities. However, near-balanced interpolation often collapses, and task-level results reveal a seesaw effect in which gains on some capabilities coexist with regressions on others. These results show that simple parameter averaging, when paired with lightweight dimensional adaptation and carefully controlled ratios, is a surprisingly strong baseline for heterogeneous LLM merging, suggesting that the limits of direct weighted fusion may also bound what more complex heterogeneous merging methods can achieve at scale.

summary.takeaway: Direct weighted averaging of heterogeneous LLMs can be effective without training or semantic alignment.
summary.problem: Existing methods for merging heterogeneous LLMs often require complex machinery and training.
summary.method: The paper proposes a training-free dimensional adaptation followed by ratio-controlled interpolation for merging.
summary.evidence: Union-style merging with small-ratio interpolation shows performance improvements over strong source checkpoints, achieving an average score of 0.5551.
summary.limitations: The study is limited to Qwen-family checkpoints and does not address broader contexts like multilingual or long-context settings.
summary.why_for_you: This research provides insights into efficient LLM merging strategies relevant for scalable model integration.

signals.text: Deterministic dimensional adaptation allows for effective direct weighted averaging across heterogeneous LLMs, preserving source model functions.
Union-style merging expands the smaller model into the larger parameter space, while intersection-style merging truncates the larger model to the smaller space.
Small-ratio interpolation can enhance model capabilities, but near-balanced ratios may lead to performance collapse, indicating a seesaw effect in task-level results.

deep_dive.overview: This research investigates whether large language models with different parameter spaces can be merged through direct weighted averaging without training or semantic alignment. The authors propose a method involving training-free dimensional adaptation followed by controlled interpolation ratios. Their findings indicate that simple parameter averaging, when combined with dimensional adaptation, serves as a strong baseline for heterogeneous LLM merging. Notably, the results demonstrate that while small-ratio interpolation can yield improvements, it also risks performance collapse at near-balanced ratios, highlighting the complexity of merging strategies.

methodology.title: Dimensional Adaptation
methodology.detail: The method involves expanding the smaller model to fit the larger model's parameter space or truncating the larger model to match the smaller model's dimensions, enabling compatibility for merging.

methodology.title: Weighted Averaging
methodology.detail: After dimensional adaptation, the models are merged using a weighted average based on a controlled mixing ratio, which is crucial for maintaining performance.

methodology.title: Union and Intersection Merging
methodology.detail: Union-style merging expands the smaller model, while intersection-style merging truncates the larger model, allowing for different approaches to model integration.

mechanism.title: Ratio Sensitivity
mechanism.detail: The study identifies that the mixing ratio significantly influences performance, with severe collapses observed at ratios outside the optimal range.

experiments.title: Qwen Model Evaluation
experiments.detail: The experiments evaluate Qwen2.5 and Qwen3 model pairs across various benchmarks, including GSM8K and MATH-500, demonstrating performance improvements in merged models.

experiments.title: Union Merging Results
experiments.detail: Union merging results show that the merged model can outperform both source models, achieving an aggregate score of 0.7525, indicating effective capability transfer.

experiments.title: Intersection Merging Results
experiments.detail: Intersection merging results reveal that while some configurations yield improvements, others lead to regressions, emphasizing the seesaw effect in task-level performance.

findings.title: Performance Improvement
findings.detail: Union-style merging with a small ratio achieved an average score of 0.5551, closely competing with more complex methods.

findings.title: Seesaw Effect
findings.detail: The merging process can lead to gains in some capabilities while causing regressions in others, as seen in the task-level evaluations.

findings.title: Compatibility Operator
findings.detail: Dimensional adaptation acts as a compatibility operator, enabling effective weighted averaging without additional training or alignment.

contributions: Introduces a simple, training-free method for merging heterogeneous LLMs.
Demonstrates the effectiveness of direct weighted averaging in model merging.
Highlights the importance of dimensional adaptation in achieving compatibility.
limitations: Focuses exclusively on Qwen-family checkpoints, limiting generalizability.
Does not explore long-context, multilingual, or tool-use scenarios.
open_questions: How can the proposed method be adapted for broader contexts beyond the Qwen-family models?
What are the implications of the seesaw effect for practical applications of merged LLMs?

papers.title: Natural Language Access to Domain-Specific Metadata: A Reusable Framework for LLM Query Generation
papers.abstract: Researchers need to answer ad-hoc questions about the contents of domain-specific archives but often lack the expertise to write structured queries on the metadata. We show that when domain vocabulary and semantics are captured in a well-designed Web Ontology Language (OWL) ontology, Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate accurate structured queries zero-shot, without fine-tuning, retrieval augmentation, or multi-agent orchestration. We present the Natural Language Knowledge Graph Query (NLKGQ) system, a framework and development process that enables natural language access to metadata in such archives. The framework includes a web interface that helps researchers pose natural language questions, which a domain-agnostic harness translates to SPARQL via an LLM and executes against a knowledge graph. The development process begins with capturing domain vocabulary and semantics in a formal OWL ontology. Domain-specific code then extracts metadata from archive sources and imports it into a knowledge graph defined by the ontology. Both are designed for reuse across domains. We demonstrate the system on metadata derived from a large-scale neuroimaging research archive, evaluating multiple LLMs and ontology representations. The best configurations achieve 100% accuracy on a competence and regression question set developed with domain experts. An ablation study across eight ontology representations reveals that readable entity names and semantic annotations are the dominant factors in accuracy, more significant than model choice or prompt engineering. We also compare SPARQL to an auto-generated SQL database as query backends, showing that OWL's structural features provide a substantial advantage over SQL DDL for LLM-driven query generation. Our demonstration domain also requires local LLMs on modest institutional hardware to address privacy concerns for human subject data.

summary.takeaway: The NLKGQ framework enables accurate zero-shot query generation for domain-specific metadata using LLMs and OWL ontologies.
summary.problem: Researchers struggle to formulate structured queries for domain-specific archives due to a lack of expertise.
summary.method: The framework employs a web interface and an ontology-first approach to translate natural language questions into SPARQL queries.
summary.evidence: The best configurations achieved 100% accuracy on a competency and regression question set developed with domain experts.
summary.limitations: The evaluation is limited to a single metadata domain, and the competency question set is small.
summary.why_for_you: This framework provides a novel approach to enhance LLM-driven query generation, relevant for trustworthy AI applications.

signals.text: The NLKGQ system achieved 100% accuracy on a competency and regression question set, demonstrating the effectiveness of the ontology-first approach in generating accurate queries.
The framework utilizes a domain-agnostic harness to translate natural language questions into SPARQL queries, showcasing a reusable method for accessing metadata.
An ablation study revealed that semantic annotations and readable entity names significantly impact accuracy, with a 19 percentage point drop in SPARQL accuracy when annotations were stripped.

deep_dive.overview: This research addresses the challenge of querying domain-specific archives by presenting the NLKGQ framework, which leverages OWL ontologies to enable LLMs to generate structured queries from natural language inputs. The framework includes a web interface for user interaction and a systematic development process that captures domain vocabulary and semantics. The strongest evidence of its efficacy is the achievement of 100% accuracy on a competency question set, underscoring the importance of ontology design in enhancing query generation accuracy.

methodology.title: Ontology Development
methodology.detail: The process begins with capturing domain vocabulary and semantics in a formal OWL ontology, which serves as the foundation for query generation and knowledge graph construction.

methodology.title: ETL Pipeline
methodology.detail: A domain-specific Extract-Transform-Load (ETL) pipeline maps metadata from archives to the ontology, producing a knowledge graph that facilitates structured query generation.

methodology.title: Test Driver Framework
methodology.detail: The test driver evaluates LLM performance by comparing generated queries against reference SPARQL queries, supporting various configurations to assess accuracy and variability.

methodology.title: SPARQL and SQL Comparison
methodology.detail: The framework allows for a systematic comparison between SPARQL and auto-generated SQL databases, highlighting the advantages of OWL's structural features for LLM-driven query generation.

mechanism.title: Query Generation Mechanism
mechanism.detail: The LLM generates queries zero-shot using the full ontology or derived schema provided in the system prompt, ensuring context is maintained for accurate query formulation.

experiments.title: Evaluation on Neuroimaging Archive
experiments.detail: The framework was demonstrated on an MRI neuroimaging research archive, evaluating multiple LLMs and ontology representations, achieving 100% accuracy on SPARQL.

experiments.title: Ablation Study
experiments.detail: An ablation study across eight ontology representations showed that semantic annotations and readable entity names are critical for maintaining high accuracy in query generation.

experiments.title: Model Evaluation
experiments.detail: Eight locally deployed LLM variants were evaluated, with the best model achieving 100% accuracy on SPARQL and 57% on SQL, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness.

findings.title: Accuracy Achievement
findings.detail: The NLKGQ framework achieved 100% accuracy on a competency question set, validating the effectiveness of the ontology-first approach.

findings.title: Impact of Annotations
findings.detail: Stripping semantic annotations from the ontology resulted in a 19 percentage point decrease in SPARQL accuracy, emphasizing their importance.

findings.title: Comparison of Backends
findings.detail: SPARQL queries outperformed SQL queries, achieving 100% accuracy compared to 57% for SQL, highlighting OWL's advantages in query generation.

contributions: Development of the NLKGQ framework for natural language access to domain-specific metadata.
Systematic evaluation of LLM-driven SPARQL generation across multiple models and configurations.
Creation of a generic OWL KG-to-SQL schema generator for comparative analysis of query backends.
limitations: The evaluation is limited to a single metadata domain, requiring further validation for generalization.
The competency question set is small, which may not fully represent end-user query performance.
open_questions: How can the framework be adapted for cross-domain applications?
What strategies can enhance the complexity of the ontology while maintaining LLM performance?

papers.title: It's Not What You Say, It's How You Say It: Evaluating LLM Responses to Expressions of Belief
papers.abstract: Users frequently express their beliefs to large language models (LLMs). In some situations, the LLM should accept these contextual beliefs as true. In others, they should stick to their prior knowledge. Notably, users' expressions of belief (EoBs) can take linguistically diverse forms - using presuppositions, evidential and certainty markers, or varied tones - each of which may have a different persuasiveness over the LLMs. We introduce a typology to systematically evaluate how different EoBs affect whether models follow context versus prior knowledge. The typology is grounded in four linguistically motivated dimensions: form, evidentiality, epistemic stance, and tone, spanning 17 fine-grained types. By pairing these EoBs with world knowledge facts, we generate controlled EoB-query pairs that isolate the effect of linguistic variation.
