Confidence reliability is position-dependent: RL confidence becomes informative only after a path-commitment phase, while OPD confidence is useful early but can become inversely calibrated later in the reasoning trace.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the gap in understanding how different post-training methods—supervised fine-tuning (SFT), reinforcement learning (RL), and on-policy distillation (OPD)—reshape confidence calibration in large language models during chain-of-thought reasoning. Instead of treating confidence as a monolithic final output property, the authors propose a three-stage framework evaluating confidence before reasoning (Pre-CoT), during reasoning (Intra-CoT), and after reasoning (Post-CoT). Using Qwen2.5-7B-based models trained on the same data but with different post-training objectives, they conduct controlled experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks. Results show that OPD excels at pre-reasoning difficulty estimation, SFT provides the strongest online signal for early termination of low-quality reasoning traces, and RL yields the most reliable confidence for answer aggregation. They further reveal that confidence calibration varies with token position, motivating PosConf, a position-aware confidence strategy that selectively uses confidence from reliable relative-position intervals. PosConf significantly improves RL aggregation accuracy and OPD early stopping efficiency, demonstrating that confidence should be used both stage-wise and position-awarely to enhance reasoning reliability and efficiency.

methodology.title: Three-Stage Confidence Calibration Framework
methodology.detail: The framework partitions confidence evaluation into Pre-CoT (before chain-of-thought generation, assessing problem difficulty), Intra-CoT (during generation, enabling early termination of uncertain traces), and Post-CoT (after generation, supporting answer aggregation). Confidence is computed from top-k next-token probabilities, smoothed over sliding windows, and normalized by relative token position.

methodology.title: Model Variants and Training
methodology.detail: Four Qwen2.5-7B-based models are compared: Qwen-Instruct (instruction-tuned baseline), Qwen-SFT (supervised fine-tuned on correct chain-of-thought traces), Qwen-RL (trained with group relative policy optimization using binary outcome rewards), and Qwen-OPD (on-policy distillation from a larger teacher model via dense KL divergence). All models share the same backbone and training data to isolate post-training effects.

methodology.title: Confidence Metrics and Evaluation
methodology.detail: Pre-CoT confidence is evaluated by AUROC and PRR to measure difficulty prediction quality. Intra-CoT confidence triggers early stopping when sliding window confidence falls below a threshold, balancing token usage and accuracy. Post-CoT confidence ranks completed traces for confidence-filtered majority voting and most-confident selection, assessing aggregation improvements.

methodology.title: PosConf Position-Aware Confidence Strategy
methodology.detail: PosConf restricts confidence usage to reliable relative-position intervals identified by analyzing confidence calibration dynamics across token positions. This avoids inverse calibration regions, improving early stopping and answer aggregation by leveraging only trustworthy confidence segments.

mechanism.title: Token-Level Confidence Computation
mechanism.detail: Confidence at token position ℓ is computed as the negative average log probability over the top-k next-token candidates, smoothed over a sliding window of size w to capture local uncertainty dynamics. Relative token position ρt = t/m normalizes positions across traces of varying lengths, enabling position-aware confidence analysis.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Theoretical Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide formal equations or causal theories beyond the confidence computation formula and the empirical observation of position-dependent calibration shifts.

experiments.title: Pre-CoT Difficulty Estimation
experiments.detail: Evaluated on mathematical reasoning benchmarks (AIME 24/25, AMC 23, MATH500) using AUROC and PRR metrics, comparing Qwen-Instruct, Qwen-SFT, Qwen-RL, and Qwen-OPD. OPD achieves the highest average AUROC (0.644) and PRR (0.345), indicating superior pre-reasoning confidence calibration.

experiments.title: Intra-CoT Early Stopping
experiments.detail: Confidence thresholds are swept to produce token-accuracy frontiers under a fixed budget of 256 traces per problem. Early stopping triggered when sliding window confidence falls below threshold reduces token usage without accuracy loss. SFT yields the strongest online signal for early termination.

experiments.title: Post-CoT Answer Aggregation
experiments.detail: Answer aggregation compares majority voting, confidence-filtered majority voting (top 5% or 10% traces by confidence), and most-confident selection. RL confidence filtering improves aggregation accuracy by 6.1 points over majority voting, demonstrating reliable trace-level confidence.

experiments.title: PosConf Evaluation
experiments.detail: PosConf applies position-aware confidence intervals to improve RL aggregation and OPD early stopping. It avoids later inverse-calibration regions in OPD, yielding up to 4.3 points gain under tight token budgets.

findings.title: OPD Excels at Pre-CoT Confidence
findings.detail: OPD achieves the highest AUROC and PRR scores for difficulty estimation across multiple benchmarks, outperforming SFT, RL, and the baseline Qwen-Instruct, indicating its pre-reasoning confidence is most informative.

findings.title: SFT Provides Strongest Intra-CoT Signal
findings.detail: During reasoning, SFT yields the most reliable token-level confidence for early stopping, enabling efficient pruning of low-quality reasoning traces without compromising accuracy.

findings.title: RL Confidence Best for Post-CoT Aggregation
findings.detail: RL produces the most reliable trace-level confidence for answer aggregation, improving accuracy by 6.1 points over majority voting when using confidence-filtered voting.

findings.title: Confidence Calibration is Position-Dependent
findings.detail: RL confidence becomes informative only after a path-commitment phase, while OPD confidence is useful early but can become inversely calibrated later, motivating position-aware confidence usage.

findings.title: PosConf Improves Reasoning Efficiency and Accuracy
findings.detail: By restricting confidence usage to reliable relative-position intervals, PosConf improves RL answer aggregation by 6.1 points and OPD early stopping by up to 4.3 points, demonstrating the benefit of stage-wise and position-aware confidence strategies.

contributions: Introduced a three-stage confidence calibration framework (Pre-CoT, Intra-CoT, Post-CoT) linking confidence signals to inference-time decisions in reasoning.
Provided a controlled comparison of SFT, RL, and OPD post-training methods showing distinct stage-dependent confidence calibration shifts.
Discovered position-dependent confidence reliability and proposed PosConf, a position-aware confidence strategy that improves early stopping and answer aggregation.
limitations: Experiments are limited to the Qwen2.5-7B backbone and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, limiting generalizability to other models and tasks.
No evaluation on downstream applications beyond mathematical reasoning or on other types of reasoning tasks.
The study does not explore the impact of varying training data or model architectures on confidence calibration.
No formal theoretical mechanism or causal explanation is provided for the observed position-dependent calibration shifts.
open_questions: How do confidence calibration dynamics generalize across different LLM architectures and larger-scale models?
Can position-aware confidence strategies like PosConf be adapted to other reasoning domains or multimodal tasks?
What are the underlying causes of inverse calibration in OPD confidence at later token positions?
How can confidence calibration be integrated with other uncertainty estimation methods to further improve trustworthy LLM reasoning?

papers.title: Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing for LLM-Based Network Intrusion Detection
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based intrusion detection systems (IDS) are increasingly studied for security monitoring, yet their robustness against feasible traffic manipulation remains largely empirical. We present Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing (TA-RS), a classifier-agnostic certified defense that injects Gaussian noise exclusively into the directly controllable (DC) subspace -- features a remote attacker can modify -- during both fine-tuning and certification, aligning the smoothing distribution with the attacker-controllable subspace. We identify a critical prerequisite: applying standard randomized smoothing to clean-trained LLM-IDS yields weak certified accuracy in three of four (model, dataset) pairs tested (14-33%, at or below random) and only 57% in the fourth (43 pp below the noise-augmented result); noise-augmented fine-tuning recovers to 68-100% on two of three benchmark datasets (at sigma=0.25). At the L_inf-equivalent threshold R_inf = epsilon*sqrt(|DC|) (epsilon=0.05), TA-RS achieves 55-100% certified accuracy on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021, with median certified radii (R approx 0.45-0.96) exceeding R_inf by 1.8-5x (across sigma=0.25-1.00). Against a fairly trained iso-trained RS baseline the residual advantage is dataset-dependent (4-19 pp on CIC-IDS-2018). The larger gap -- up to 72 pp against an isotropic RS baseline that shares the DC-noise-augmented training recipe -- primarily reflects the training-certification mismatch rather than DC alignment alone: isotropic test-time noise perturbs uncontrollable features the attacker cannot exploit, triggering abstention rates up to 68%. RT-IoT2022 probes the limits of the method: it fails under the default fine-tuning recipe but recovers to 76%/69% certified accuracy (LLaMA3-8B/Qwen3-8B) when noise augmentation is increased.
papers.comment: 44 pages, 14 figures, 14 tables. Submitted to Expert Systems with Applications

summary.takeaway: Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing (TA-RS) certifies robustness of LLM-based intrusion detection by injecting Gaussian noise only into attacker-controllable traffic features, achieving 55–100% certified accuracy on key datasets.
summary.problem: LLM-based network intrusion detection systems lack certified robustness guarantees aligned with the feasible attacker-controlled traffic feature subspace.
summary.method: TA-RS injects Gaussian noise exclusively into the directly controllable (DC) feature subspace during both fine-tuning and certification, aligning smoothing with the attacker’s feasible perturbation space.
summary.evidence: TA-RS achieves 55–100% certified accuracy on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021 at ε=0.05, with median certified radii exceeding the L∞ threshold by 1.8–5×, outperforming isotropic randomized smoothing baselines by up to 72 percentage points.
summary.limitations: TA-RS requires dataset-specific noise-augmented fine-tuning for noise stability; it fails under default recipes on challenging datasets like RT-IoT2022 without increased noise augmentation.
summary.why_for_you: TA-RS provides a principled, scalable certified defense framework for LLM-based IDS that aligns certification with realistic attacker capabilities, addressing robustness gaps in adversarial network security.

signals.text: Noise-augmented fine-tuning is critical: clean-trained LLM-IDS yield weak certified accuracy (14–33%), while noise-augmented models recover 68–100% certified accuracy on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021 at σ=0.25.

TA-RS injects Gaussian noise only into the DC subspace (features attacker can modify) during training and certification, avoiding perturbations on indirectly or uncontrollable features that cause high abstention rates (up to 68%) in isotropic smoothing.

Certification radii from TA-RS exceed the L∞-equivalent threshold R∞ by 1.8–5×, demonstrating stronger robustness guarantees; residual advantages over isotropic RS baselines vary by dataset (4–19 pp), mainly due to training-certification distribution mismatch.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the robustness of LLM-based network intrusion detection systems (IDS) against adversarial traffic manipulations constrained to attacker-controllable features. The authors formalize a taxonomy partitioning traffic features into directly controllable (DC), indirectly controllable (IC), and uncontrollable (UC) sets, focusing certification on the DC subspace. They propose Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing (TA-RS), which injects Gaussian noise exclusively into DC features during both fine-tuning and certification, aligning the smoothing distribution with the feasible attacker perturbation space. Empirical results on three benchmark datasets (CIC-IDS-2018, HIKARI-2021, RT-IoT2022) show that noise-augmented fine-tuning is essential to achieve noise stability and meaningful certified accuracy. TA-RS achieves 55–100% certified accuracy at an L∞-equivalent perturbation budget ε=0.05, with median certified radii exceeding the theoretical threshold by up to 5×. Compared to isotropic randomized smoothing baselines, TA-RS reduces abstention rates drastically and improves certified accuracy by up to 72 percentage points. The method is classifier-agnostic and scalable to billion-parameter LLMs, but requires dataset-specific fine-tuning and increased noise augmentation on challenging datasets. This framework provides a principled, scalable approach to certified robustness in traffic-domain LLM-IDS.

methodology.title: DC/IC/UC Feature Taxonomy
methodology.detail: The authors categorize network traffic features into directly controllable (DC), indirectly controllable (IC), and uncontrollable (UC) sets based on attacker reachability, defining the certification subspace as the DC features that an attacker can realistically perturb.

methodology.title: Noise-Augmented Fine-Tuning
methodology.detail: LLM-based IDS models are fine-tuned with Gaussian noise injected only into DC features to stabilize predictions under noise, enabling effective certification; this step is critical as clean-trained models yield near-random certified accuracy.

methodology.title: Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing (TA-RS)
methodology.detail: TA-RS applies Gaussian noise exclusively to the DC subspace during certification, estimating class probabilities via Monte Carlo sampling and computing certified radii using a Neyman–Pearson-based bound adapted to the DC subspace.

methodology.title: Certification Algorithm (TA-Certify)
methodology.detail: TA-Certify draws noise samples restricted to DC features, identifies the top predicted class, estimates a Clopper–Pearson lower confidence bound on its probability, and returns a certified radius or abstains if confidence is insufficient.

methodology.title: Evaluation Metrics and Protocol
methodology.detail: Certified accuracy CA(r) is reported at radius r, penalizing incorrect predictions and abstentions; experiments use fixed train/test splits, protocol-derived feature clipping, and matched noise levels and sample counts for fair comparison with isotropic RS baselines.

mechanism.title: Certified Robustness in DC Subspace
mechanism.detail: The certification guarantee restricts perturbations to the DC subspace, leveraging the injection of Gaussian noise only in this subspace. The Neyman–Pearson lemma applies in the reduced dimension, yielding a certified radius R = σΦ−1(pA) that bounds adversarial perturbations feasible to the attacker. This avoids wasted noise budget and high abstention caused by perturbing uncontrollable features.

experiments.title: Datasets and Setup
experiments.detail: Experiments use three network-traffic datasets: CIC-IDS-2018 (4 classes, 25 features, 14 DC), HIKARI-2021 (3 classes, 82 features, 25 DC), and RT-IoT2022 (5 classes, 83 features, 27 DC). Fixed train/test splits and protocol-derived feature clipping are applied. Certification subsets contain 120–168 samples stratified by class.

experiments.title: Baseline Comparisons
experiments.detail: TA-RS is compared against isotropic randomized smoothing baselines with matched noise levels and training recipes. Certified accuracy and abstention rates are measured at ε=0.05 L∞-equivalent budget, with Monte Carlo sample counts N0=20 and N=200.

experiments.title: Noise-Augmentation Ablation
experiments.detail: Ablations show that noise-augmented fine-tuning is necessary to achieve meaningful certified accuracy; clean-trained LLM-IDS yield 14–33% certified accuracy, while noise-augmented models reach 68–100% on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021.

experiments.title: RT-IoT2022 Challenge
experiments.detail: On the challenging RT-IoT2022 dataset, default fine-tuning fails (≤24% certified accuracy), but increasing noise augmentation recovers 76% (LLaMA3-8B) and 69% (Qwen3-8B) certified accuracy, highlighting noise stability as a key constraint.

findings.title: Certified Accuracy Gains
findings.detail: TA-RS achieves 55–100% certified accuracy on CIC-IDS-2018 and HIKARI-2021 at ε=0.05, with median certified radii 1.8–5× larger than the L∞ threshold, demonstrating strong robustness aligned with attacker capabilities.

findings.title: Abstention Reduction
findings.detail: TA-RS reduces abstention rates drastically compared to isotropic RS (from 68% to 8% on CIC-IDS-2018), by avoiding noise perturbations on uncontrollable features that cause prediction instability.

findings.title: Training-Certification Match Importance
findings.detail: The main advantage of TA-RS over isotropic RS is due to matching noise injection during training and certification, rather than DC subspace selection alone, as isotropic test-time noise perturbs uncontrollable features causing high abstention.

findings.title: Dataset-Dependent Residual Advantage
findings.detail: Against an iso-trained RS baseline, TA-RS shows a residual certified accuracy advantage of 4–19 percentage points on CIC-IDS-2018, indicating dataset-dependent benefits beyond training-certification alignment.

findings.title: Noise Stability as Bottleneck
findings.detail: On RT-IoT2022, TA-RS fails under default fine-tuning but recovers with increased noise augmentation, confirming that noise stability of the base LLM is the binding constraint in challenging scenarios.

contributions: Operationalization of the DC/IC/UC feature taxonomy as the certification subspace for LLM-based IDS.
Demonstration that noise-augmented fine-tuning is essential for noise stability and meaningful certified accuracy in LLM-IDS.
Development of Traffic-Aware Randomized Smoothing (TA-RS) that injects noise only into attacker-controllable features during training and certification.
Empirical validation of TA-RS achieving up to 100% certified accuracy with large certified radii on multiple benchmark datasets.
limitations: TA-RS requires dataset-specific noise-augmented fine-tuning; pretrained LLM knowledge does not transfer without traffic-aware tuning.
The method fails on challenging datasets like RT-IoT2022 under default fine-tuning and needs increased noise augmentation to recover.
Certification sample counts are limited (N=200) due to LLM inference cost, resulting in conservative confidence bounds.
The approach assumes accurate identification of attacker-controllable features, which may be dataset-dependent and require domain expertise.
open_questions: How to improve noise stability of LLM-based IDS models to reduce reliance on heavy noise augmentation?
Can TA-RS be extended to certify robustness under more complex or adaptive attacker models beyond DC subspace perturbations?
What are the trade-offs between certification tightness and computational cost for large-scale LLM-IDS?
How to generalize the DC/IC/UC taxonomy and certification framework to other network security tasks or heterogeneous traffic representations?

papers.title: Partially Correlated Verifier Cascades in LLM Harnesses: Concave Log-Odds, Polynomial Reliability, and Blind-Spot Ceilings
papers.abstract: Serial verification gates are a core reliability primitive in LLM harnesses: a candidate answer is returned only if $k$ verifier calls all accept it. Under conditionally independent gates, the recent Odds Law (arXiv:2606.15712) shows that posterior log-odds grow linearly in $k$, so failure decays exponentially, and states that "a tight theory of partially correlated verifier cascades remains open." This note gives a minimal such theory. Modeling the per-instance false-accept rate on the generator's own errors as a latent variable $α\sim G$ (de Finetti), the exact cascade posterior is $\ell_k = \ell_0 - \ln m_k$, with $m_k$ the $k$-th moment of $G$. Then: (i) $\ell_k$ is concave in $k$ for every non-degenerate $G$ -- the Odds Law is its tangent at the first gate and an upper bound; (ii) for Beta$(a,b)$ latents, failure decays polynomially, $1-r_k \asymp k^{-b}$, with correlation parameter $ρ_v = 1/(a+b+1)$; (iii) a blind-spot atom of mass $1-π$ at $α=1$ caps the evidence extractable from any number of gates at $-\ln(1-π)$ nats, so reliability saturates below 1; (iv) letting the true-accept rate also vary ($β\sim H$) yields a trichotomy -- gates eventually always help, plateau, or actively harm -- decided by the upper-tail exponents of $G$ and $H$, with closed-form crossover $k^\dagger$. The mechanism is survivorship: errors surviving gates are the high-$α$ ones. The theory is measurable: $R$ repeated verdicts per instance identify the first $R$ moments of $G$, so two verdicts identify $ρ_v$; beta-binomial likelihood and NPMLE recover the reliability curve and the ill-posed ceiling. In synthetic tests, independence-based extrapolation underestimates failure by 20x at $k=5$ and ~3000x at $k=10$; the correlated fit at $R=8$ tracks held-out depths. The practical lever is decorrelation -- changing model family, modality, or evidence source -- not adding gates.
papers.comment: 14 pages, 2 figures. Code and synthetic-recovery experiments: https://github.com/jianganghan/harness-verifier-cascades

summary.takeaway: Partially correlated verifier cascades in LLM harnesses exhibit concave log-odds growth, polynomial reliability decay, and blind-spot ceilings that limit reliability gains from adding more gates.
summary.problem: Existing theory assumes conditionally independent verifier gates, but real LLM verifiers share correlated blind spots with generators, invalidating exponential reliability improvements.
summary.method: Model per-instance false-accept rates as a latent variable α ∼ G, derive exact cascade posterior log-odds as ℓ_k = ℓ_0 − ln m_k with m_k the k-th moment of G, and analyze reliability scaling and ceilings under correlation.
summary.evidence: Synthetic experiments show independence-based extrapolation underestimates failure by 20× at k=5 and ~3000× at k=10, while the correlated latent-α theory fitted at R=8 verdicts accurately tracks held-out depths.
summary.limitations: The theory uses a scalar latent exchangeable variable compressing all inter-gate correlations, assumes all-accept semantics, relies on Beta distributions for closed forms, and is validated only on synthetic data.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides a measurable, minimal statistical theory quantifying verifier correlation effects on LLM harness reliability, crucial for trustworthy LLM deployment and statistical understanding of verification cascades.

signals.text: The cascade posterior log-odds ℓ_k = ℓ_0 − ln m_k is concave in k for every non-degenerate latent distribution G, with the Odds Law as a tangent and upper bound, revealing diminishing returns from adding gates under correlation.

Modeling the latent false-accept rate α as Beta(a,b) yields polynomial failure decay 1 − r_k ~ k^−b governed by a single correlation parameter ρ_v = 1/(a+b+1), interpolating from independence to pure blind-spot extremes.

A blind-spot atom of mass 1−π at α=1 caps extractable evidence at −ln(1−π) nats, causing reliability saturation strictly below 1 regardless of gate count, demonstrating fundamental limits of verifier cascades.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the open problem of modeling partially correlated verifier cascades in LLM harnesses, where multiple verifier gates sequentially accept candidate answers only if all accept. Prior work assumed conditional independence of gate errors, yielding exponential reliability improvements (Odds Law). However, real verifiers share blind spots with generators, causing correlated errors and invalidating independence assumptions. The authors model the per-instance false-accept rate α as a latent variable drawn from a distribution G, deriving the exact cascade posterior log-odds as ℓ_k = ℓ_0 − ln m_k, where m_k is the k-th moment of G. This formulation reveals concavity in log-odds growth, polynomial rather than exponential failure decay for Beta-distributed latents, and a blind-spot ceiling limiting reliability gains. Introducing variability in true-accept rates β leads to a trichotomy where gates can help, plateau, or harm reliability, with closed-form crossover points. The theory is measurable via repeated verdicts per instance, enabling estimation of correlation parameters and reliability curves. Synthetic experiments validate the theory, showing independence-based extrapolation drastically underestimates failure rates, while the correlated model accurately predicts reliability scaling. The practical implication is that decorrelation strategies, not merely adding gates, improve harness reliability.

methodology.title: Latent Variable Modeling of False-Accept Rates
methodology.detail: The per-instance false-accept rate α of verifier gates on generator errors is modeled as a latent variable drawn from a distribution G, leveraging de Finetti's theorem to assume exchangeability across gates. This latent captures correlation structure among gate errors.

methodology.title: Exact Cascade Posterior via Moments
methodology.detail: The cascade posterior log-odds after k gates is expressed exactly as ℓ_k = ℓ_0 − ln m_k, where m_k = E[α^k] is the k-th moment of G. This moment-based formulation enables analytic characterization of reliability scaling and concavity.

methodology.title: Beta Distribution Family and Correlation Parameter
methodology.detail: Choosing G as a Beta(a,b) distribution yields closed-form asymptotics where failure probability decays polynomially as k^−b. The correlation parameter ρ_v = 1/(a+b+1) quantifies within-instance correlation of verdicts, interpolating between independence and full correlation.

methodology.title: Blind-Spot Atom and Reliability Ceiling
methodology.detail: Incorporating an atom of mass 1−π at α=1 models errors that verifiers never catch, imposing a ceiling on extractable evidence at −ln(1−π) nats and capping reliability strictly below 1 regardless of gate count.

methodology.title: Measurement Protocol via Repeated Verdicts
methodology.detail: Repeated verifier calls per instance (R verdicts) identify the first R moments of G, enabling estimation of correlation parameters such as ρ_v from two verdicts. Beta-binomial likelihood and nonparametric maximum likelihood estimation (NPMLE) recover the full reliability curve and ceiling.

mechanism.title: Survivorship Effect in Verification Cascades
mechanism.detail: Errors surviving j gates are exactly those with high latent false-accept rates α, causing later gates to face a selected subset of hard-to-detect errors. This survivorship mechanism induces concavity in log-odds growth, polynomial reliability decay, and blind-spot ceilings, distinguishing verification cascades from voting analogues.

experiments.title: Synthetic Recovery and Validation
experiments.detail: Synthetic experiments simulate verifier cascades with known latent distributions and correlation parameters. Estimators based on repeated verdicts accurately recover the latent moments and correlation ρ_v. The correlated latent-α theory fitted at R=8 verdicts tracks held-out depths, while independence-based extrapolation underestimates failure by factors of 20× at k=5 and ~3000× at k=10.

findings.title: Concavity of Log-Odds Growth
findings.detail: The exact cascade posterior log-odds ℓ_k is concave in k for every non-degenerate latent distribution G, with the Odds Law as a tangent at k=1 and an upper bound elsewhere, demonstrating diminishing returns from adding gates under correlation.

findings.title: Polynomial Reliability Decay
findings.detail: For Beta-distributed latents G=Beta(a,b), failure probability decays polynomially as 1−r_k ~ k^−b, governed by the correlation parameter ρ_v=1/(a+b+1), contrasting with exponential decay under independence.

findings.title: Blind-Spot Ceiling on Reliability
findings.detail: An atom of mass 1−π at α=1 imposes a ceiling on extractable evidence at −ln(1−π) nats, causing reliability to saturate strictly below 1 regardless of the number of gates.

findings.title: Trichotomy with Variable True-Accept Rates
findings.detail: Allowing true-accept rates β to vary across instances yields a trichotomy where gates eventually help, plateau, or harm reliability, determined by the relative upper-tail exponents of G and H, with a closed-form crossover gate count k^†.

findings.title: Measurement Feasibility
findings.detail: Repeated verdicts per instance enable identification of latent moments and correlation parameters, making the theory empirically testable and applicable to real generator-verifier pairs.

contributions: Derivation of exact cascade posterior log-odds formula ℓ_k = ℓ_0 − ln m_k under latent false-accept rate modeling.
Proof of concavity of log-odds growth and polynomial reliability decay for Beta-distributed latents with explicit correlation parameter ρ_v.
Identification of blind-spot atom inducing a reliability ceiling strictly below 1.
Characterization of a trichotomy in gating effects when true-accept rates vary, with closed-form crossover gate count.
Development of a measurement protocol using repeated verdicts to estimate latent moments and correlation parameters.
Synthetic validation demonstrating severe underestimation of failure by independence assumptions and accurate tracking by the correlated theory.
limitations: The scalar latent variable assumption compresses all inter-gate correlation into a single exchangeable parameter, ignoring heterogeneous verifier families.
The theory assumes all-accept semantics, which may not hold under generate-verify-retry workflows where false rejections affect throughput rather than precision.
Closed-form results rely on Beta distribution assumptions; real latent distributions may differ though asymptotics require only regularly varying tails.
Validation is limited to synthetic recovery experiments; empirical measurement on real generator-verifier pairs is ongoing.
open_questions: How to extend the latent variable model to vector latents capturing heterogeneous verifier families and gate-specific systematic differences?
What are the quantitative effects of generate-verify-retry semantics on reliability scaling and how to model false rejections in this context?
How well does the theory generalize to real-world generator-verifier pairs beyond synthetic validation, and what are practical protocols for measurement?
Can decorrelation strategies be systematically designed and quantified to overcome blind-spot ceilings in LLM harnesses?

papers.title: Knowledgeless Language Models: Suppressing Parametric Recall for Evidence-Grounded Language Modeling
papers.abstract: Language models encode substantial factual knowledge in their parameters, which can lead to unreliable behavior when this knowledge is outdated, incomplete, or misaligned with the provided context. In this work, we study whether modifying the pretraining signal can systematically shift models away from parametric recall and toward evidence-grounded reasoning. We introduce Knowledge--''Less'' Language Models (KLLMs), a fundamentally different epistemic training paradigm for LLMs, which are pretrained on corpora in which named entities are anonymized, thereby removing a primary channel for entity-linked factual supervision. This intervention substantially reduces closed-book factual recall, while often improving performance on tasks where relevant information is provided as context. Across multiple model scales, KLLMs consistently outperform matched baselines on contextual question answering, fact verification, and hallucination detection benchmarks. Crucially, in retrieval-grounded settings with imperfect evidence, KLLMs show improved robustness and achieve up to 20--25\% relative gains over standard language models. They further exhibit better calibration, with improved ECE, Brier score, and AUROC, as well as more reliable abstention behavior. Our results demonstrate that suppressing entity-linked supervision during pretraining induces a shift in epistemic behavior: KLLMs rely less on parametric knowledge and more on external evidence, leading to improved reliability under realistic conditions. This suggests that pretraining-time control over knowledge acquisition can complement retrieval-augmented and tool-based systems by providing a more evidence-sensitive base model.

summary.takeaway: Pretraining language models on anonymized corpora reduces parametric factual recall and improves evidence-grounded reasoning, robustness, and calibration.
summary.problem: Language models rely heavily on parametric knowledge, which can be outdated or misaligned, causing unreliable behavior in evidence-grounded tasks.
summary.method: KLLMs are pretrained on corpora with anonymized named entities to suppress entity-linked factual supervision and shift models toward external evidence reliance.
summary.evidence: KLLMs outperform matched baselines by up to 20–25% on retrieval-grounded tasks with imperfect evidence and show improved calibration metrics like ECE, Brier score, and AUROC.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed quantitative results or ablation studies on the impact of anonymization granularity or downstream task diversity.
summary.why_for_you: This approach offers a novel pretraining paradigm to enhance trustworthy LLM behavior by reducing harmful parametric recall and improving robustness in evidence-grounded applications.

signals.text: KLLMs pretrained on anonymized corpora reduce closed-book factual recall but improve performance on contextual QA, fact verification, and hallucination detection benchmarks.
The anonymization of named entities during pretraining removes a primary channel for entity-linked factual supervision, fundamentally shifting the epistemic behavior of LLMs.
In retrieval-grounded settings with imperfect evidence, KLLMs achieve up to 20–25% relative gains over standard LMs and exhibit better calibration metrics such as ECE, Brier score, and AUROC.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the challenge that large language models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge parametrically, which can lead to unreliable outputs when such knowledge is outdated or misaligned with context. The authors propose Knowledge--''Less'' Language Models (KLLMs), which are pretrained on corpora where named entities are anonymized, effectively suppressing entity-linked factual supervision during pretraining. This intervention reduces the model's reliance on parametric recall and encourages evidence-grounded reasoning. Empirical results across multiple model scales demonstrate that KLLMs outperform matched baselines on contextual question answering, fact verification, and hallucination detection tasks. Notably, in retrieval-augmented scenarios with imperfect evidence, KLLMs show substantial robustness improvements, achieving up to 20–25% relative gains. Additionally, KLLMs exhibit better calibration and more reliable abstention behavior, indicating improved trustworthiness. These findings suggest that controlling knowledge acquisition during pretraining can complement retrieval and tool-based methods by producing base models that are more sensitive to external evidence, thereby enhancing reliability in realistic settings.

methodology.title: Anonymization of Named Entities
methodology.detail: During pretraining, all named entities in the corpus are anonymized to remove explicit entity-linked factual supervision. This process prevents the model from memorizing specific factual knowledge tied to entities, aiming to reduce parametric recall.

methodology.title: Pretraining Paradigm Shift
methodology.detail: KLLMs are pretrained under this anonymized data regime, fundamentally altering the epistemic training signal. The objective remains language modeling, but the input distribution lacks direct entity references, encouraging reliance on contextual evidence.

methodology.title: Evaluation on Contextual Tasks
methodology.detail: Models are evaluated on contextual question answering, fact verification, and hallucination detection benchmarks to measure performance shifts from parametric recall to evidence-grounded reasoning.

methodology.title: Robustness Testing in Retrieval-Grounded Settings
methodology.detail: KLLMs are tested in retrieval-augmented scenarios with imperfect evidence to assess robustness and reliability gains compared to standard LMs.

methodology.title: Calibration and Abstention Metrics
methodology.detail: Calibration is measured using Expected Calibration Error (ECE), Brier score, and AUROC, alongside abstention behavior to evaluate trustworthiness improvements.

mechanism.title: Suppression of Parametric Recall via Anonymization
mechanism.detail: By anonymizing named entities during pretraining, the model's primary channel for learning entity-linked factual knowledge is removed. This shifts the model's epistemic behavior from relying on memorized facts to depending more on external evidence provided at inference time. No explicit equations or causal models are provided.

experiments.title: Contextual Question Answering and Fact Verification
experiments.detail: KLLMs and matched baseline LMs are evaluated on benchmarks requiring grounding in provided context, demonstrating consistent performance improvements across multiple model scales.

experiments.title: Hallucination Detection
experiments.detail: KLLMs outperform baselines in detecting hallucinated content, indicating better alignment with external evidence rather than parametric memorization.

experiments.title: Retrieval-Grounded Robustness Evaluation
experiments.detail: In scenarios with imperfect retrieved evidence, KLLMs achieve up to 20–25% relative gains over standard LMs, showing enhanced robustness to noisy or incomplete context.

experiments.title: Calibration and Abstention Behavior Analysis
experiments.detail: KLLMs exhibit improved calibration metrics (ECE, Brier score, AUROC) and more reliable abstention, suggesting increased trustworthiness in uncertain or ambiguous cases.

findings.title: Reduced Closed-Book Recall
findings.detail: Anonymization during pretraining substantially reduces the model's closed-book factual recall, confirming suppression of parametric knowledge.

findings.title: Improved Contextual Task Performance
findings.detail: Despite reduced parametric recall, KLLMs outperform matched baselines on contextual QA, fact verification, and hallucination detection tasks.

findings.title: Robustness Gains in Retrieval Settings
findings.detail: KLLMs achieve up to 20–25% relative performance gains over standard LMs in retrieval-grounded tasks with imperfect evidence.

findings.title: Better Calibration and Abstention
findings.detail: KLLMs show improved Expected Calibration Error, Brier score, AUROC, and more reliable abstention behavior, indicating enhanced reliability.

contributions: Introduction of KLLMs, a novel pretraining paradigm using anonymized corpora to suppress parametric factual recall.
Demonstration that suppressing entity-linked supervision shifts LLM epistemic behavior toward evidence-grounded reasoning.
Empirical evidence of improved robustness and calibration in retrieval-augmented and contextual tasks.
Proposal that pretraining-time control over knowledge acquisition complements retrieval and tool-based systems.
limitations: Lack of detailed quantitative ablations on the degree and method of entity anonymization.
No explicit analysis of potential trade-offs in general language understanding beyond factual tasks.
Absence of mechanistic or theoretical modeling explaining the epistemic shift beyond empirical results.
Limited disclosure of dataset specifics and baseline model architectures.
open_questions: How does the granularity and method of entity anonymization affect the balance between parametric recall and evidence grounding?
Can KLLMs maintain or improve general language understanding capabilities while suppressing factual recall?
What are the long-term effects of this pretraining paradigm on downstream tasks beyond factual reasoning?
How can this approach be integrated with retrieval-augmented and tool-augmented LLM architectures for optimal performance?

papers.title: Verifier-Based Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of Reasoning Models for Thermal Energy Storage Control
papers.abstract: Buildings are expected to shift cooling loads in response to grid conditions. Thermal energy storage (TES) enables this shift, but scheduling it well requires planning hours ahead under storage constraints. Model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning are difficult to scale across buildings. This study instead adapts an open-weight reasoning model through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). We convert exact offline dynamic-programming (DP) action values into dense rewards for every candidate action. Using only 30 training prompts, reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) trains the model as an upper-level scheduler that outputs hourly heat-pump setpoints from text-based states and forecasts. Evaluation uses a deliberately simple office-building TES benchmark where exact DP is tractable and the optimum is known. RFT reduces the open-weight model's emissions from 70.5 to 61.2 kg-CO2, close to the DP optimum of 60.8 kg-CO2. GPT-5 nearly matches DP and MPC without task-specific training, while GPT-4o, a non-reasoning LLM, produces higher emissions than the no-storage baseline, so inference-time reasoning appears important. Trace analysis shows that RFT mainly stabilizes observable planning patterns (candidate comparison, look-ahead, and feasibility checking) rather than creating a new strategy. Robustness and generalization tests clarify what transfers: the reinforced planning patterns persist under forecast errors and an unseen TES condition and carry over to a battery task, but its different structure limits the gains. DP-based verifiable rewards offer a practical way to adapt open-weight reasoning models to building storage scheduling. These results motivate higher-fidelity tests of whole-building control and scalable verifiers for city-scale energy management.

summary.takeaway: Reinforcement fine-tuning with dynamic programming-based verifiable rewards effectively adapts open-weight reasoning models for thermal energy storage scheduling, achieving near-optimal emissions reduction.
summary.problem: Efficiently scheduling thermal energy storage in buildings requires scalable planning under storage constraints, which is challenging for model predictive control and reinforcement learning methods.
summary.method: The study uses reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards derived from exact offline dynamic programming action values to fine-tune an open-weight reasoning model as an upper-level scheduler.
summary.evidence: Reinforcement fine-tuning reduces emissions from 70.5 to 61.2 kg-CO2, closely approaching the dynamic programming optimum of 60.8 kg-CO2 on a simple TES benchmark.
summary.limitations: The approach’s gains are limited when transferring to structurally different tasks like battery control, and higher-fidelity tests on whole-building control remain to be conducted.
summary.why_for_you: This work demonstrates a practical method to leverage verifiable rewards for efficient adversarial training of reasoning LLMs in energy management, relevant for trustworthy and scalable LLM control applications.

signals.text: Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) stabilizes planning patterns such as candidate comparison, look-ahead, and feasibility checking rather than inventing new strategies, indicating the model learns to reliably execute known reasoning steps.

The method converts exact offline dynamic programming (DP) action values into dense, verifiable rewards for every candidate action, enabling precise reinforcement learning signal without requiring extensive training data.

Evaluation on a simple office-building TES benchmark shows RFT reduces emissions from 70.5 to 61.2 kg-CO2, nearly matching the DP optimum of 60.8 kg-CO2, while GPT-4o without reasoning produces worse emissions than no storage.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the challenge of scheduling thermal energy storage (TES) in buildings to shift cooling loads efficiently under storage constraints, a task difficult for traditional model predictive control (MPC) and reinforcement learning due to scalability issues. The authors propose reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), leveraging exact offline dynamic programming (DP) action values as dense rewards to fine-tune an open-weight reasoning model. Using only 30 training prompts, reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) trains the model to output hourly heat-pump setpoints from text-based states and forecasts. The approach is evaluated on a simple TES benchmark where the DP optimum is known, demonstrating that RFT achieves emissions close to the optimum and outperforms non-reasoning LLMs. Trace analysis reveals that RFT stabilizes existing planning patterns rather than creating new strategies. Robustness tests show these reinforced patterns generalize under forecast errors and to an unseen TES condition, with partial transfer to a battery control task. The study highlights DP-based verifiable rewards as a practical adaptation mechanism for reasoning models in building storage scheduling, motivating future work on higher-fidelity and scalable energy management applications.

methodology.title: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT)

papers.title: Can LLMs Write Reliable Rubrics? A Meta-Evaluation for Experiment Reproduction
papers.abstract: Rubric-based evaluation is a promising approach for assessing open-ended outputs from LLM-based research agents, particularly in paper reproduction, where direct paper-to-repository comparison is prone to hallucination. However, constructing paper-specific rubrics requires substantial expert effort, limiting the scalability of benchmarks such as PaperBench. In this work, we present, to our knowledge, the first systematic meta-evaluation of LLM-generated rubrics for paper reproduction. We reformulate rubrics into a checklist-style format and evaluate four generation settings across two backbone models. We meta-evaluate generated rubrics intrinsically by semantic similarity and extrinsically by score alignment with ground-truth rubrics. Our results show that the augmented settings substantially improves downstream evaluation alignment, with the strongest setting approaching the human baseline, while intrinsic gains are more modest. Further analyses reveal that LLM-generated rubrics are often overly fine-grained, biased toward high scores, and less adaptive to paper domains, highlighting both the affordances and limitations.

summary.takeaway: Augmented LLM-generated rubrics substantially improve alignment with human evaluation in paper reproduction tasks, nearing human baseline performance.
summary.problem: Constructing paper-specific rubrics for evaluating LLM-based paper reproduction is expert-intensive and limits benchmark scalability.
summary.method: The study meta-evaluates LLM-generated rubrics reformulated into checklist format across four generation settings and two backbone models using intrinsic semantic similarity and extrinsic score alignment.
summary.evidence: Augmented rubric generation settings show substantial improvement in downstream evaluation alignment, with the best setting approaching human baseline, despite modest intrinsic semantic gains.
summary.limitations: LLM-generated rubrics tend to be overly fine-grained, biased toward high scores, and less adaptive to diverse paper domains.
summary.why_for_you: This work provides critical insights into automating rubric generation for trustworthy evaluation of LLM research agents, addressing hallucination-prone direct comparisons.

signals.text: The strongest augmented rubric generation setting achieves downstream evaluation alignment close to human baseline, demonstrating effective rubric automation for paper reproduction.
Rubrics are reformulated into a checklist-style format and evaluated across four generation settings and two backbone LLMs, enabling systematic meta-evaluation of rubric quality.
Intrinsic evaluation via semantic similarity shows only modest gains, indicating that semantic closeness alone is insufficient to guarantee evaluation alignment.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the challenge of scalable, reliable evaluation of LLM-generated research outputs in paper reproduction tasks, where direct comparison to repositories is prone to hallucination. The authors propose automating rubric generation using LLMs and conduct the first systematic meta-evaluation of these rubrics. They convert rubrics into checklist-style formats and test four generation settings across two backbone models. Evaluation is twofold: intrinsic semantic similarity and extrinsic score alignment with ground-truth rubrics. Results reveal that augmented rubric generation settings significantly improve downstream evaluation alignment, nearly matching human baselines, while intrinsic semantic similarity gains remain modest. Further analysis uncovers that LLM-generated rubrics are often overly detailed, biased toward higher scores, and less adaptable across paper domains. These findings highlight both the potential and current limitations of LLM-generated rubrics for trustworthy, scalable evaluation in LLM-based research agent benchmarks.

methodology.title: Rubric Reformulation
methodology.detail: Original rubrics are reformulated into a checklist-style format to standardize evaluation criteria and facilitate systematic comparison across generation settings and models.

methodology.title: Generation Settings
methodology.detail: Four distinct rubric generation settings are tested, varying augmentation strategies to assess their impact on rubric quality and downstream evaluation alignment.

methodology.title: Backbone Models
methodology.detail: Two backbone LLMs serve as the basis for rubric generation, enabling analysis of model-dependent effects on rubric reliability and adaptability.

methodology.title: Intrinsic Meta-Evaluation
methodology.detail: Generated rubrics are evaluated intrinsically by measuring semantic similarity to ground-truth rubrics, assessing content closeness independent of scoring outcomes.

methodology.title: Extrinsic Meta-Evaluation
methodology.detail: Rubrics are extrinsically evaluated by aligning their scoring outcomes with ground-truth rubric scores, measuring practical evaluation reliability.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal mechanisms but focuses on empirical meta-evaluation of rubric generation and scoring alignment.

experiments.title: Rubric Generation and Evaluation
experiments.detail: Experiments involve generating rubrics under four settings using two backbone LLMs, reformulating rubrics into checklist format, and evaluating via intrinsic semantic similarity and extrinsic score alignment metrics.

findings.title: Augmented Settings Improve Alignment
findings.detail: Augmented rubric generation settings substantially improve downstream evaluation alignment, with the strongest setting approaching human baseline performance.

findings.title: Modest Intrinsic Gains
findings.detail: Intrinsic semantic similarity between generated and ground-truth rubrics shows only modest improvement, indicating semantic closeness is not fully predictive of evaluation quality.

findings.title: Overly Fine-Grained Rubrics
findings.detail: LLM-generated rubrics tend to be overly detailed, which may complicate evaluation and reduce practical usability.

findings.title: Bias Toward High Scores
findings.detail: Generated rubrics exhibit a bias toward assigning higher scores, potentially skewing evaluation outcomes.

findings.title: Limited Domain Adaptability

contributions: First systematic meta-evaluation of LLM-generated rubrics for paper reproduction tasks.
Introduction of checklist-style rubric reformulation to standardize evaluation.
Demonstration that augmented rubric generation settings improve downstream evaluation alignment near human baselines.
Identification of key limitations in LLM-generated rubrics including fine-grained detail, scoring bias, and domain adaptability.

Bias toward high scores in generated rubrics may distort evaluation fairness.
Limited adaptability of rubrics across diverse paper domains restricts generalizability.
Intrinsic semantic similarity metrics do not strongly correlate with downstream evaluation alignment.
open_questions: How can rubric generation be improved to reduce scoring bias and increase fairness?
What methods can enhance rubric adaptability across diverse research domains?
Can intrinsic evaluation metrics be developed that better predict downstream evaluation alignment?
How to balance rubric granularity to optimize usability without sacrificing evaluation fidelity?

papers.title: The Illusion of Robustness: Aggregate Accuracy Hides Prediction Flips under Task-Irrelevant Context
papers.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) grow more capable, they are increasingly deployed in context-rich settings where task inputs are often accompanied by long, partially irrelevant context. In a controlled setting, we find that state-of-the-art models often appear robust to task-irrelevant context at the aggregate level: prepending it to benchmark questions causes little change in overall accuracy. This aggregate stability, however, masks significant per-example instability. Even semantically meaningless pseudo-words, formed by randomly combining characters, can markedly shift model predictions on a small fraction of examples, degrading performance on some while improving it on others. This two-sided effect holds consistently across a wide range of models and datasets, yet the affected examples are largely model-specific. We further show that this instability is modulated by context type, context length, test-time compute, and model development stage. Together, our findings reveal context-induced tail risks concealed by aggregate accuracy, motivating per-example reliability evaluation of language models.

summary.takeaway: Aggregate accuracy metrics obscure significant per-example prediction instability caused by task-irrelevant context in state-of-the-art LLMs.
summary.problem: LLMs deployed with long, partially irrelevant context appear robust at the aggregate level but exhibit unstable predictions on individual examples.
summary.method: The study prepends task-irrelevant context, including semantically meaningless pseudo-words, to benchmark questions and analyzes prediction changes across multiple models and datasets.
summary.evidence: Prepending pseudo-words shifts model predictions on a small fraction of examples, with effects varying by context type, length, compute, and model development stage.
summary.limitations: The analysis is limited to controlled settings and does not provide mechanistic explanations for the observed instability.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding per-example prediction flips under irrelevant context is critical for trustworthy LLM deployment in real-world, context-rich environments.

signals.text: State-of-the-art LLMs show stable aggregate accuracy when irrelevant context is prepended, yet individual examples experience significant prediction flips.
The method uses semantically meaningless pseudo-words formed by random character combinations to isolate the effect of irrelevant context on model predictions.
Prediction instability is modulated by factors including context type, context length, test-time compute, and model development stage, indicating nuanced sensitivity.

deep_dive.overview: This research investigates the robustness of large language models to task-irrelevant context by prepending such context to benchmark questions and measuring prediction stability. While aggregate accuracy remains largely unchanged, the study reveals significant per-example prediction flips, including both degradations and improvements, when irrelevant context is introduced. The use of pseudo-words as irrelevant context isolates semantic effects, demonstrating that even meaningless input can alter model behavior. This instability is consistent across diverse models and datasets but affects examples in a model-specific manner. Furthermore, the degree of instability depends on context characteristics and model factors such as development stage and computational budget at test time. These findings expose hidden tail risks in LLM reliability that aggregate metrics fail to capture, underscoring the need for per-example evaluation to ensure trustworthy deployment in context-rich scenarios.

methodology.title: Prepending Task-Irrelevant Context
methodology.detail: The study prepends long, partially irrelevant context, including semantically meaningless pseudo-words created by random character combinations, to benchmark questions to test model robustness to irrelevant input.

methodology.title: Controlled Evaluation Across Models and Datasets
methodology.detail: Multiple state-of-the-art LLMs and benchmark datasets are evaluated under identical conditions to assess the consistency and specificity of prediction instability caused by irrelevant context.

methodology.title: Analysis of Prediction Flips
methodology.detail: Per-example prediction changes are tracked to identify instances where irrelevant context causes shifts in model outputs, measuring both performance degradation and improvement.

methodology.title: Modulation Factors Study
methodology.detail: The impact of context type, context length, test-time compute resources, and model development stage on prediction stability is systematically analyzed to understand factors influencing instability.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide a mechanistic or theoretical explanation for why irrelevant context induces prediction flips, focusing instead on empirical observation.

experiments.title: Benchmark Question Evaluation with Irrelevant Context
experiments.detail: Models are tested on standard benchmark questions with and without prepended irrelevant context, including pseudo-words, to measure changes in aggregate accuracy and per-example predictions.

experiments.title: Cross-Model and Dataset Consistency Checks
experiments.detail: Experiments span a wide range of state-of-the-art LLMs and datasets to verify that the two-sided effect of irrelevant context on prediction flips is consistent yet model-specific.

experiments.title: Context and Model Factor Ablations
experiments.detail: Ablation studies vary context type, length, test-time compute, and model development stage to quantify their modulation of prediction instability.

findings.title: Aggregate Accuracy Masks Instability
findings.detail: Despite little change in overall accuracy when irrelevant context is prepended, individual examples frequently experience prediction flips, revealing hidden instability.

findings.title: Pseudo-Words Cause Prediction Shifts
findings.detail: Even meaningless pseudo-words significantly alter model predictions on a subset of examples, demonstrating sensitivity to non-semantic context.

findings.title: Two-Sided Effect on Performance
findings.detail: Irrelevant context can both degrade and improve performance on different examples, indicating complex, example-specific effects.

findings.title: Model-Specific Affected Examples
findings.detail: The examples impacted by irrelevant context vary across models, suggesting that instability is not uniform but dependent on model architecture or training.

findings.title: Instability Modulated by Multiple Factors
findings.detail: Context type, length, test-time compute, and model development stage all influence the degree of prediction instability observed.

contributions: Demonstration that aggregate accuracy conceals significant per-example prediction instability under task-irrelevant context.
Introduction of semantically meaningless pseudo-words as a tool to isolate context effects on LLM predictions.
Empirical evidence that prediction instability is two-sided and model-specific across diverse LLMs and datasets.
Identification of factors modulating instability, including context characteristics and model development parameters.
Motivation for per-example reliability evaluation metrics in LLM deployment.
limitations: Lack of mechanistic or theoretical explanation for the observed prediction flips.
Experiments conducted in controlled settings may not fully capture real-world context complexity.
No quantitative metrics or numerical results are provided in the abstract to gauge effect sizes.
The study does not explore mitigation strategies for the identified instability.
open_questions: What underlying mechanisms cause LLMs to be sensitive to semantically meaningless context?
How can per-example prediction instability be effectively measured and mitigated in deployed systems?
To what extent do different model architectures or training regimes influence susceptibility to irrelevant context?
Can model design or training be adapted to reduce context-induced tail risks without sacrificing aggregate accuracy?

papers.title: LLM Judges Can Be Too Generous When There Is No Reference Answer
papers.abstract: LLM judges are increasingly being used to evaluate open-ended model responses, often in no-reference settings where a ground-truth answer is unavailable. However, can they reliably assess in such evaluation setups? We explore this question in this paper through a two stage pipeline with a) calibration experiments that assess the judge model's knowledge of the task it is evaluating, and b) sensitivity experiments that assess how the judge model's performance is impacted by the presence and positioning of the reference answer in the prompt. Across experiments covering three languages, we show that the judge models we evaluated tend to over-credit incorrect answers in the absence of a reference answer, and adding reference answer information to the prompt flips the judge model's correct/incorrect decisions by as much as 85% in some experimental settings. Comparison with a subset of human annotations shows that these reference-driven changes generally align with human judgments. Our results emphasize the need for calibrating the LLM judges with a sample with reference-aware evaluation before using them in reference-free setups reliably, and our methodology provides a blueprint for researchers and practitioners in doing such calibration of LLM judges for other tasks.

summary.takeaway: LLM judges tend to over-credit incorrect answers without reference answers, and their decisions shift drastically when reference answers are included.
summary.problem: Can LLM judges reliably evaluate open-ended model responses in no-reference settings where ground-truth answers are unavailable?
summary.method: A two-stage pipeline involving calibration experiments to assess judge model task knowledge and sensitivity experiments to measure impact of reference answer presence and positioning.
summary.evidence: Experiments across three languages show up to 85% flips in judge decisions when reference answers are added, aligning with human annotations.
summary.limitations: The study does not provide quantitative metrics beyond decision flip rates or detailed analysis of judge model architectures.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding and calibrating LLM judges is critical for trustworthy evaluation of open-ended LLM outputs in reference-free scenarios.

signals.text: LLM judges over-credit incorrect answers in no-reference settings, indicating a systematic bias in their evaluation without ground-truth context.
The two-stage pipeline includes calibration experiments to verify judge model task knowledge and sensitivity experiments to test how reference answer presence affects judgments.
Adding reference answers to prompts causes up to 85% of judge model decisions to flip between correct and incorrect, demonstrating high sensitivity to reference information.

deep_dive.overview: This paper investigates the reliability of large language model (LLM) judges when evaluating open-ended responses without access to ground-truth reference answers. The authors propose a two-stage evaluation pipeline: first, calibration experiments assess whether the judge model understands the task it is evaluating; second, sensitivity experiments measure how the presence and positioning of reference answers in the prompt influence the judge's decisions. Conducted across three languages, the experiments reveal that LLM judges systematically over-credit incorrect answers when no reference is provided. Introducing reference answers into the prompt causes dramatic shifts in evaluation outcomes, with up to 85% of decisions flipping from correct to incorrect or vice versa. These shifts align well with human annotations, suggesting that reference-aware calibration is essential for trustworthy LLM judging. The methodology offers a practical blueprint for calibrating LLM judges before deploying them in no-reference evaluation settings, addressing a critical gap in reliable automated evaluation of open-ended LLM outputs.

methodology.title: Calibration Experiments
methodology.detail: These experiments assess the judge model's understanding of the evaluation task by testing its ability to correctly judge responses when reference answers are present, ensuring the model has task-relevant knowledge before no-reference evaluation.

methodology.title: Sensitivity Experiments
methodology.detail: These experiments evaluate how the judge model's decisions change when reference answers are added or repositioned in the prompt, quantifying the impact of reference information on judgment reliability.

mechanism.title: No explicit mechanism provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present a formal mechanism or theoretical model explaining why LLM judges over-credit incorrect answers without references or why reference presence causes decision flips.

experiments.title: Multilingual Evaluation
experiments.detail: Experiments were conducted across three languages to test judge model behavior in diverse linguistic contexts, measuring decision flips and comparing judge outputs to human annotations.

findings.title: Over-crediting Incorrect Answers
findings.detail: LLM judges tend to assign credit to incorrect model responses when no reference answer is provided, indicating unreliable evaluation in no-reference settings.

findings.title: High Sensitivity to Reference Answers
findings.detail: Inclusion of reference answers in prompts causes up to 85% of judge decisions to flip, demonstrating that reference information strongly influences evaluation outcomes.

findings.title: Alignment with Human Judgments
findings.detail: Changes in judge decisions driven by reference answer presence generally align with human annotations, validating the importance of reference-aware calibration.

contributions: Identification of systematic over-crediting by LLM judges in no-reference evaluation settings.
Development of a two-stage pipeline combining calibration and sensitivity experiments to assess judge reliability.
Empirical demonstration of up to 85% decision flips caused by reference answer inclusion across three languages.
Provision of a practical methodology blueprint for calibrating LLM judges before no-reference deployment.
limitations: Lack of detailed quantitative metrics beyond decision flip percentages limits understanding of judge accuracy.
No analysis of the impact of different judge model architectures or sizes on evaluation reliability.
Absence of a formal theoretical mechanism explaining observed judge behavior.
Limited information on dataset specifics or task domains used in experiments.
open_questions: How do different LLM judge architectures or training regimes affect over-crediting behavior in no-reference settings?
Can formal theoretical models explain why reference answers cause large decision flips in LLM judges?
What are effective calibration strategies to improve judge reliability across diverse tasks and languages?
How does judge performance vary with different types of open-ended tasks beyond those tested?

papers.title: UMoE:Unlocking Every Expert in Domain-Specific Training
papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale capacity without proportional compute cost and have become a key architecture for frontier large language models (LLMs). Yet domain-specific post-training inherits an expert pool shaped by mixed-domain pre-training: a substantial subset of experts contributes little on the target domain, and standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) leaves the composition of this pool unchanged. We propose a simple, budget-preserving pipeline that realigns the expert pool to the target domain before fine-tuning. Given a target domain, we (1) prune the experts with lowest domain-aligned saliency, (2) regrow the expert pool to its original size through perturbation-based expert expansion, and (3) apply standard SFT. The resulting model preserves the original expert count, parameter count, and inference cost. With a single frozen recipe and no per-domain hyperparameter tuning, UMoE consistently improves over direct sft across two MoE architectures (Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), five domains (math, code, science, tool-use, and agentic coding), and 12 benchmarks. Representative improvements are 3.4 points in math average accuracy, 6.0 points on SWE-bench Verified. On a strong in-house math corpus, direct sft already surpasses Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking (82.81 vs.\ 81.06), yet UMoE further raises the average to 84.17, an additional 1.36 points, demonstrating robustness to a substantially stronger SFT regime. Data-scaling experiments further show that the gain persists as training data grows. Analysis reveals that the direct-SFT model allocates substantial routed-expert compute to a low-saliency subset that can be removed post hoc with little average degradation; UMoE turns this redundant capacity into useful domain capacity and achieves lower training loss, with gains spanning all difficulty levels in downstream evaluation.

summary.takeaway: UMoE reorganizes the expert pool of pretrained MoE LLMs by pruning low-saliency experts and regrowing them via perturbation, yielding consistent domain-specific performance gains without increasing model size or inference cost.
summary.problem: Standard supervised fine-tuning of pretrained MoE models leaves many experts poorly aligned to the target domain, wasting capacity and limiting domain-specific adaptation.
summary.method: UMoE prunes the least domain-salient experts using a calibration set, regrows the expert pool by perturbation-based expansion to restore original size, then applies standard supervised fine-tuning.
summary.evidence: UMoE improves benchmark averages across five domains and two MoE architectures, e.g., +3.4 points math accuracy and +6.0 points on SWE-bench Verified, while preserving parameter count and inference cost.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed analysis of UMoE’s impact on inference latency or memory beyond parameter count, nor does it explore alternative pruning ratios or perturbation scales extensively.
summary.why_for_you: UMoE offers an efficient, budget-preserving approach to enhance domain-specific fine-tuning of large MoE LLMs by better utilizing expert capacity, relevant for improving trustworthy and efficient LLM adaptation.

signals.text: UMoE achieves a 3.4-point average accuracy improvement on math benchmarks and a 6.0-point gain on SWE-bench Verified by reorganizing experts before fine-tuning, demonstrating robust domain adaptation across multiple datasets.

The method uses REAP saliency scores on a calibration subset to prune the bottom 50% of experts per layer, then regenerates pruned experts by copying and symmetrically perturbing surviving experts’ MLP weights and router rows.

Analysis shows direct supervised fine-tuning routes substantial compute to low-saliency experts that can be pruned with minimal degradation, whereas UMoE reallocates this capacity to domain-aligned experts, reducing training loss and improving downstream performance.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the inefficiency in domain-specific fine-tuning of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models, where many experts pretrained on mixed domains contribute little to the target domain. The authors propose UMoE, a three-step pipeline that first prunes experts with the lowest domain-aligned saliency using a calibration dataset, then regrows the expert pool to its original size by perturbation-based expansion of surviving experts, and finally applies standard supervised fine-tuning. This preserves the original model architecture, parameter count, and inference cost, ensuring deployment budget consistency. Evaluations on two MoE architectures (Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B) across five domains (math, code, science, tool-use, agentic coding) and 12 benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements, including a 3.4-point gain in math accuracy and 6.0 points on SWE-bench Verified. The approach is robust to stronger fine-tuning regimes and scales well with training data size. The key insight is that direct fine-tuning wastes capacity on low-saliency experts, whereas UMoE reallocates this capacity to domain-relevant experts, improving training efficiency and downstream task performance.

methodology.title: Domain-Aligned Expert Pruning
methodology.detail: UMoE scores each expert’s domain relevance using REAP saliency on a calibration subset of the target domain data, combining router gate values and activation norms. It prunes the bottom 50% of experts per layer, retaining those most relevant to the domain to form a domain-aligned expert subset.

methodology.title: Budget-Preserving Expert Expansion
methodology.detail: To restore the original expert count, each pruned slot is reinitialized by copying MLP weights and router rows from surviving experts in a round-robin fashion. Both the parent and regrown experts are independently perturbed with Gaussian noise scaled by parameter standard deviation (σ=0.05) to promote specialization and avoid initialization asymmetry.

methodology.title: Standard Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)
methodology.detail: After expert pool reorganization, the model undergoes standard supervised fine-tuning on the full domain-specific dataset using cross-entropy loss. This step updates the domain-aligned experts to improve downstream task performance without changing model size or inference cost.

methodology.title: Evaluation Across Architectures and Domains
methodology.detail: UMoE is evaluated on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B MoE architectures across five domains (math, code, science, tool-use, agentic coding) using multiple benchmarks and varying SFT data scales to validate generality and robustness.

mechanism.title: Domain-Aligned Saliency Scoring
mechanism.detail: Experts are scored by REAP saliency, which integrates router gate weights and activation norms over a calibration set, reflecting each expert’s functional importance under the target domain distribution. This guides pruning decisions to retain domain-relevant experts.

mechanism.title: Symmetric Perturbation for Expert Expansion
mechanism.detail: Copied experts are perturbed symmetrically on both the parent and regrown copies by adding Gaussian noise scaled by parameter standard deviation, applied to both MLP weights and router rows. This symmetric perturbation avoids initialization bias and encourages functional specialization.

mechanism.title: Fixed Budget Constraint
mechanism.detail: UMoE maintains the original expert count E and active expert count K, preserving parameter count and inference cost. This ensures that domain adaptation does not increase deployment resource requirements.

experiments.title: Domain-Specific Fine-Tuning on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-35B-A3B
experiments.detail: UMoE is tested on two MoE architectures with 128 and 256 routed experts respectively, across five domains with domain-specific SFT datasets and multiple benchmarks, including math competitions (AIME, HMMT), code reasoning (LiveCodeBench), science (GPQA-Diamond), tool-use (τ-bench), and agentic coding (SWE-bench Verified).

experiments.title: Data-Scaling Experiments
experiments.detail: UMoE’s performance gains persist across varying amounts of supervised fine-tuning data, demonstrating robustness to training data scale and confirming that improvements are not limited to small data regimes.

experiments.title: Ablation on Saliency Metrics and Perturbation Design
experiments.detail: Comparisons among REAP saliency, activation frequency, and Expert Activation Norm (EAN) show REAP and frequency are competitive, with EAN weaker. Perturbing both parent and regrown experts symmetrically outperforms one-sided perturbation, and perturbing both router and MLP weights yields complementary benefits.

findings.title: UMoE Improves Domain-Specific Accuracy
findings.detail: UMoE consistently outperforms direct supervised fine-tuning, e.g., raising math average accuracy by 3.4 points and SWE-bench Verified pass@1 by 6.0 points, demonstrating effective domain adaptation.

findings.title: Robustness to Stronger Fine-Tuning Regimes
findings.detail: On a strong in-house math corpus where direct SFT already surpasses a strong baseline (82.81 vs. 81.06), UMoE further improves average accuracy to 84.17, showing gains under stronger SFT conditions.

findings.title: Expert Pool Reorganization Reduces Redundancy
findings.detail: Direct SFT routes substantial compute to low-saliency experts that can be pruned post hoc with little degradation, whereas UMoE reallocates this capacity to domain-aligned experts, lowering training loss and improving performance across difficulty levels.

findings.title: Perturbation Design is Critical
findings.detail: Symmetric perturbation of both parent and regrown experts on MLP and router parameters is essential; one-sided perturbation leads to routing decline and performance degradation.

contributions: Proposed UMoE, a domain-aware expert pool reorganization method that prunes and regrows experts to improve domain-specific fine-tuning without increasing model size or inference cost.
Introduced a budget-preserving expert expansion technique using symmetric perturbation of copied experts to promote specialization.
Demonstrated consistent performance gains across multiple MoE architectures, five diverse domains, and 12 benchmarks, including strong math and agentic coding tasks.
