Provided analysis showing that direct fine-tuning wastes capacity on low-saliency experts, which UMoE effectively reallocates to domain-relevant experts.
Validated robustness of UMoE gains across varying supervised fine-tuning data scales and stronger fine-tuning regimes.
limitations: The impact of UMoE on inference latency and memory usage beyond parameter count is not analyzed.
The pruning ratio is fixed at 50% without extensive exploration of alternative ratios or adaptive pruning strategies.
The perturbation scale σ is fixed at 0.05; sensitivity to this hyperparameter is not deeply studied.
UMoE relies on a calibration subset for saliency scoring, but the effect of calibration set size and representativeness is not detailed.
open_questions: How does UMoE affect inference efficiency metrics such as latency and memory footprint in deployment scenarios?
Can adaptive or dynamic pruning ratios based on domain complexity further improve expert pool reorganization?
What is the sensitivity of UMoE performance to the choice and size of the calibration dataset used for saliency scoring?
Could alternative perturbation schemes or learned expert regeneration methods yield better specialization and downstream gains?

papers.title: HyperSafe: Inference-Time Safety Recovery for Fine-Tuned Language Models
papers.abstract: Safety alignment in large language models can be fragile under fine-tuning, as even benign task adaptation may increase harmful compliance. Existing defenses mainly follow two directions: they either intervene during or after fine-tuning through retraining or weight modification, which can be costly and may hurt task performance, or they use model-agnostic safety classifiers, which may miss failures specific to a given fine-tuned checkpoint. These limitations motivate a post hoc, model-specific, and non-invasive approach to safety restoration. To meet these requirements, we propose HyperSafe, a framework that restores safety behavior by generating a model-specific Safe Side Network (SSN) for each fine-tuned checkpoint. HyperSafe uses layer-wise activation fingerprints to capture how fine-tuning changes the model's inner representations. With a small set of given calibration prompts, the hypernetwork maps these fingerprints to the parameters of the \ssn{} in a single forward pass. The generated \ssn{} runs alongside the frozen fine-tuned model and performs prompt-level safety classification: harmful prompts are routed to refusal, while safe prompts are answered by the original fine-tuned model. Thus, HyperSafe requires no gradient updates, no safety data at deployment time, and no modification to the deployed model weights. We evaluate HyperSafe on two model families, Qwen2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B, across multiple safety benchmarks. HyperSafe reduces harmful response rates from 19-31% to below 1% on every held-out checkpoint, while keeping downstream task accuracy within 1% of the fine-tuned baseline on average. Code is available at https://github.com/nokronim/project-safety-remedy.

summary.takeaway: HyperSafe generates model-specific Safe Side Networks at inference time to restore safety in fine-tuned LLMs, reducing harmful outputs below 1% while preserving task accuracy within 1%.
summary.problem: Fine-tuning safety-aligned large language models often degrades their safety alignment, increasing harmful response rates significantly.
summary.method: HyperSafe uses layer-wise activation fingerprints from calibration prompts to generate a Safe Side Network via a hypernetwork that classifies prompts at inference, routing harmful ones to refusal without modifying model weights.
summary.evidence: Evaluations on Qwen2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B across multiple safety benchmarks show HyperSafe reduces harmful response rates from 19–31% to below 1% on all held-out checkpoints while maintaining task accuracy within 1% of fine-tuned baselines.
summary.limitations: The method relies on a calibration set and may degrade if instruction-following data is excluded; it has been evaluated primarily on LoRA fine-tuned checkpoints and two model families.
summary.why_for_you: HyperSafe offers a non-invasive, model-specific, and efficient inference-time safety recovery approach that preserves downstream task performance, addressing fine-tuning-induced safety degradation without retraining or weight modification.

signals.text: HyperSafe reduces harmful response rates from 19–31% in LoRA fine-tuned Qwen2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B models to below 1% across 12 held-out datasets, demonstrating strong zero-shot safety generalization.

The Safe Side Network (SSN) is generated by a hypernetwork that maps layer-wise activation fingerprints from a small calibration prompt set to SSN parameters in a single forward pass, enabling prompt-level safety classification without weight updates.

Ablation studies show removing safe-probe supervision or domain-specific calibration degrades task accuracy and safety, indicating the importance of functional supervision and diverse calibration data for SSN effectiveness.

deep_dive.overview: Fine-tuning aligned large language models often compromises their safety, increasing harmful outputs despite benign task adaptation. Existing defenses either intervene during fine-tuning with costly constraints, modify model weights post hoc risking task performance degradation, or use model-agnostic classifiers that miss fine-tuning-specific failures. HyperSafe addresses these limitations by generating a model-specific Safe Side Network (SSN) at inference time using a hypernetwork conditioned on layer-wise activation fingerprints extracted from a small calibration prompt set. The SSN runs alongside the frozen fine-tuned model, classifying prompts as harmful or safe and routing harmful prompts to refusal, thus restoring safety without retraining or weight modification. Evaluations on Qwen2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B across multiple safety benchmarks demonstrate that HyperSafe reduces harmful response rates from 19–31% to below 1% while preserving task accuracy within 1%. Ablations confirm the necessity of functional supervision and calibration diversity. This approach enables deployment of fine-tuned models with restored safety guarantees efficiently and non-invasively.

methodology.title: Layer-wise Activation Fingerprints
methodology.detail: Extracts activation patterns from multiple layers of the fine-tuned model using a small set of calibration prompts to capture fine-tuning-induced representation changes, serving as input to the hypernetwork.

methodology.title: Hypernetwork Parameter Generation
methodology.detail: A hypernetwork maps the extracted activation fingerprints to the parameters of the Safe Side Network in a single forward pass, enabling rapid generation of a model-specific safety classifier without gradient updates.

methodology.title: Safe Side Network (SSN) Architecture
methodology.detail: The SSN is a lightweight classifier with 12 side layers and reduced hidden size (h/4) that runs alongside the frozen fine-tuned model, performing prompt-level safety classification to route harmful prompts to refusal.

methodology.title: Prompt-level Safety Classification
methodology.detail: The SSN classifies each input prompt as harmful or safe; harmful prompts are refused, while safe prompts are answered by the original fine-tuned model, preserving task utility.

methodology.title: Training Objective and Calibration
methodology.detail: The hypernetwork and SSN are trained using a combination of functional supervision losses including safe-probe supervision and domain calibration prompts, ensuring discriminative safety classification and minimal over-blocking.

mechanism.title: No explicit mechanism equations provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not provide formal equations or causal models but explains that layer-wise activation fingerprints capture fine-tuning changes, which the hypernetwork uses to generate SSN parameters for prompt-level safety classification.

experiments.title: Model Families and Fine-tuning
experiments.detail: Evaluations conducted on Qwen2-7B-Instruct and LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct models fine-tuned with LoRA (rank 16, α=32) across 22 diverse datasets spanning QA, reasoning, math, classification, code, and instruction-following.

experiments.title: Safety Benchmarks and Evaluation Protocol
experiments.detail: Safety evaluated on BeaverTails (700 prompts, 14 categories), AdvBench (520 prompts), and HEx-PHI (330 prompts, 11 categories) with disjoint training and evaluation splits; harmful rate and task accuracy metrics reported.

experiments.title: Comparison Baselines
experiments.detail: Compared against base aligned models, LoRA fine-tuned models without safety mechanisms, and Llama Guard 4 (12B) external classifier, demonstrating superior safety reduction and task accuracy preservation.

experiments.title: Ablation Studies
experiments.detail: Ablations on LLaMA-3-8B show removing safe-probe supervision or domain calibration degrades accuracy and safety; calibration prompt set size impacts fingerprint quality and SSN performance; SSNs trained on LoRA checkpoints transfer to full fine-tuning.

findings.title: Safety Restoration
findings.detail: HyperSafe reduces harmful response rates from 19–31% in fine-tuned models to below 1% across all held-out datasets and model families, achieving over 95% relative reduction in harmful outputs.

findings.title: Task Accuracy Preservation
findings.detail: Task accuracy remains within 1 percentage point of the fine-tuned baseline on average, indicating minimal utility loss despite safety restoration.

findings.title: Generalization and Transfer
findings.detail: SSNs generated from LoRA fingerprints transfer unchanged to fully fine-tuned counterparts, maintaining harmful rates ≤0.1% and stable task accuracy.

findings.title: Calibration Data Importance
findings.detail: Instruction-following calibration data is critical for safety; removing it substantially increases harmful rates, while removing other categories has minimal effect.

findings.title: Efficiency
findings.detail: SSN adds only 3–4% of backbone parameters and requires a single hypernetwork forward pass amortized over prompts; safe prompts bypass SSN during decoding, keeping generation cost unchanged.

contributions: Proposed HyperSafe, a novel inference-time safety recovery framework generating model-specific Safe Side Networks without weight modification or retraining.
Introduced layer-wise activation fingerprints as a representation of fine-tuning changes for hypernetwork conditioning.
Demonstrated strong safety restoration reducing harmful outputs below 1% while preserving task accuracy within 1% across two large LLM families and multiple safety benchmarks.
Provided extensive ablations showing the importance of functional supervision, calibration diversity, and prompt set size.
Showed SSN transferability from LoRA to full fine-tuning, enabling practical deployment without re-alignment.
limitations: Dependence on a sufficiently diverse and representative calibration prompt set, especially instruction-following data, for effective safety classification.
Evaluations limited to two model families (Qwen2-7B and LLaMA-3-8B) and LoRA fine-tuning; generalization to other architectures or fine-tuning methods is unverified.
No explicit theoretical mechanism or formal guarantees provided for safety restoration effectiveness.
Potential residual harmful outputs remain (up to 0.7% in some datasets), indicating non-zero failure risk.
open_questions: How well does HyperSafe generalize to other fine-tuning methods beyond LoRA and to larger or different LLM architectures?
Can the calibration prompt set be optimized or minimized further without degrading safety and accuracy?
What are the theoretical limits and guarantees of safety restoration achievable by model-specific SSNs generated from activation fingerprints?
How does HyperSafe perform against adaptive adversarial harmful prompts designed to evade the SSN?

papers.title: Proxy Exploration and Reusable Guidance: A Modular LLM Post-Training Paradigm via Proxy-Guided Update Signals
papers.abstract: Post-training is essential for refining the domain-specific capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet existing reward optimization and distribution matching methods tightly couple policy exploration with distribution alignment. This coupling forces expensive exploration directly on the policy model and severely hinders the asynchronous generation, reuse, and cross-model transfer of optimization signals. In this paper, we propose Proxy-guided Update Signal Transfer (PUST), a novel post-training framework that fundamentally decouples update-signal exploration from distribution alignment. Instead of utilizing the primary model for costly exploration, PUST employs a lightweight proxy model as an efficient testbed to discover high-reward behaviors. We extract the relative improvement signal between the proxy's initial and optimized states, transferring this directional update to the primary model to guide its policy alignment. This decoupled pipeline, comprising proxy exploration, update-signal extraction, and signal transfer, significantly reduces computational overhead and enables optimization signals to be asynchronously generated, cached, and reused. Crucially, by transferring relative improvements rather than absolute policy distributions, PUST naturally supports weak-to-strong improvement and seamless cross-model transfer. Systematic evaluations on Qwen3-family models across math and code domains demonstrate that update signals extracted from substantially weaker proxies can robustly and adjustably enhance stronger primary models. Ultimately, PUST transforms post-training from a monolithic online optimization process into a highly modular, reusable, and cost-efficient paradigm.

summary.takeaway: The Proxy-guided Update Signal Transfer (PUST) framework enhances post-training efficiency for LLMs by decoupling exploration from alignment.
summary.problem: Existing methods couple policy exploration with distribution alignment, leading to high computational costs and inefficiencies.
summary.method: PUST employs a lightweight proxy model to explore high-reward behaviors and transfers relative improvement signals to the primary model.
summary.evidence: Systematic evaluations on Qwen3-family models show that weaker proxies can effectively enhance stronger primary models through extracted update signals.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed quantitative results on the performance of the proposed method compared to existing baselines.
summary.why_for_you: This research offers a novel approach to improve the efficiency of post-training processes in LLMs, relevant for enhancing model adaptability.

signals.text: PUST allows for asynchronous generation and caching of optimization signals, significantly reducing computational overhead compared to traditional methods.
The framework utilizes a proxy model for exploration, which enables the extraction of relative improvement signals that guide the primary model's policy alignment.
Experiments demonstrate that update signals from weaker proxies can robustly enhance stronger models, indicating effective cross-model transfer capabilities.

deep_dive.overview: The research addresses the inefficiencies in post-training for LLMs caused by tightly coupling policy exploration with distribution alignment. By introducing the PUST framework, the authors propose a decoupled approach that utilizes a proxy model for exploration, allowing for the extraction and transfer of relative improvement signals to primary models. Evaluations on Qwen3-family models across math and code domains reveal that this method not only reduces computational costs but also enhances the adaptability of stronger models using insights from weaker proxies.

methodology.title: Proxy Model Utilization
methodology.detail: A lightweight proxy model is employed to explore high-reward behaviors, allowing for efficient signal extraction without burdening the primary model.

methodology.title: Signal Extraction
methodology.detail: The relative improvement signal between the proxy's initial and optimized states is extracted, which serves as a directional update for the primary model.

methodology.title: Signal Transfer Mechanism
methodology.detail: The extracted signals are transferred to the primary model, enabling it to align its policy based on the improvements identified during proxy exploration.

mechanism.title: Decoupling Exploration and Alignment
mechanism.detail: The PUST framework separates the stages of policy exploration and alignment, allowing for more efficient post-training processes.

experiments.title: Evaluation on Qwen3-family Models
experiments.detail: Systematic evaluations demonstrate that update signals from weaker proxies can effectively enhance stronger primary models, showcasing the framework's adaptability.

experiments.title: Convergence Analysis
experiments.detail: Comparative analysis reveals that OPD variants achieve rapid convergence, while traditional methods like GRPO require longer exploratory phases.

findings.title: Efficiency of PUST
findings.detail: PUST significantly reduces exploration costs by delegating sampling and reward evaluation to a smaller proxy model.

findings.title: Scalability of Update Signals
findings.detail: The framework allows for update signals to be asynchronously generated, cached, and reused across different training runs.

findings.title: Cross-Model Transfer
findings.detail: Signals explored by weaker proxies can be flexibly applied to stronger primary models, enhancing their performance.

contributions: Reinterpretation of post-training as distinct stages of policy exploration and alignment.
Introduction of the PUST framework that transfers relative improvement signals for flexible policy updates.
Demonstration of the reusability and scalability of update signals across models.
limitations: Lack of detailed quantitative comparisons with existing baselines.
No exploration of the impact of different proxy model architectures on performance.
open_questions: How can the PUST framework be adapted for different types of LLM architectures?
What are the optimal conditions for selecting proxy models to maximize performance gains?

papers.title: Requential Coding: Pushing the Limits of Model Compression with Self-Generated Training Data
papers.abstract: Compression is fundamental to intelligence. A model that can represent its training data as a short code has discovered regularities that enable generalization. Large neural networks may learn functions far simpler than their parameter counts suggest, but it is challenging to construct codes that realize this simplicity. Parameter-based methods such as quantization produce code lengths that scale with model size, insensitive to how much information the parameters store. Prequential coding bypasses this issue by compressing the training trajectory, but codes the exact data sequence regardless of how much the model learns, yielding large codes when the data has high entropy. We introduce requential coding, where a teacher model selects training samples drawn from the student's own distribution. The student's code records only these selections, which cost bits only where teacher and student disagree. The resulting code length is independent of parameter count and data entropy, and often orders of magnitude shorter than the prequential counterpart, with an advantage that grows with scale. This compression sheds light on phenomena inaccessible to prior compressors. Holding loss fixed, larger models and ensembles compress to much smaller sizes despite more parameters. Plugged into a PAC-Bayes bound, the requential code yields state-of-the-art generalization guarantees for billion-parameter LLMs, outperforming bounds built on aggressive post-training quantization even granted zero error. The bound tightens with scale in the compute-optimal regime, as models become increasingly compressible relative to dataset size. The same code predicts that models gradually overfit when trained for multiple epochs. It also isolates the learnable information in a dataset from its unpredictable, random content, revealing that lower-entropy text holds far more learnable structure than higher-entropy image data.

summary.takeaway: Requential coding compresses large neural networks by encoding only teacher-selected training samples from the student's distribution, achieving code lengths independent of parameter count and data entropy, enabling state-of-the-art generalization bounds for billion-parameter LLMs.
summary.problem: Existing model compression methods scale code length with parameter count or data entropy, failing to capture the actual information learned by large neural networks.
summary.method: Requential coding iteratively trains a student model on samples selected by a teacher model from the student's own distribution, encoding only the indices of accepted samples via relative entropy coding to minimize code length.
summary.evidence: Experiments show requential coding yields code lengths orders of magnitude shorter than prequential coding, with compression improving with model scale and producing tighter PAC-Bayes generalization bounds than aggressive post-training quantization.
summary.limitations: Encoding time can be prohibitively slow due to the need for many proposals in relative entropy coding, and the method requires a teacher model trained on real data with similar architecture and hyperparameters.
summary.why_for_you: This method offers a principled, scalable approach to quantify and leverage the compressibility of large LLMs beyond parameter counts, directly relevant to data selection and statistical theory for LLM generalization.

signals.text: Requential coding achieves code lengths roughly equal to the cumulative KL divergence between teacher and student distributions, enabling compression rates near 1 bit per parameter for compute-optimal LLMs.

The method uses relative entropy coding (REC) with a pseudorandom number generator to generate candidate samples from the student, encoding only the index of the teacher-accepted sample, reducing communication cost to KL(Q∥P) bits.
Empirical results demonstrate that larger models and ensembles compress to smaller sizes despite more parameters, and the requential code predicts gradual overfitting with multiple training epochs.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the challenge that traditional model compression methods, such as parameter quantization or prequential coding, produce code lengths scaling with model size or data entropy, failing to reflect the actual information learned by large neural networks. Requential coding innovates by having a teacher model select training samples from the student's own distribution, encoding only the indices of accepted samples via relative entropy coding. This approach yields code lengths independent of parameter count and data entropy, often orders of magnitude shorter than prequential coding. The method is implemented by iteratively training a student model on teacher-selected samples, with the teacher evolving by training on real data. The resulting compression reveals phenomena inaccessible to prior compressors, such as improved compressibility with scale and tighter PAC-Bayes generalization bounds for billion-parameter LLMs. Experiments on transformers trained on text and images validate the approach, showing strong compression and predictive insights into overfitting and dataset learnability. The method requires shared randomness and incurs computational overhead but offers a principled framework for understanding and leveraging model compressibility at scale.

methodology.title: Requential Coding Protocol
methodology.detail: At each training step t, the student model Pt generates candidate samples Yt,i from its distribution using a pseudorandom number generator with a shared seed. The teacher model Qt selects an accepted sample Xt by choosing an index i⋆ such that Xt is marginally distributed as Qt. The encoder transmits the index i⋆ using relative entropy coding (REC), which requires approximately KL(Qt ∥ Pt) bits. The student then trains on Xt to update Pt+1. This iterative process compresses the training trajectory by encoding only the teacher's selections.

methodology.title: Relative Entropy Coding (REC)
methodology.detail: REC reduces the communication of a sample from distribution Q to communicating an index of a proposal from distribution P, leveraging shared randomness. The encoder and decoder share a pseudorandom number generator to produce identical candidate sequences. The encoder transmits a prefix-free code of the accepted proposal's index, achieving an expected code length bounded by KL(Q∥P) plus small logarithmic overheads, approaching the information-theoretic lower bound.

methodology.title: Teacher Model and Training Dynamics
methodology.detail: The teacher model Qt is trained on real data batches and shares architecture and hyperparameters with the student to maintain low divergence. Enhancements include teacher smoothing via exponential moving average of checkpoints to reduce noise and iso-loss projection to periodically reset the teacher closer to the student, balancing divergence and pulling the student toward the target distribution.

methodology.title: Code Length Evaluation and Runtime
methodology.detail: Code length is evaluated by simulating the stochastic process where REC encoding/decoding is replaced by sampling from the teacher. This requires roughly 2× memory and 2.33× FLOPs compared to ordinary training. Encoding time can be reduced by dividing batches into smaller blocks, trading off code length for encoding speed. Decoding cost remains close to ordinary training.

mechanism.title: Compression via Teacher-Student KL Divergence
mechanism.detail: The code length accumulates approximately as the sum over training steps of KL divergences between the teacher and student distributions, reflecting the information difference the student must learn. This mechanism decouples code length from parameter count and data entropy, focusing on the actual information transferred during training.

mechanism.title: REC Index Encoding with Elias Delta Code
mechanism.detail: Indices of accepted samples are encoded using the parameter-free Elias delta universal integer code, which adds negligible overhead and avoids requiring the decoder to know the teacher-student KL. This ensures prefix-free coding with expected length bounded by KL(Qt ∥ Pt) plus small logarithmic terms.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism for Overfitting Prediction
mechanism.detail: While the code predicts gradual overfitting with multiple epochs, the paper does not provide explicit equations or causal mechanisms for this phenomenon.

experiments.title: Compression Comparison on Transformers
experiments.detail: Requential coding is evaluated against prequential coding and quantization on transformer models trained on text and image datasets. Results show requential coding achieves orders of magnitude shorter code lengths, with compression rates near 1 bit per parameter for compute-optimal LLMs.

experiments.title: Generalization Bound Evaluation
experiments.detail: The requential code is plugged into a PAC-Bayes generalization bound, evaluated on billion-parameter LLMs. It outperforms bounds based on aggressive 4-bit post-training quantization, even assuming zero training error, and tightens with scale in the compute-optimal regime.

experiments.title: Teacher Smoothing and Iso-Loss Projection Ablations
experiments.detail: Improvements such as teacher smoothing via EMA and iso-loss projection are introduced to reduce noise and maintain low divergence between teacher and student, improving code length and training stability.

experiments.title: Runtime and Encoding Tradeoffs
experiments.detail: Experiments analyze the computational overhead of requential coding, showing it requires roughly double memory and 2.33× FLOPs compared to ordinary training. Encoding time can be reduced by block-wise transmission at the cost of longer codes.

findings.title: Code Length Independent of Parameter Count and Data Entropy
findings.detail: Requential coding produces code lengths that do not scale with model size or data entropy, unlike parameter quantization or prequential coding, enabling compression orders of magnitude shorter than prequential codes.

findings.title: Larger Models Compress Better Despite More Parameters
findings.detail: Holding loss fixed, larger models and ensembles achieve smaller code lengths, indicating increased compressibility with scale, a phenomenon inaccessible to prior compressors.

findings.title: State-of-the-Art Generalization Bounds
findings.detail: When plugged into PAC-Bayes bounds, requential coding yields tighter generalization guarantees for billion-parameter LLMs than aggressive post-training quantization bounds, with the bound tightening as model scale increases.

findings.title: Prediction of Overfitting Dynamics
findings.detail: The requential code predicts that models gradually overfit when trained for multiple epochs, isolating learnable information from unpredictable random content in datasets.

findings.title: Lower-Entropy Text Holds More Learnable Structure
findings.detail: Analysis reveals that lower-entropy text data contains far more learnable structure than higher-entropy image data, as reflected in compression behavior.

contributions: Introduction of requential coding, a novel compression scheme encoding only teacher-selected samples from the student's distribution, independent of parameter count and data entropy.
Demonstration of orders of magnitude shorter code lengths than prequential coding on large transformers trained on text and images.
Integration of requential coding into PAC-Bayes bounds yielding state-of-the-art generalization guarantees for billion-parameter LLMs.
Empirical insights into model compressibility scaling with size and dataset learnability, including overfitting prediction and data entropy analysis.
Development of practical encoding schemes using relative entropy coding with universal integer codes and shared randomness.
limitations: Encoding time can be prohibitively slow due to the need for many proposals in relative entropy coding, limiting practical transmission speed.
The method requires a teacher model trained on real data with similar architecture and hyperparameters, which may not always be available or efficient.
The approach incurs roughly double memory and more than double FLOPs compared to ordinary training, increasing computational cost.
No explicit causal mechanism or equations are provided for phenomena such as overfitting prediction.
open_questions: How can encoding time be further reduced without significantly increasing code length, enabling practical model transmission?
Can requential coding be extended or adapted to settings without access to a teacher model trained on real data?
What are the theoretical limits of compressibility for different model architectures and data modalities under requential coding?
How does requential coding interact with other compression techniques such as pruning or knowledge distillation in large-scale LLMs?

papers.title: From Expressivity to Sample Complexity: Narrow Teachers for Transformers via C-RASP
papers.abstract: A theoretical understanding of Transformers is crucial to better understand the capacities and limitations of large language models (LLMs). There is much work analyzing the expressivity of attention-based models. By proposing handcrafted weights or using computational complexity arguments, a large amount of past theoretical works have sought to characterize which tasks are and which are not in the hypothesis class of Transformer models. However, little work investigates the learnability of such solutions. In this work, we make progress towards this goal. Inspired by recent loss landscape analysis work, we propose preliminary sample complexity bounds for learning C-RASP constructions with Transformers.

summary.takeaway: The paper establishes sample complexity bounds for learning C-RASP constructions with Transformers.
summary.problem: Existing theoretical analyses of Transformers focus on expressivity but neglect learnability.
summary.method: The authors propose a framework that connects expressivity results to sample complexity bounds.
summary.evidence: The results indicate that constant-size constructions like Dyck-1 can be easily learned by Transformers.
summary.limitations: The paper lacks empirical validation of the theoretical findings regarding loss landscape impacts.
summary.why_for_you: This work bridges expressivity and learnability, which is crucial for understanding LLM training dynamics.

signals.text: The paper demonstrates that C-RASP Transformers can yield sample complexity bounds, specifically showing that constructions like Dyck-1 are easily learned.
A novel learning algorithm based on a Guess and Check (G&C) procedure is proposed, which samples weights and computes empirical risk to ensure zero training error.
The authors derive a sample complexity bound that relates the probability of sampling a teacher model to the architecture of the Transformer, providing a theoretical foundation for learning.

deep_dive.overview: This research addresses the gap in understanding the learnability of Transformers by proposing sample complexity bounds for C-RASP constructions. The authors extend existing frameworks to show how wide student networks can implement narrow teacher networks, thus linking expressivity with learnability. Their findings suggest that certain constant-size constructions, such as Dyck-1, can be effectively learned by Transformers, providing a theoretical basis for future explorations in LLM training dynamics.

methodology.title: Sample Complexity Bounds
methodology.detail: The authors derive bounds based on the architecture of Transformers and the characteristics of C-RASP programs, focusing on the relationship between model width, depth, and the number of variables.

methodology.title: Guess and Check Learning Algorithm
methodology.detail: The learning algorithm samples weights uniformly at random and computes the empirical risk until zero training error is achieved, linking the success rate to the volume of generalizing solutions.

methodology.title: C-RASP Framework Extension
methodology.detail: The paper extends the C-RASP framework to include a broader class of constructions, allowing for the analysis of their learnability in the context of Transformers.

mechanism.title: Teacher-Equivalent Models
mechanism.detail: The paper defines a teacher-equivalent model in relation to a data distribution, establishing a framework for understanding how well a predictor can match a teacher model.

experiments.title: Learning Dyck-1
experiments.detail: The authors illustrate their theoretical results by demonstrating that a single-head student Transformer can learn a C-RASP program for Dyck-1 with a sample complexity bound better than traditional Occam's razor arguments.

findings.title: Expressivity and Learnability Link
findings.detail: The work is among the first to connect expressivity results of Transformers to sample complexity, showing that expressive capabilities can be learned.

findings.title: Sample Complexity for C-RASP
findings.detail: The derived sample complexity bounds indicate that a narrow teacher can be effectively learned by a wider student Transformer under specific conditions.

findings.title: Impact of Model Architecture
findings.detail: The findings suggest that the architecture of Transformers significantly influences their ability to learn specific tasks, such as those defined by C-RASP.

contributions: The paper extends the framework of Buzaglo et al. to Transformers.
It provides a constraint-counting argument for implementing narrow teachers with wide student networks.
It bridges the gap between expressivity and learnability in the context of Transformers.
limitations: The lack of empirical validation for the theoretical findings.
The current approach only accounts for a single encoding of the teacher within the student.
open_questions: How does the loss landscape impact length generalization in Transformers?
Can the bounds on the probability of sampling a teacher model be further tightened?

papers.title: VoxENES 2026: Benchmarking Generalization of Speech Spoofing Detectors Against LLM-Era TTS and Voice Conversion
papers.abstract: Modern LLM-driven text-to-speech (TTS) and voice conversion (VC) systems produce synthetic speech that differs from the generators represented in many legacy spoofing benchmarks. This mismatch creates a temporal generalization gap that can overestimate detector robustness under real-world post-processing conditions. We bridge this gap by introducing VoxENES 2026, a bilingual (English and Spanish) benchmark of 53,628 audio samples generated using 10 contemporary speech synthesis methods and evaluated under 10 standardized post-processing conditions. Using VoxENES 2026, we benchmark eight pretrained detectors without fine-tuning and observe substantial performance degradation: the best model achieves 28.98\% EER overall, while most perform near or below random chance across modern generators and perturbations. Our results highlight the reliance on brittle artifacts in current detectors and establish VoxENES 2026 as a practical testbed for developing robust audio spoofing countermeasures.

summary.takeaway: VoxENES 2026 reveals that current pretrained speech spoofing detectors degrade significantly against modern LLM-driven TTS and VC systems, achieving at best 28.98% EER and often near random chance.
summary.problem: Legacy spoofing benchmarks fail to capture the acoustic characteristics of synthetic speech generated by contemporary LLM-driven TTS and VC systems, causing overestimated detector robustness.
summary.method: The authors introduce VoxENES 2026, a bilingual benchmark with 53,628 audio samples from 10 modern LLM-driven speech synthesis methods, augmented by 10 standardized post-processing conditions, to evaluate pretrained detectors without fine-tuning.
summary.evidence: Evaluation of eight pretrained detectors on VoxENES 2026 shows substantial performance degradation compared to legacy benchmarks, with the best model achieving only 28.98% EER overall and most near or below random chance.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide fine-tuning or adaptation experiments to improve detector robustness on the new benchmark, nor mechanistic explanations for why detectors fail on modern generators.
summary.why_for_you: This benchmark exposes critical generalization failures of current spoofing detectors against LLM-era synthetic speech, highlighting the need for robust countermeasures aligned with evolving generative models.

signals.text: The best pretrained detector evaluated on VoxENES 2026 achieves only 28.98% equal error rate (EER), indicating severe degradation compared to legacy benchmarks.

VoxENES 2026 includes 53,628 audio samples generated by 10 state-of-the-art LLM-driven TTS and VC methods, covering English and Spanish, and applies 10 standardized post-processing augmentations to simulate real-world conditions.

Performance degradation is attributed to detectors relying on brittle artifact cues tied to older synthesis methods, which are progressively suppressed or concealed by modern LLM-driven generators and post-processing.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the temporal generalization gap in speech spoofing detection caused by the rapid evolution of LLM-driven text-to-speech (TTS) and voice conversion (VC) systems. Legacy benchmarks predominantly contain synthetic speech from pre-2024 generators, which differ acoustically from modern LLM-based methods such as autoregressive, flow-matching, diffusion, and hybrid architectures. This mismatch leads to overestimated robustness of detectors when deployed in real-world scenarios involving new generation pipelines and common audio post-processing like compression and noise. To bridge this gap, the authors introduce VoxENES 2026, a bilingual benchmark dataset with over 53,000 samples generated from 10 contemporary LLM-driven TTS and VC systems, augmented by 10 standardized post-processing conditions. Evaluating eight pretrained detectors without fine-tuning reveals substantial performance degradation, with the best model achieving only 28.98% EER and most detectors performing near or below random chance. These results demonstrate that current detectors rely on fragile artifact cues that do not generalize to modern synthetic speech, establishing VoxENES 2026 as a critical testbed for developing robust spoofing countermeasures aligned with the evolving synthesis frontier.

methodology.title: Dataset Construction
methodology.detail: VoxENES 2026 comprises 53,628 audio samples generated from 10 modern LLM-driven speech synthesis methods, including 7 TTS and 3 VC systems, covering English and Spanish languages. Real speech samples from LibriSpeech and VoxPopuli corpora are included for reference.

methodology.title: Post-Processing Augmentation
methodology.detail: To simulate real-world transmission and manipulation effects, the dataset applies 10 standardized audio augmentations such as codec compression, additive noise, resampling, speed perturbation, and loudness normalization, modeling common distortions that affect detector performance.

methodology.title: Evaluation Protocol
methodology.detail: Eight pretrained speech spoofing detectors are evaluated on VoxENES 2026 without any fine-tuning to measure out-of-distribution generalization. Performance is quantified primarily using equal error rate (EER) across all synthetic and augmented samples.

methodology.title: Benchmarking Modern Generators
methodology.detail: The benchmark explicitly includes state-of-the-art LLM-driven TTS architectures such as VoxCPM, Qwen3-TTS, GLM-TTS, CosyVoice 3, Chatterbox, FlashLabs Chroma, and VibeVoice, as well as VC methods like Seed-VC, OpenVoice v2, and RVC v2, representing the current synthesis frontier.

mechanism.title: Data Drift and Artifact Reliance
mechanism.detail: No explicit mechanistic equations are provided; however, the paper theorizes that detectors trained on legacy datasets learn brittle artifact cues specific to older synthesis methods. Modern LLM-driven generators and post-processing steps suppress or conceal these cues, causing detectors to fail due to distributional shifts and data drift.

experiments.title: Pretrained Detector Evaluation
experiments.detail: Eight pretrained speech spoofing detectors are benchmarked on VoxENES 2026 without fine-tuning. The evaluation covers synthetic speech from 10 modern generators and 10 post-processing conditions, measuring equal error rate (EER) to assess robustness and generalization.

experiments.title: Dataset Composition
experiments.detail: The dataset includes 3,028 real speech samples, 4,600 original synthetic samples, and 46,000 augmented synthetic samples, sourced from LibriSpeech and VoxPopuli corpora for real speech, and 10 LLM-driven TTS and VC systems for synthetic speech.

findings.title: Severe Performance Degradation
findings.detail: The best performing pretrained detector achieves only 28.98% EER on VoxENES 2026, a substantial drop from reported results on legacy benchmarks, indicating poor generalization to modern LLM-driven synthetic speech.

findings.title: Near Random Chance Performance
findings.detail: Most evaluated detectors perform near or below random chance levels across modern generators and post-processing augmentations, demonstrating reliance on brittle artifact cues that do not generalize.

findings.title: Impact of Post-Processing
findings.detail: Standardized post-processing augmentations such as compression, noise, and resampling further degrade detector performance, highlighting the importance of modeling real-world audio transformations.

contributions: Introduction of VoxENES 2026, a large-scale bilingual benchmark dataset with 53,628 samples from 10 modern LLM-driven TTS and VC systems.
Inclusion of 10 standardized post-processing augmentations to simulate real-world audio transmission and manipulation effects.
Comprehensive evaluation of eight pretrained speech spoofing detectors without fine-tuning, revealing significant generalization failures.
Demonstration that current detectors rely on brittle artifact cues tied to legacy synthesis methods, motivating development of robust countermeasures.
Provision of a practical testbed for advancing speech spoofing detection aligned with the evolving LLM-driven synthesis frontier.
limitations: Lack of experiments involving fine-tuning or adaptation of detectors on VoxENES 2026 to improve robustness.
Absence of mechanistic or theoretical analysis explaining why detectors fail on modern LLM-driven synthetic speech.
No exploration of new detector architectures or training strategies to address the identified generalization gap.
Limited discussion on multilingual performance differences beyond English and Spanish inclusion.
open_questions: How can speech spoofing detectors be adapted or retrained to generalize effectively to LLM-driven TTS and VC systems?
What novel artifact cues or features can be leveraged to detect synthetic speech generated by modern LLM-based architectures?
How do different post-processing augmentations individually and jointly affect detector robustness, and can detectors be made invariant to them?
Can theoretical frameworks be developed to model the data drift and distributional shifts caused by evolving speech synthesis methods?

papers.title: UltraX: Refining Pre-Training Data at Scale with Adaptive Programmatic Editing
papers.abstract: As available training data approaches its physical limit, gains from Scaling Laws have begun to diminish. Consequently, improving Large Language Models (LLMs) now depends less on data expansion and more on higher-quality data utilization. However, in the context of large-scale corpora, existing refinement methodologies face significant limitations in quality, efficiency, and reliability: Rule-based approaches are constrained by fixed heuristics and struggle with instance-level variations; LLM-based approaches improve quality but fail to meet the efficiency and reliability requirements of large-scale data processing. To address these challenges, we propose UltraX, a function-calling refinement framework for large-scale pre-training data that completes the editing function space by introducing insertion in addition to deletion and modification, enabling fine-grained instance-level editing. Specifically, UltraX builds a reliable program-supervision generation pipeline. In this pipeline, dataset-adaptive prompt optimization first guides an expert LLM to produce high-quality end-to-end refined texts, and Line Alignment Mapping and Dynamic Context Replacement then convert original-refined text pairs into structured program supervision. Meanwhile, UltraX improves supervision quality and stabilizes the training distribution with low-confidence example filtering and ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination. During inference and execution, it normalizes and validates model outputs through sliding-window prediction, global operation aggregation, and systematic post-processing, improving the stability and reliability of large-scale execution. Experiments show that UltraX achieves the highest average performance across all corpora and also matches or surpasses baselines with fewer training tokens, demonstrating stronger data efficiency and refinement reliability.

summary.takeaway: UltraX introduces a function-calling refinement framework with insertion, deletion, and modification operations, achieving superior data refinement quality and efficiency for large-scale LLM pre-training.
summary.problem: Existing large-scale pre-training data refinement methods either lack fine-grained editing capabilities or fail to scale efficiently and reliably to massive corpora.
summary.method: UltraX constructs a program-supervision pipeline using dataset-adaptive prompt optimization, line alignment mapping, dynamic context replacement, and robust execution with sliding-window prediction and post-processing.
summary.evidence: Experiments with 1B parameter models pretrained on multiple corpora show UltraX surpasses baselines by over 2% relative improvement on multiple datasets while using fewer training tokens.
summary.limitations: The paper does not provide detailed analysis of UltraX’s performance on extremely long documents beyond sliding-window segmentation nor does it address potential biases inherited from expert LLMs used in supervision generation.
summary.why_for_you: UltraX offers a scalable, reliable, and fine-grained data refinement approach that improves pre-training data quality and efficiency, directly addressing challenges in trustworthy and efficient LLM data utilization.

signals.text: UltraX achieves over 2% relative improvement on multiple datasets in downstream tasks using 1B parameter models pretrained from scratch, demonstrating stronger data efficiency and refinement reliability compared to baselines.

UltraX’s program-supervision pipeline includes dataset-adaptive prompt optimization guiding an expert LLM to generate high-quality refined texts, followed by line alignment mapping and dynamic context replacement to convert text pairs into structured editing programs.

UltraX stabilizes training distribution and improves supervision quality via low-confidence example filtering and ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination, while inference uses sliding-window prediction and global operation aggregation to ensure stable large-scale execution.

deep_dive.overview: UltraX addresses the diminishing returns of scaling LLM training data by focusing on improving data quality through fine-grained, programmatic editing of pre-training corpora. Unlike prior rule-based or LLM-based refinement methods limited by fixed heuristics or computational inefficiency, UltraX completes the editing function space by adding insertion to deletion and modification, enabling nuanced instance-level edits. It constructs a reliable program supervision pipeline where an expert LLM, guided by dataset-adaptive prompts, produces end-to-end refined texts. These are converted into structured editing operations via line alignment mapping and dynamic context replacement. To ensure training stability and quality, UltraX filters low-confidence examples and controls sampling ratios of operation types. During inference, it segments long documents with sliding windows, predicts local operations, aggregates them globally, and applies systematic post-processing to produce stable, executable refinement programs. Experiments with 1B models pretrained on multiple corpora demonstrate UltraX’s superior average performance and data efficiency, with relative improvements exceeding 2% on several datasets, validating its approach to scalable, reliable, and fine-grained data refinement for LLM pre-training.

methodology.title: Dataset-Adaptive Prompt Optimization
methodology.detail: UltraX first optimizes prompts tailored to each dataset to guide an expert LLM in generating high-quality, end-to-end refined texts from raw inputs, ensuring that the refinement captures dataset-specific nuances and semantic improvements.

methodology.title: Line Alignment Mapping and Dynamic Context Replacement
methodology.detail: These techniques convert original and refined text pairs into structured program supervision by aligning lines between versions and replacing context dynamically, enabling the extraction of precise editing operations such as insertion, deletion, and modification.

methodology.title: Low-Confidence Example Filtering and Ratio-Controlled Sampling
methodology.detail: To improve supervision quality and stabilize training, UltraX filters out examples with low confidence scores and controls the sampling ratio of different operation combinations, balancing the training distribution across insertion, deletion, and modification operations.

methodology.title: Sliding-Window Segment-wise Operation Prediction
methodology.detail: During inference, UltraX segments long documents using a sliding-window approach, normalizes line numbers, and independently predicts editing operation sequences for each segment to handle length constraints and maintain local context.

methodology.title: Global Operation Aggregation and Systematic Post-Processing
methodology.detail: Local operation sequences from segments are merged into a global program by mapping operations to global line numbers, filtering duplicates, merging adjacent or interfering operations, and applying fallback mechanisms to ensure stable, executable refinement programs.

mechanism.title: Programmatic Editing with Complete Operation Space
mechanism.detail: UltraX extends the editing function space by including insertion alongside deletion and modification, enabling fine-grained instance-level edits that preserve semantic coherence and restore missing information, overcoming limitations of prior deletion-only or replacement-only frameworks.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Theoretical Equations Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models but describes a deterministic function executor that applies predicted editing operations to original texts, ensuring auditable and interpretable refinement.

experiments.title: Pretraining 1B Parameter Models on Multiple Corpora
experiments.detail: UltraX was evaluated by pretraining 1B parameter language models from scratch on multiple large-scale corpora, comparing downstream task performance against baselines including raw data and ProX refinement, measuring average accuracy improvements and data efficiency.

experiments.title: Downstream Task Evaluation Across Ten Tasks
experiments.detail: Performance was assessed on ten downstream tasks including ARC-C, ARC-E, CSQA, HellaS, MMLU, OBQA, PIQA, SIQA, WinoG, and SciQ, with varying numbers of training tokens, demonstrating consistent gains and surpassing baselines with fewer tokens.

experiments.title: Ablation on Operation Combination Sampling
experiments.detail: The effect of ratio-controlled sampling by operation combination was analyzed to understand its impact on training stability and refinement quality, showing that balanced sampling improves model performance.

findings.title: Superior Average Performance
findings.detail: UltraX achieves the highest average performance across all evaluated corpora, with relative improvements exceeding 2% on multiple datasets compared to baseline methods.

findings.title: Improved Data Efficiency
findings.detail: UltraX matches or surpasses baseline refinement methods while using fewer training tokens, indicating stronger data efficiency in pre-training.

findings.title: Fine-Grained Refinement Balances Noise Removal and Preservation
findings.detail: Analyses suggest UltraX’s inclusion of insertion operations alongside deletion and modification enables better balance between removing noise and preserving useful information, reducing semantic fragmentation.

findings.title: Stable Large-Scale Execution
findings.detail: The sliding-window prediction, global aggregation, and systematic post-processing pipeline improve the stability and reliability of large-scale data refinement execution.

contributions: Proposed UltraX, a function-calling refinement framework introducing insertion to complete the editing function space for fine-grained instance-level editing.
Developed a reliable seed-supervision pipeline using dataset-adaptive prompt optimization, line alignment mapping, and dynamic context replacement to generate structured program supervision.
Designed a robust large-scale execution pipeline with systematic post-processing to handle duplicate matching, ambiguous replacements, and operation interference.
Demonstrated consistent downstream performance improvements and stronger data efficiency across multiple large-scale pre-training corpora.
limitations: Lack of detailed evaluation on extremely long documents beyond sliding-window segmentation and its impact on refinement quality.
Potential biases and errors inherited from expert LLMs used in generating seed supervision are not explicitly analyzed.
No formal theoretical or causal mechanism is provided to explain the editing operation interactions or their effect on model performance.
Limited discussion on the computational cost and scalability trade-offs compared to other LLM-based refinement methods.
open_questions: How does UltraX perform on extremely long documents or streaming data beyond the sliding-window segmentation approach?
What are the effects of expert LLM biases on the quality and reliability of generated program supervision?
Can the programmatic editing framework be extended to incorporate semantic or syntactic constraints to further improve refinement quality?
How does UltraX compare in computational efficiency and cost to other state-of-the-art LLM-based refinement methods at larger model scales?

papers.title: Do You Need a Frontier Model as a Citation Verifier? Benchmarking Rubric LLMs for Deep-Research Source Attribution
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning increasingly relies on an LLM judge to score each rubric criterion, and that judge acts as the reward model during training. Before such a signal can be trusted, we need to know how capable the judge must be and how biased it is. We study this calibration question for citation quality in deep-research systems, where a search-grounded LLM must support each claim it writes with a cited source. Citation quality is a structured rubric task in which each attribution-citation pair is judged along two dimensions that require an LLM, source relevance and factual support. On an adversarial long-form benchmark, we score 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges from 3 model families against gold labels over 1,248 rubric decisions, all of which were human-reviewed and 378 of which were hard cases adjudicated from judge disagreements. Cheaper judges remain competitive across both dimensions, with GPT-5-mini attaining the strongest source-relevance pass-class F1 at 0.908 ($κ$=0.636), while on factual support the judges are statistically indistinguishable (overlapping confidence intervals), so no single model dominates. At comparable F1, the judges still differ substantially in pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate. Scalar F1 obscures this directional bias, yet it is exactly what a downstream reinforcement learning loop would reinforce. Calibrating the judge is therefore a prerequisite for using citation rubrics as reward signals, and our results show that this calibration does not require the most expensive available model.

summary.takeaway: Cheaper off-the-shelf LLM judges can reliably evaluate citation quality for source relevance and factual support without requiring the most expensive frontier models.
summary.problem: Determining how capable and unbiased an LLM judge must be to serve as a trustworthy reward model for citation quality in deep-research systems.
summary.method: Benchmarking 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges from 3 model families on an adversarial long-form citation quality task with human-reviewed gold labels across source relevance and factual support dimensions.
summary.evidence: GPT-5-mini achieved the highest source-relevance pass-class F1 of 0.908 (κ=0.636), and judges were statistically indistinguishable on factual support, with detailed bias metrics revealing differences in pass-rate drift, false positive, and false negative rates.
summary.limitations: The study does not provide evidence on how judge calibration impacts downstream reinforcement learning training quality or explore mechanisms to correct directional biases in judges.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding judge calibration and bias in citation verification enables efficient and trustworthy reward modeling for RL training in deep-research LLM applications.

signals.text: GPT-5-mini attained the strongest source-relevance pass-class F1 at 0.908 with Cohen’s κ=0.636, outperforming more expensive models on this dimension.
The evaluation framework uses a rubric with two LLM-judged criteria—source relevance and factual support—each scored binarily with rationale, enabling structured and interpretable judge assessments.

Despite comparable F1 scores, judges differ substantially in pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate, indicating that scalar F1 metrics obscure directional biases critical for reinforcement learning reward signals.

deep_dive.overview: This work addresses the calibration of LLM judges used as reward models in reinforcement learning for citation quality in deep-research systems. The authors construct an adversarial benchmark spanning 25 diverse topics with 1,248 human-reviewed rubric decisions on source relevance and factual support. They evaluate 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI families, measuring pass-class F1, Cohen’s κ, and bias metrics such as pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate. Results show that smaller, cheaper models like GPT-5-mini can match or exceed the performance of larger frontier models on source relevance, while factual support judgments are statistically indistinguishable across judges. However, differences in directional bias metrics reveal that scalar accuracy metrics alone are insufficient to characterize judge reliability for downstream RL training. The study concludes that careful calibration of judges is essential but does not require the most expensive models, enabling more cost-effective and trustworthy citation verification in RL pipelines.

methodology.title: Benchmark Construction
methodology.detail: The Deep-Research Citation Benchmark includes 25 diverse topics with long-form summaries and adversarially edited claims using 19 strategies. Attribution-citation pairs are parsed and scored on three criteria: link accessibility (deterministic), source relevance, and factual support (both LLM-judged). A council of 6 LLM judges independently labels pairs, with human review validating all 1,248 decisions and adjudicating 378 hard cases.

methodology.title: Judge Evaluation Metrics
methodology.detail: Judges produce binary pass/fail scores per criterion with free-text rationales. Metrics include pass-class F1, Cohen’s κ for agreement, pass-rate drift (judge vs. gold pass rate), false positive rate (accepting bad citations), and false negative rate (rejecting good citations). These metrics characterize both accuracy and directional bias relevant for RL reward signals.

methodology.title: Judge Models and Setup
methodology.detail: Eight LLM judges from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI families are evaluated via cloud inference APIs. Each judge scores all 624 source relevance and 624 factual support pairs. Two judges (GPT-5-mini and Claude Opus 4.6) also contributed to gold labels, enabling council-independent comparisons.

methodology.title: Prompt Design
methodology.detail: Prompts instruct judges to provide binary scores and rationales for source relevance and factual support, emphasizing expert evaluation criteria such as topical relevance, claim support, factual consistency, and contradiction detection. The same prompts are applied uniformly across all judges.

mechanism.title: No Explicit Mechanism Provided
mechanism.detail: The paper does not present formal equations or causal models explaining judge behavior or bias mechanisms, focusing instead on empirical benchmarking and metric analysis.

experiments.title: Adversarial Long-Form Citation Benchmark
experiments.detail: The benchmark contains 1,248 rubric decisions over 624 attribution-citation pairs, with 378 hard cases adjudicated by humans. Judges are evaluated on source relevance and factual support dimensions using pass-class F1, Cohen’s κ, pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate.

experiments.title: Judge Cost-Quality Tradeoff Analysis
experiments.detail: The study compares judge accuracy metrics against estimated cost per decision on a logarithmic scale, showing that cheaper judges like GPT-5-mini achieve competitive or superior performance relative to more expensive models.

findings.title: Cheaper Judges Competitive on Source Relevance
findings.detail: GPT-5-mini achieves the highest source-relevance pass-class F1 of 0.908 and Cohen’s κ of 0.636, outperforming larger models, demonstrating that smaller judges can reliably assess topical relevance.

findings.title: No Single Judge Dominates Factual Support
findings.detail: On factual support, judges’ performance overlaps within confidence intervals, indicating no statistically significant difference in accuracy among the evaluated models.

findings.title: Directional Biases Vary Across Judges
findings.detail: Despite similar F1 scores, judges differ substantially in pass-rate drift, false positive rate, and false negative rate, revealing biases that scalar metrics like F1 fail to capture but that affect RL reward signals.

contributions: Introduces a large adversarial benchmark for citation quality evaluation with human-reviewed gold labels across diverse topics.
Comprehensively evaluates 8 off-the-shelf LLM judges on source relevance and factual support, including bias metrics critical for RL reward modeling.
Demonstrates that smaller, cheaper LLM judges can match or exceed frontier models in citation verification tasks.
Highlights the importance of calibrating judges to account for directional biases that scalar accuracy metrics obscure.
limitations: Does not analyze the impact of judge calibration on downstream reinforcement learning training outcomes.
Lacks exploration of methods to mitigate or correct directional biases in judge models.
No mechanistic or theoretical explanation is provided for observed judge biases or performance differences.
Evaluation is limited to off-the-shelf models accessed via APIs, without fine-tuning or adaptation experiments.
open_questions: How do directional biases in LLM judges affect the stability and quality of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards?
What calibration or debiasing techniques can effectively reduce false positive and false negative rates in LLM judges?
Can smaller LLM judges be fine-tuned or adapted to further close gaps in factual support evaluation?
How does retrieval quality interact with judge performance and bias in citation verification pipelines?

papers.title: When the Judge Changes, So Does the Measurement: Auditing LLM-as-Judge Reliability
papers.abstract: An LLM-as-judge score can move even when the candidate responses stay fixed, simply because the evaluator has changed. We treat this evaluator-replacement ambiguity as a measurement-validity problem. Across four judgment datasets, we compare two upgrade paths available in practice: scaling Qwen3 dense judges from 1.7B to 32B parameters and moving across MiniMax M2-M2.7 released APIs. The main pattern is that judge upgrades are not interchangeable: only Qwen3 1.7B to 4B gives a robust adjacent gain, while MiniMax adjacent releases do not. Stronger judges reduce but do not remove position and verbosity bias. Repeated-sample juries add little when errors are correlated. Structured debate can move decisions substantially, but without parser and fallback logs those shifts cannot be attributed to deliberation. We argue that LLM-as-judge reports should include dataset slices, bias probes, error-dependence estimates, and protocol audit trails.

summary.takeaway: LLM-as-judge reliability varies with evaluator changes, showing that judge upgrades are not interchangeable and that stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate biases or correlated errors.
summary.problem: Replacing an LLM evaluator changes measured scores even with fixed candidate responses, creating evaluator-replacement ambiguity that challenges measurement validity.
summary.method: The study compares two evaluator upgrade paths—Qwen3 parameter scaling (1.7B to 32B) and MiniMax M2–M2.7 API releases—across four judgment datasets, analyzing accuracy, bias, error correlation, and protocol auditability.
summary.evidence: Empirical results show only Qwen3 1.7B→4B scaling yields robust adjacent gains, MiniMax releases lack consistent gains, stronger judges reduce position and verbosity bias but do not remove them, and jury aggregation gains are limited by high error correlation.
summary.limitations: The study does not establish causal claims about MiniMax internals and lacks parser and fallback logs to fully attribute debate-induced decision shifts.
summary.why_for_you: Understanding evaluator-replacement ambiguity and multi-dimensional reliability components is critical for trustworthy LLM evaluation and designing robust LLM-as-judge protocols.

signals.text: Only the Qwen3 parameter scaling from 1.7B to 4B parameters produces a robust adjacent gain in judge reliability, while MiniMax M2 to M2.7 API upgrades do not yield consistent improvements across datasets.

The study operationalizes LLM-as-judge reliability into four components—judgment validity, bias robustness, aggregation independence, and protocol auditability—measured via accuracy, Cohen’s κ, position flip rates, error correlation ρ, and parse status.
High intra-class error correlations (ρ up to 0.972 for Qwen3 juries) limit jury aggregation gains, as majority voting fails to amplify reliability when errors are dependent rather than independent.

deep_dive.overview: This paper addresses the evaluator-replacement ambiguity in LLM-as-judge evaluation, where changing the evaluator model alters measured scores despite fixed candidate responses. It investigates whether improvements in judge reliability arise from increased evaluator capability or other factors like bias and protocol design. The authors compare two upgrade paths: parameter scaling of Qwen3 judges (1.7B to 32B parameters) and released-model upgrades of MiniMax M2 to M2.7 APIs, across four diverse judgment datasets. They decompose reliability into four operational components—accuracy, bias robustness, error correlation, and auditability—and analyze how these interact with evaluator scaling and aggregation protocols. Results show that only Qwen3 scaling from 1.7B to 4B yields robust gains, while MiniMax upgrades do not consistently improve reliability. Stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate position and verbosity biases. Jury aggregation gains are limited by high correlated errors, and debate protocols require audit trails to attribute decision shifts properly. The study advocates for comprehensive reporting standards including dataset slices, bias probes, error-dependence estimates, and protocol logs to improve measurement validity in LLM-as-judge evaluations.

methodology.title: Evaluator Upgrade Comparison
methodology.detail: Two evaluator upgrade paths are compared: Qwen3 dense judges scaled from 1.7B to 32B parameters, and MiniMax M2 to M2.7 released APIs. This comparison isolates parameter scaling effects from released-model changes without causal claims about MiniMax internals.

methodology.title: Reliability Operationalization
methodology.detail: LLM-as-judge reliability is decomposed into four constructs: judgment validity (accuracy, Cohen’s κ, Spearman correlation), bias robustness (position flip, verbosity bias, granularity sensitivity), aggregation independence (error correlation ρ, jury gain), and protocol auditability (parse status, fallback behavior, intermediate verdicts).

methodology.title: Datasets and Judges
methodology.detail: Eight judges (Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, 14B, 32B; MiniMax M2, M2.1, M2.5, M2.7) are evaluated on four datasets: LLMBar (419 adversarial pairs), PandaLM testset-v1 (894 pairwise examples), Chatbot Arena seed-42 (1,997 pairwise examples), and Judge’s Verdict (200 TechQA-derived examples with pointwise labels).

methodology.title: Aggregation and Debate Protocols
methodology.detail: Jury aggregation experiments estimate intra-class error correlation ρ to assess independence assumptions. Debate experiments analyze decision shifts but highlight the need for parser and fallback logs to attribute changes to deliberation.

mechanism.title: Evaluator-Replacement Ambiguity
mechanism.detail: The paper conceptualizes the measurement pipeline as comprising candidate responses, benchmark slice, judge model, prompt/decoding, parser, and aggregation/debate. Changes in any component, especially the judge model, can alter reported scores, creating ambiguity about the source of score changes.

mechanism.title: Error Correlation and Jury Aggregation
mechanism.detail: High intra-class error correlation ρ among jurors violates independence assumptions of Condorcet-style majority voting, limiting jury accuracy gains. The beta-binomial model corrected by ρ accurately predicts jury accuracy, showing that correlated errors constrain aggregation benefits.

experiments.title: Judge Upgrade Evaluation
experiments.detail: Evaluated eight judges across four datasets using fixed main prompts. Metrics include accuracy, Cohen’s κ, and Spearman correlation. The study compares adjacent judge upgrades along parameter scaling and released-model axes to assess reliability gains.

experiments.title: Bias Probing
experiments.detail: Position-flip rates, verbosity bias, and granularity sensitivity are measured to assess bias robustness. Results show stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate these biases, with position-flip rates decreasing from 0.320 (Qwen3-1.7B) to 0.117–0.147 (MiniMax releases).

experiments.title: Jury Aggregation Experiment
experiments.detail: Homogeneous and heterogeneous juries are formed to test aggregation gains. Error correlation ρ is estimated from vote matrices, showing high correlation (up to 0.972) that limits majority voting improvements. Beta-binomial models corrected by ρ closely predict observed jury accuracy.

experiments.title: Debate Protocol Case Study
experiments.detail: Structured debate experiments reveal substantial decision shifts, but lack of parser and fallback logs prevents attribution of these shifts to deliberation, highlighting the need for audit trails in debate protocols.

findings.title: Non-Interchangeability of Judge Upgrades
findings.detail: Only Qwen3 parameter scaling from 1.7B to 4B parameters yields a robust adjacent gain in judge reliability; MiniMax M2 to M2.7 API upgrades do not show consistent improvements across datasets.

findings.title: Bias Reduction but Persistence
findings.detail: Stronger judges reduce position-flip rates from 0.320 to approximately 0.117–0.147 and verbosity bias from 0.547 to about 0.13, but biases remain nonzero, indicating capability improves but does not eliminate bias.

findings.title: Limited Jury Gains Due to Correlated Errors
findings.detail: High intra-class error correlations (ρ = 0.944–0.972 for Qwen3 juries) cause majority voting to yield minimal accuracy improvements, with jury size increases from 1 to 5 only marginally improving accuracy (e.g., 0.463 to 0.482 on LLMBar).

findings.title: Debate Shifts Require Audit Trails
findings.detail: Structured debate can substantially change decisions, but without parser and fallback logs, these shifts cannot be confidently attributed to deliberation processes.

findings.title: Dataset-Specific Evaluator Strength
findings.detail: No single judge dominates all datasets: GLM-5.1 leads on LLMBar, MiniMax-M2.7 leads on PandaLM, and mimo-v2-pro leads on Chatbot Arena, emphasizing slice-specific measurement validity.

contributions: Formulation of evaluator-replacement ambiguity as a measurement-validity problem in LLM-as-judge evaluation.
A two-axis empirical study comparing parameter scaling and released-model upgrades across multiple datasets and judges.
Decomposition of LLM-as-judge reliability into judgment validity, bias robustness, aggregation independence, and protocol auditability.
Demonstration that stronger judges reduce but do not eliminate biases and that jury aggregation gains are limited by correlated errors.
Proposal of a reporting standard including dataset slices, bias probes, error-dependence estimates, and protocol audit trails.
limitations: No causal claims are made about MiniMax internal model changes due to lack of controlled ablation.
Absence of parser and fallback logs limits attribution of debate-induced decision shifts to actual deliberation.
Bias and reliability analyses are limited to the evaluated datasets and judge panels, restricting generalizability.
Prompt sensitivity is treated as a robustness check but not systematically explored, leaving prompt effects under-specified.
open_questions: How can audit trails be designed to reliably attribute decision shifts in multi-agent debate protocols?
What mechanisms underlie the persistence of bias despite increased evaluator capability?
Can error correlation among heterogeneous juries be reduced to improve aggregation gains?
How do prompt variations interact with evaluator scaling to affect measurement validity?

papers.title: DT-Guard: Intent-Driven Reasoning-Active Training for Reasoning-Free LLM Safety Guardrail
papers.abstract: Large language models deployed in open-world applications require safety guardrails that are both robust to complex risks and efficient enough for low-latency runtime moderation. Existing guardrails face a practical trade-off between lightweight classification-based models, which are efficient but often struggle with concealed intent, ambiguous semantics, and borderline safety decisions, and reasoning-based guards, which improve judgment quality but introduce additional token generation and inference latency. We present DT-Guard, a content safety guardrail model based on a Reasoning-Active Training, Reasoning-Free Inference paradigm. The key idea is to use reasoning supervision during training while emitting only structured safety labels at inference time. DT-Guard formulates safety judgment as a progressive decision process, Intent - Category - Safety, and constructs an intent-driven dataset with intent labels, risk categories, safety labels, and structured reasoning trajectories. To further improve hard-case robustness, we propose Rollout-Guided Progressive Hard-Case Optimization (RG-PHO), which uses multi-rollout consistency to identify stably mastered, persistently failed, and preference-unstable samples, and applies targeted supervised and preference optimization accordingly. At inference time, DT-Guard directly generates structured labels without explicit reasoning traces, preserving deployment efficiency. Experiments on prompt-side and response-side safety benchmarks show that DT-Guard achieves average F1 scores of 0.886 and 0.870, respectively. With only a 4B backbone, it reaches a dual-side average F1 of 0.878, outperforming strong 8B guardrail baselines. These results demonstrate that reasoning supervision can be effectively internalized into low-latency safety discrimination.

summary.takeaway: DT-Guard internalizes reasoning supervision during training to achieve efficient, reasoning-free inference for robust LLM safety guardrails.
summary.problem: Existing LLM safety guardrails trade off between efficient but shallow classification and robust but slow reasoning-based methods.
